_0bKM3s0SMs.title: The New Zealand Story – Did Ocean Get the Arcade Adventure Right on C64?
_0bKM3s0SMs.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/the-new-zealand-story/

Released in 1989 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, The New Zealand Story is a colourful arcade-style platformer based on Taito’s popular coin-op hit starring Tiki the Kiwi.

Players take control of Tiki as he journeys across varied landscapes to rescue his kidnapped friends from cages and enemy creatures before time runs out. Gameplay combines precise jumping with a quirky selection of weapons, tools, and hidden routes.

Levels encourage exploration and experimentation, rewarding players who uncover secret paths and power-ups. Tight controls and clever level layouts help balance the game’s increasing difficulty.

Visually, the C64 version features vibrant sprite work and cheerful backgrounds that closely reflect the arcade original. The presentation is enhanced by standout music composed by Jonathan Dunn, which remains one of the game’s most memorable features.

Despite hardware limitations, Ocean delivered a faithful and engaging conversion. Contemporary reviews praised its addictive challenge and strong arcade feel, even with tighter time limits and occasional sprite quirks.

Today, The New Zealand Story is remembered as one of the finest late-1980s platformers on the Commodore 64, showcasing how arcade licenses could shine on 8-bit home computers.

Released in 1991 for the Commodore 64, Toki is an arcade-style platformer developed by Taito and converted by Ocean Software. Players take control of Toki, a man transformed into a monkey by an evil sorcerer, as he battles through hostile worlds to rescue his girlfriend and reclaim his human form.

The game focuses on fast, demanding platform action, with Toki firing powerful fireballs, dodging enemies, and navigating dangerous terrain filled with traps and vertical hazards. Despite the hardware limitations, the C64 version delivers a strong sense of momentum and challenge that reflects the spirit of the arcade original.

Levels are packed with varied enemy types and large boss encounters that test timing and positioning. Controls are responsive, encouraging aggressive play while still punishing mistakes, keeping the action intense throughout.

Audio is handled by Allister Brimble, whose energetic soundtrack complements the frantic gameplay and helps drive the pace forward. Combined with colourful presentation and solid level design, Toki stands as one of the more impressive late-era arcade conversions on the Commodore 64.

_4amISEt0mM.title: Jet Set Willy – 60 Rooms of Housework Before Maria Lets You Sleep on the C64
_4amISEt0mM.description:
🕹️ Jet Set Willy (1984) – Commodore 64 Non-Linear Platforming Icon
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/jet-set-willy/

Released in 1984 by Software Projects and designed by Matthew Smith, Jet Set Willy is a defining non-linear platform game that pushed 8-bit ambition to its limits. On the Commodore 64, you guide Willy through a vast mansion of 60 interconnected rooms, collecting glowing objects while surviving a maze of hazards and roaming guardians.

Controls are deceptively simple—left, right, jump—but the challenge lies in precision. You’re free to explore in almost any order, climbing ropes, tackling awkward staircases, timing jumps perfectly, and learning how each room behaves. Progress demands memory, patience, and an understanding of how the mansion fits together.

The C64 version carries over many of the quirks that made the game legendary. Respawning behaviour can be unforgiving, some layouts border on the cruel, and the infamous Attic Bug originally made the game impossible to complete until later fixes appeared. These rough edges are part of its reputation as much as its design.

Music adds to the experience, with Bach’s Invention No. 1 playing during gameplay and Moonlight Sonata on the title screen, giving the mansion an oddly refined atmosphere that contrasts with its deadly traps.

Today, Jet Set Willy stands as a landmark of early non-linear platforming, remembered for its scale, difficulty, and the sheer audacity of its design on 8-bit hardware.

💬 Did you map the mansion methodically, or get hopelessly lost chasing that last item?

_GIULKywK78.title: The Train: Escape to Normandy – Steal Back France’s Art and Drive It to Freedom on the C64
_GIULKywK78.description:
🕹️ The Train: Escape to Normandy (1987) – Commodore 64 WWII Action Simulation
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/the-train-escape-to-normandy/

Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, The Train: Escape to Normandy is an action-simulation title developed by Artech Digital Entertainment and published by Accolade. Inspired by the 1964 film The Train, the game places players in the role of French Resistance fighter Pierre LeFeu during a daring World War II mission to hijack a Nazi-controlled steam train carrying priceless artworks.

Gameplay unfolds across multiple interconnected phases. The opening sequence involves a tense shootout as Pierre covers his ally Le Duc while critical track switches are thrown. Once the train is moving, players must manage the steam locomotive itself, balancing speed, pressure, and water levels while navigating hostile territory.

Combat adds another layer of pressure, with German fighter planes and gunboats attacking at key moments. Players take control of defensive weapons to repel these assaults, while station stops require securing enemy-held locations to resupply and gather intelligence. Success depends on careful planning as much as quick reactions.

With atmospheric static screens, detailed train operations, and a strong sense of historical tension, The Train: Escape to Normandy stands out for blending simulation depth with action-driven gameplay. It remains a distinctive and ambitious entry in the Commodore 64 library.

_HQKCEBff1w.title: Project Firestart – Survival Horror on the C64 Seven Years Before Resident Evil
_HQKCEBff1w.description:
🕹️ Project Firestart (1989) – Commodore 64 Sci-Fi Survival Horror Pioneer
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/project-firestart/

Released in 1989 by Electronic Arts and developed by Dynamix, Project Firestart is widely regarded as one of the earliest true survival horror games on the Commodore 64. Set aboard the orbital research station Prometheus above Titan in the year 2061, you play government agent Jon Hawking, sent to investigate a catastrophic loss of contact.

Exploration unfolds through side-scrolling corridors with clever pseudo-3D depth, as you move between decks, access computer terminals, and uncover logs detailing a genetic experiment that has spiralled out of control. The station is no longer abandoned, and every encounter forces you to balance survival, limited resources, and time pressure.

Tension is driven by deliberate pacing, atmospheric music, and cinematic scripted moments that build dread rather than relying on constant action. Player choices affect outcomes, leading to multiple endings and giving the experience lasting replay value.

Despite criticisms at the time for frequent disk swapping and slower scrolling, Project Firestart left a lasting mark on game design. Its influence can be felt in later genre-defining titles, and today it’s celebrated as a bold, forward-thinking classic that pushed storytelling and atmosphere on the C64.

💬 Did the atmosphere pull you in, or did the time pressure keep you constantly on edge?

Released in 1984 by David and Richard Darling and published by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Magic Carpet is a fast-paced arcade-style action game that challenges players to guide a carpet-riding hero through a series of dangerous underground caverns.

Presented in a side-scrolling format, the game tasks players with dodging falling rocks, stalactites, and hostile enemies while collecting treasure and useful power-ups. Each stage demands sharp reactions and careful timing, with hazards often appearing suddenly and leaving little room for error.

As progress is made, the level layouts become more complex and the pace intensifies, pushing players to master precise movement and pattern recognition. Success relies on memorising trap placements and maintaining control under pressure.

Visually, Magic Carpet makes effective use of colour and smooth animation to create lively cave environments within the limits of the C64 hardware. Its energetic soundtrack adds momentum to the action, reinforcing the game’s arcade-style atmosphere.

Known for its high difficulty and uncompromising design, Magic Carpet earned a reputation as a tough but rewarding challenge. Today, it remains a memorable example of early budget-label arcade gaming and a favourite among fans of demanding retro titles.

_KRx_UxPWTM.title: Play Expo Blackpool 2022 – John Romero, Retro Games and Norbreck Castle
_KRx_UxPWTM.description:

🌐 For more Retro Events, visit:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/collections/retro-events.html

A full weekend of gaming nostalgia and retro mischief at Play Expo Blackpool 2022, filmed at the iconic Norbreck Castle Hotel. This video captures the atmosphere, characters, and chaos of one of the UK’s premier retro gaming events, packed with classic machines, Commodore throwbacks, and plenty of unexpected moments along the way.

From hands-on sessions with Commodore 64 favourites like Paradroid and IK+ to rows of arcade cabinets begging for “just one more go,” the event delivers wall-to-wall nostalgia. Add in rare retro merchandise, quirky hardware finds, and a buzzing crowd of like-minded fans, and it’s everything a retro gaming weekend should be.

One of the standout moments is a live appearance by legendary game designer John Romero, co-creator of DOOM and Quake. From meet-and-greets to candid moments on the show floor, it’s a rare chance to see a true icon of gaming history up close. And because it’s Play Expo, things don’t stop there—expect breakdancing, DJ beats, and more than a hint of ‘80s-style chaos.

Whether you grew up with a joystick in one hand and a pocket full of Space Raiders in the other, or you’re discovering retro gaming for the first time, this video captures the spirit, humour, and community that make Play Expo Blackpool such a special event.

_LTR9gNp_5c.title: IK+ on the Amiga – Still One of the Slickest Fighting Games of Its Era?
_LTR9gNp_5c.description:
🕹️ International Karate Plus (1988) – Commodore Amiga Three-Way Fighting Action Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/ik-amiga/

Released in 1988 by System 3 and developed by Archer MacLean for the Commodore Amiga, International Karate Plus—commonly known as IK+—is a refined and expanded sequel to the original International Karate. This fast-paced top-down fighting game introduced the unique concept of three fighters battling simultaneously on a single screen, creating constant tension and chaotic fun.

Gameplay focuses on precise joystick control, responsive combat, and smart positioning, as players must defend themselves from two opponents at once. A wide range of punches, kicks, and special moves encourages aggressive play, while careful timing and spacing are essential for survival in later rounds.

Progression is driven by skill mastery and adaptability, as enemy fighters become faster and more unpredictable. Alongside its competitive mechanics, the Amiga version adds playful background animations and hidden gags, including roaming Pac-Man characters, periscopes, spiders, and cheeky visual tricks that give the game its distinctive personality.

Visually, IK+ delivers smooth animation, colourful arenas, and crisp character sprites that showcase the Amiga’s strengths. The experience is elevated further by Dave Lowe’s superb musical arrangements, which provide energy and atmosphere throughout every bout.

Widely regarded as one of the finest home computer fighting games of its era, International Karate Plus remains a benchmark for multiplayer-friendly action. Its blend of tight controls, humour, and competitive depth has secured its status as a timeless favourite among Amiga fans.

_m3v-nWDFPQ.title: 720 Degrees – Could the C64 Handle Atari’s Skateboarding Arcade Hit?
_m3v-nWDFPQ.description:
🕹️ 720° (1987) – Commodore 64 Isometric Skateboarding Arcade Sports Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/720-degrees/

Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64 by Tiertex Design Studios and published by U.S. Gold, 720° is a faithful home conversion of Atari Games’ iconic arcade skateboarding hit.

Players skate through the vibrant Skate City hub, earning tickets by scoring points in order to unlock access to four challenge parks: Ramp, Downhill, Slalom, and Jump.

Each park features timed stunt events that test balance, speed, and precision, with trick spins, slalom gates, and hazardous obstacles standing between you and high scores.

Fail to complete events quickly enough and Skate City becomes even more dangerous, introducing hazards such as water traps and swarms of bees.

Between events, players can visit in-game shops to spend prize money on upgraded boards, pads, and helmets that improve performance and survivability.

The UK and European C64 version is especially praised for its smoother scrolling, weightier controls, and strong SID soundtrack by Ben Daglish.

Many fans consider this release superior to the US Mindscape version, which suffered from slower visuals and limited audio.

Combining arcade accuracy with clever progression and replay value, the game captures the thrill of competitive skateboarding on 8-bit hardware.

Today, 720° is remembered as one of the finest sports arcade conversions on the Commodore 64 and a standout of the late 1980s era.

💬 Did you manage to conquer all four parks, or did Skate City get the better of you?

_syDxx6aJEA.title: Times of Lore – The Vast C64 RPG That Helped Inspire Ultima VI
_syDxx6aJEA.description:
🕹️ Times of Lore (1988) – Commodore 64 Action RPG Fantasy Epic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/times-of-lore/

Released in 1988 by Origin Systems, Times of Lore is an ambitious action role-playing game for the Commodore 64 designed by Chris Roberts. Set in the troubled medieval kingdom of Albareth, the story begins with the mysterious disappearance of High King Valwyn, plunging the land into unrest as rival factions battle for control.

Players choose between three distinct heroes: a powerful barbarian, a heavily armoured knight, or a swift and agile valkyrie, each offering different strengths and playstyles. The game is presented from a top-down perspective and features real-time action as players explore a vast world made up of thousands of interconnected screens.

Combat is immediate and accessible, focusing on melee encounters with enemies such as brigands and orcs, while progress also depends on exploration, puzzle-solving, and interaction with non-player characters via a menu-driven dialogue system. The scale of the world encourages curiosity and persistence, rewarding those willing to take their time.

Visually, Times of Lore features detailed character sprites and environments that give the world a strong sense of place. Martin Galway’s atmospheric soundtrack reinforces the medieval tone and remains one of the game’s standout elements. Although sometimes criticised for its slow pacing and simple combat, Times of Lore is remembered as a bold early example of action RPG design on the Commodore 64 and a key stepping stone in the evolution of the genre.

_ThSf8hdKWQ.title: Beach-Head – Minefields, Tanks and a Final Fortress in One C64 Invasion
_ThSf8hdKWQ.description:
🕹️ Beach-Head (1983) – Commodore 64 Multi-Stage WWII Action Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/beach-head/

Released in 1983 by Access Software for the Commodore 64, Beach-Head is a landmark World War II action game that tasks players with launching a full-scale assault on a heavily fortified enemy island. Rather than focusing on a single gameplay style, the game unfolds across multiple distinct stages, each representing a different phase of the invasion.

The opening sequence sees players navigating a fleet of ships through dangerous waters, choosing between a direct route under enemy fire or a hidden passage filled with mines and torpedoes. This is followed by a shift to anti-aircraft defence, where quick reflexes are required to protect the fleet from waves of enemy planes.

Later stages introduce artillery combat against enemy battleships and a side-scrolling beach assault, where tanks must survive long enough to reach the enemy fortress. The number of tanks that make it ashore directly affects the difficulty of the final confrontation, adding strategic weight to earlier performance.

The climactic fortress assault demands precise timing and accurate fire to destroy the enemy gun emplacement while under heavy retaliation. This varied structure, combined with constant pressure, keeps the action intense from start to finish.

Beach-Head was one of Access Software’s biggest successes and is remembered for its ambitious design and cinematic pacing. It later received a sequel, Beach Head II: The Dictator Strikes Back, further cementing its place as a Commodore 64 classic.

_WsFBiB8U34.title: Rocket Ranger – Jetpacks, Villains and Cinemaware Ambition on the C64
_WsFBiB8U34.description:
🕹️ Rocket Ranger (1988) – Commodore 64 Cinematic Action-Strategy Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/rocket-ranger/

Released for the Commodore 64 by Cinemaware, Rocket Ranger drops players into an alternate-history 1940s where the Nazis have established a secret base on the Moon. Using a mysterious substance called Lunarium, they plan to reduce global intelligence levels and secure world domination. Humanity’s last hope comes from the future, as advanced jetpack technology, powerful weapons, and code-breaking tools are sent back in time for you to change the course of history.

The game follows Cinemaware’s trademark cinematic structure, blending dramatic animated sequences with a mix of action and strategy. Players must manage limited resources, deploy spies across Europe to uncover enemy rocket factories, and decide how much Lunarium to expend at each stage while avoiding capture. Strategic choices directly affect your chances of success.

Action sequences punctuate the experience, including brutal hand-to-hand combat with Nazi guards, high-speed jetpack dogfights against enemy aircraft, and daring assaults on Zeppelins and secret installations. These moments are tightly woven into the narrative, giving Rocket Ranger its distinctive movie-like pacing.

Decades later, Rocket Ranger remains one of the most iconic cinematic games of the 8-bit era. Its ambitious blend of storytelling, strategy, and arcade action set a high bar for presentation on the Commodore 64. In 2018, its legacy was celebrated with a limited Extended Collector’s Edition, featuring multi-platform versions, artwork, and even the soundtrack on vinyl.

Players control a lone commando assaulting heavily fortified enemy bases, using a distinctive crosshair aiming system that separates movement from shooting. While dodging incoming fire, players must accurately target gun emplacements, buildings, and vehicles, creating a constant push-and-pull between survival and precision.

The Commodore 64 version captures the feel of the arcade experience with solid level design and satisfying destruction, even if the action runs at a slightly reduced pace and with simplified visuals due to hardware constraints. These compromises do little to diminish the thrill of clearing screens under heavy fire.

With its unique control scheme and relentless arcade challenge, CABAL earned a strong following among home computer players. Today, it’s remembered as one of the standout arcade conversions on the C64 and a defining example of crosshair-based shooters on 8-bit systems.

Released in 1986 by Durell Software, Saboteur is a landmark stealth-action game developed by Clive Townsend and brought to the Commodore 64 by Branko Spoljaric. Players assume the role of a lone ninja infiltrating a heavily guarded warehouse complex to recover a disk containing the names of rebel leaders.

Gameplay takes place across a large network of interconnected rooms, tunnels, and hidden areas. Success relies on careful movement, observation, and timing as players avoid or confront guards, dogs, and automated gun turrets. The ninja can crouch, climb, sprint, and attack using punches, drop-kicks, and weapons such as shurikens, with improvised tools discovered along the way adding tactical variety.

An energy system governs every action, draining through combat, falls, and swimming. Resting in safe zones is essential to survive longer infiltrations, while selectable difficulty levels alter enemy density, security systems, and time pressure, allowing players to tailor the challenge.

Praised for its atmosphere and forward-thinking design, Saboteur helped define stealth gameplay on home computers. Its influence carried into the sequel Saboteur II: Avenging Angel and later inspired enhanced modern releases, cementing its status as a Commodore 64 classic.

Released in 1988 by Martech for the Commodore 64, Shoot-Out is a crosshair-based shooting game set in the dusty frontier town of Gulch Creek. Players take on the role of Quick Hand Luke, a skilled gunslinger determined to restore order to the Wild West.

The game unfolds across a series of increasingly demanding scenarios. It begins with precision-based target practice, where players must shoot appearing cans without missing a single shot. As the game progresses, moving enemies, obstacles, and time pressure are introduced, requiring fast reactions and steady aim.

Gameplay focuses on accuracy, rhythm, and memorisation, with little margin for error. Each stage demands perfect timing, making Shoot-Out a test of concentration as much as reflexes. One mistake can often mean restarting the challenge.

Visually, the game uses a fixed-screen, top-down perspective with simple yet effective Western-themed backdrops. Desert landscapes and minimal character designs help establish atmosphere without distracting from the core shooting mechanics.

A major highlight is the soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, whose energetic and memorable composition adds excitement and personality to the experience. His music helps elevate the presentation and remains one of the game’s most celebrated features.

Although reviews were mixed due to limited depth and variety, Shoot-Out has retained a nostalgic following. Today, it’s remembered as a focused, skill-based shooter that captures classic arcade shooting in an 8-bit Western setting.

Released in 1985 by Activision for the Commodore 64, Alcazar: The Forgotten Fortress is an ambitious action-adventure game designed and programmed by Tom Loughry.

Players set out on a quest to recover a stolen crown by navigating a dynamically generated world map filled with twenty-two castles, each containing unique layouts, hazards, and hidden treasures.

Gameplay is presented from a top-down perspective, with every castle forming a maze of interconnected rooms. Players must overcome traps, enemies, and environmental puzzles in order to progress.

A variety of tools and items aid exploration and combat, including pistols, grappling hooks, magic carpets, and secret passages. Limited ammunition and careful resource management add a strong strategic element.

The game features multiple difficulty levels and a built-in demonstration mode, both of which were advanced features for home computer games of the mid-1980s.

Randomised castle layouts ensure that each playthrough feels different, encouraging experimentation and long-term mastery. Success depends on learning enemy patterns and managing supplies wisely.

Praised for its originality and scope, Alcazar pushed the boundaries of what action-adventure games could achieve on 8-bit systems and influenced later exploration-based titles.

Today, it’s remembered as a challenging and rewarding classic that showcases early game design ingenuity.

Released in 1983 by Epyx and designed by Jeff McCord, Sword of Fargoal is one of the most influential dungeon-crawling RPGs on the Commodore 64. Players descend into a deadly, ever-changing dungeon on a quest to recover the legendary Sword of Fargoal, stolen by the evil wizard Umla.

Each playthrough features randomly generated dungeon layouts, ensuring no two adventures are ever the same. Players explore between 15 and 20 levels, facing over 30 different monster types including ogres, trolls, wyverns, and fearsome shadow dragons.

A key feature is the fog-of-war system, which hides unexplored areas and creates constant tension as new threats emerge from the darkness. Progression is driven by experience, levelling, and careful resource management, with temples on each level offering healing, protection, or experience in exchange for gold.

Known for its unforgiving difficulty and permanent death mechanic, Sword of Fargoal rewards cautious exploration and strategic decision-making. Its blend of randomness, risk, and atmosphere helped define early roguelike design and cemented its reputation as a true C64 classic that still challenges players today.

Players can jump into single-player or head-to-head multiplayer matches, controlling one skater at a time while switching seamlessly during play. Released in 1989 and developed by Foursfield, Ghostbusters II is a top-down action game for the Commodore 64, published by Activision and based on the hit movie sequel. Rather than a single gameplay style, the game is structured around several distinct stages that recreate key moments from the film.

The action begins in the sewers beneath New York, where players guide a Ghostbuster down vertical shafts to collect slime samples while avoiding or neutralising ghosts. This is followed by a top-down driving section through the streets of Manhattan, piloting the Ecto-1 to trap roaming spirits while dodging traffic and obstacles. The final stage shifts perspective again, delivering a side-scrolling shooter set inside the museum as players confront the game’s main threat.

Each section demands a different skill set, keeping the experience varied while staying faithful to the film’s locations and tone. While some critics noted repetition within individual stages, the constant shifts in viewpoint and mechanics help maintain momentum throughout the game.

Ghostbusters II remains a fondly remembered licensed title on the Commodore 64. Its mix of action styles and recognisable movie moments make it a nostalgic favourite for fans of the franchise and late-era C64 releases.

Known for its responsive controls and distinctive features, it stands out as one of the most memorable sports titles on the C64.

Players can choose from eight teams representing major hockey cities such as New York, Chicago, Toronto, and Montreal, and compete in exhibition matches or tournament play. The side-scrolling presentation keeps the action flowing at high speed, rewarding quick reflexes, sharp passing, and tactical positioning.

Progression relies on mastering puck control, defensive awareness, and well-timed shots on goal. Strategic line changes and smart player movement become increasingly important as matches grow more competitive, especially in two-player showdowns.

One of the game’s most iconic features is its fight system. Heavy collisions can trigger one-on-one brawls where players punch, block, and dodge in a short mini-game. Winning these fights sends the opposing player to the penalty box, adding an extra layer of risk and reward to physical play.

Despite the Commodore 64’s technical limitations, Blades of Steel delivers smooth gameplay and a convincing hockey atmosphere. Its use of a code sheet for copy protection was unusual for the era, while its blend of speed, strategy, and personality has secured its status as a lasting retro sports favourite.

Released in 1988 by Elite Systems and published by Domark for the Commodore 64, Live and Let Die is a fast-paced action game loosely inspired by the 1973 James Bond film. Originally developed as an original title called Aquablast, the game was later rebranded after Domark recognised its similarity to the movie’s famous speedboat chase sequence.

Players take control of a heavily armed high-speed boat and race through a variety of global locations, including the Florida Everglades, Arctic waters, and desert regions of the Sahara. The main objective is to battle enemy forces, avoid environmental hazards, and ultimately destroy Dr. Kananga’s heroin refinery.

Gameplay blends high-speed racing with arcade-style shooting, drawing comparisons to titles such as RoadBlasters and Overlander. Players must balance aggressive combat with careful fuel management, precise steering, and quick reactions to survive increasingly intense stages.

On the Commodore 64, the game delivers smooth scrolling, responsive controls, and clearly defined environments that maintain a strong sense of speed. Explosions, enemy formations, and varied terrain help keep the action fresh and engaging throughout the campaign.

Although it deviates from the film’s storyline, Live and Let Die captures the spirit of Bond-style spectacle through its explosive set pieces and globe-trotting structure. Today, it remains a distinctive entry in the James Bond gaming catalogue and a memorable example of late-1980s arcade action on home computers.

Released in 1984 by U.S. Gold and developed by Archer Maclean under the Arena Graphics name, Dropzone is one of the Commodore 64’s most celebrated shoot ’em ups. Inspired by the arcade classic Defender, it drops you onto the hostile surface of Jupiter’s moon Io with a jetpack-equipped astronaut and a single objective: rescue stranded scientists while surviving relentless alien attacks.

Gameplay is fast, precise, and unforgiving. You fly freely across horizontally scrolling landscapes, blasting enemies with your laser while juggling limited smart bombs and a temporary cloaking device. Every rescue adds pressure, as enemies grow more aggressive and the screen fills with threats from all directions.

With 99 progressively tougher levels, Dropzone demands sharp reflexes, spatial awareness, and total control of momentum. Its ultra-smooth scrolling, tight controls, and perfectly tuned difficulty curve make it endlessly playable, even by modern standards.

Critically acclaimed on release, Dropzone earned a legendary 95% score and a Gold Medal from Zzap!64, cementing its reputation as one of the finest arcade-style games ever made on the Commodore 64. Decades later, it remains a benchmark for how exhilarating and polished an 8-bit shoot ’em up can be.

Released in 1992, Agony is a horizontally scrolling shooter for the Commodore Amiga developed by Art & Magic and published by Psygnosis. Players take control of Alestes, a magician’s apprentice transformed into an owl, journeying through a dark, surreal fantasy world filled with twisted creatures and nightmarish landscapes.

Unlike many shooters of the era, Agony places less emphasis on relentless speed and more on exploration, positioning, and deliberate combat. Levels are densely detailed and encourage careful movement, with enemies and hazards woven into the environment rather than simply streamed in waves. Boss encounters are visually striking and contribute heavily to the game’s oppressive atmosphere.

One of Agony’s defining features is its audiovisual presentation. The richly illustrated backgrounds, fluid animations, and distinctive art style showcase the Amiga’s strengths, while the atmospheric soundtrack enhances the sense of unease and immersion throughout the journey. Every level feels handcrafted, reinforcing the game’s dreamlike tone.

Widely praised for its artistic direction and technical achievement, Agony stands as one of the Amiga’s most visually memorable shoot ’em ups. Its slower, mood-driven approach set it apart from the genre norm and has helped secure its reputation as a cult classic among retro gaming enthusiasts.

Each level challenges players to dig through dirt, manipulate the environment, and outthink falling boulders, roaming enemies, and deadly traps. Success depends on careful planning as much as quick reactions, with every movement potentially triggering chain reactions that can either clear a path or seal Rockford’s fate.

The Commodore 64 version is especially celebrated for its colourful presentation and distinctive sound effects, which bring the caves to life and heighten the tension as boulders tumble and enemies close in. Level design steadily increases in complexity, encouraging experimentation, memorisation, and mastery of the game’s physics-driven systems.

Boulder Dash’s blend of action, strategy, and puzzle-solving proved hugely influential, spawning numerous sequels and inspiring countless later games. Decades on, it remains one of the most iconic and enduring titles in the Commodore 64 library.

Released in 1986 by Melbourne House and developed by Beam Software, Asterix and the Magic Cauldron brings the famous Gaulish heroes to the Commodore 64 in a light adventure inspired by the beloved comic series. The story begins when Getafix’s magic cauldron explodes, scattering seven vital pieces across the land and leaving the village defenceless.

Players control Asterix and Obelix as they explore a network of interconnected screens representing the Gaulish village, forests, and Roman camps. Progress depends on careful exploration, collecting keys to unlock new areas, and engaging in one-on-one combat with Roman soldiers and wild boars.

Resource management plays a central role, with food needed to maintain strength and a single vial of magic potion providing temporary invincibility when used wisely. Choosing when to fight, explore, or retreat adds a strategic layer beneath the game’s cartoon charm.

The Commodore 64 version is enhanced by atmospheric music composed by Neil Brennan, helping capture the playful tone of the comics. However, the game is also infamous for a bug that places one cauldron piece out of reach, preventing completion without a cheat code.

Despite its flaws, Asterix and the Magic Cauldron remains a nostalgic entry in the C64 library, fondly remembered for its faithful presentation of the Asterix universe and its distinctive comic-book atmosphere.

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/ultima-1-the-first-age-of-darkness/

Released in 1986 by Origin Systems for the Commodore 64, Ultima I: The First Age of Darkness is a landmark role-playing game that laid the foundations for the legendary Ultima series.

Set in the fantasy world of Sosaria, players are tasked with defeating the evil wizard Mondain by travelling through time to destroy his Gem of Immortality and end his reign of darkness.

Gameplay is divided into several interconnected systems, including an overhead world map for exploration, first-person dungeon crawling, and even space combat sequences. This ambitious structure gave players an unprecedented sense of freedom.

Character creation allows players to distribute points across key attributes such as Strength, Agility, and Intelligence, while choosing from races including Human, Elf, Dwarf, and Bobbit. These choices directly affect combat and progression.

The Commodore 64 version was rewritten in assembly language and represented a major upgrade over the original Apple II release. It featured improved graphics, smoother performance, additional towns, and a more complex in-game economy.

Although the game includes minimal sound and no background music, its vast world, deep systems, and non-linear design kept players immersed for countless hours.

Ultima I introduced many concepts that would later define open-world RPGs, including free exploration, player-driven progression, and persistent world-building.

Today, it’s remembered as one of the most important role-playing games ever created and a cornerstone of computer gaming history.

Gameplay mixes trivia questions with physical challenges and obstacle-course style action. Players alternate between answering questions to build up cash and taking on fast-paced sequences that test timing, movement, and reflexes, mirroring the structure of the TV show itself. While the two versions share the same core idea, the US release leans into a more cartoon-style presentation and brisk arcade feel, while the UK version introduces small gameplay and pacing differences. Both feature bright visuals, upbeat music, and accessible mechanics designed to appeal to players of all ages.

Light-hearted but competitive, Double Dare stands out as one of the more unusual licensed titles on the Commodore 64. By blending quiz elements with arcade-style challenges, it delivers a nostalgic slice of 1980s television culture and remains a fondly remembered crossover between game shows and home computing.

Released in 1989 by Bullfrog Productions for the Commodore Amiga, Populous is widely regarded as the first true “god game,” placing players in the role of a deity guiding their followers toward domination. Instead of controlling individual units, players shape the world itself to influence the fate of their civilisation.

Gameplay is presented in an isometric view, where players raise and lower terrain to create habitable land for their people. As populations grow, followers build settlements that increase their power, allowing them to expand, defend territory, and prepare for conflict with rival gods.

Strategic depth comes from balancing population growth, land management, and divine intervention. Players can unleash powerful abilities such as earthquakes, floods, and volcanoes to disrupt enemies, destroy settlements, and shift the balance of power.

With over 500 unique levels, each featuring different landscapes and challenges, Populous offers enormous variety and long-term replay value. Every world requires a different approach, encouraging experimentation and careful planning.

A major commercial and critical success, Populous helped define the strategy and simulation genres and influenced countless games that followed. Today, it remains one of the Amiga’s most important and influential titles, celebrated for its originality and timeless design.

Released in 1992, Danny Sullivan’s Indy Heat is a fast-paced top-down racing game developed by Sales Curve and based on Leland Corporation’s 1991 arcade hit starring IndyCar champion Danny Sullivan. The Amiga version delivers a high-energy racing experience that closely mirrors the speed, intensity, and presentation of the original arcade machine.

Players race across nine international circuits, each packed with sharp corners, aggressive rivals, and demanding layouts, culminating in the dramatic Tradewest Speed Bowl finale. Every race is a balance of raw speed and strategy, with fuel levels, vehicle damage, and limited turbo boosts all playing a critical role in success.

Pit stops are central to gameplay, allowing drivers to refuel, repair damage, and restock turbos at the cost of valuable race time. The AI is famously unforgiving, particularly Danny Sullivan’s yellow car, which uses heavy rubber-banding to keep the pressure on until the final lap.

With colourful car animations, detailed track design, and relentless arcade pacing, Indy Heat stands as one of the most memorable top-down racers on the Amiga. Its blend of tactical pit management and flat-out racing has earned it cult status among retro racing fans and arcade enthusiasts alike.

Released in 1990 by The Bitmap Brothers and published by Image Works for the Commodore Amiga, Cadaver is an isometric action-adventure that places you in the boots of Karadoc, a dwarf thief exploring the deadly halls of Castle Wulf in search of treasure.

The game focuses on exploration and puzzle-solving rather than direct combat. Each of the five large levels is packed with traps, locked doors, pressure plates, monsters, and environmental hazards that require careful observation and planning to overcome. Progress depends on understanding the castle’s layout and using items intelligently rather than relying on brute force.

Gameplay revolves around object manipulation and logical thinking. Players push barrels, collect keys, trigger mechanisms, and cast spells to navigate rooms safely. With no traditional fighting system, timing, positioning, and clever use of the environment are essential for survival.

Visually, Cadaver stands out thanks to its detailed isometric environments and strong atmosphere. The castle feels oppressive and mysterious, with level design that rewards experimentation and patience. The freedom to tackle challenges in different ways helped the game feel deep and rewarding for its time.

Today, Cadaver is remembered as one of the defining isometric puzzle adventures on the Amiga and a prime example of The Bitmap Brothers’ distinctive design approach, combining atmosphere, intelligence, and challenge into a memorable experience.

Casting the player as a journalist for The Clarion, the game sets up a serious narrative rarely seen on the Commodore 64 at the time.

Your mission is to infiltrate a Colombian drug lord’s heavily guarded headquarters, rescue a kidnapped colleague, and uncover vital information hidden throughout the complex. Progress depends on answering 32 key questions, each unlocked by discovering clues scattered across the building, giving the game a strong investigative core.

Gameplay combines stealth, exploration, and combat, drawing comparisons with Impossible Mission and Kung Fu Master. You move between multiple floors, interact with characters, avoid detection, and fight only when necessary. The balance between careful movement and sudden action keeps tension high throughout.

One of Nexus’s most striking features is its use of digitised character portraits, lending a sense of realism and atmosphere that stood out on the C64. Combined with its mature storyline and layered mechanics, it offered something notably different from typical action games of the era.

Today, Nexus is remembered as an ambitious and atmospheric title, earning a loyal following for its blend of storytelling, puzzle-solving, and stealth-driven gameplay within the Commodore 64 library.

Released in 1985 by Starcade Software and developed by Gwyll Jones, Up Up and Away is a distinctive side-scrolling action game for the Commodore 64 that puts players in control of a hot air balloon drifting across a hazardous landscape. Its unusual theme and mechanics set it apart from more conventional arcade titles of the era.

Gameplay revolves around careful balloon control as the screen scrolls relentlessly forward. Players must dodge clouds, trees, kites, birds, and even people hurling rocks from below, all while managing a limited fuel supply that drains whenever the balloon ascends. To stay aloft, players can drop sandbags to reduce weight—these also double as weapons, used to hit targets marked with a “P” for bonus points.

Strategic planning is key, as landing at checkpoints allows players to refuel and restock sandbags before pressing on. With five selectable difficulty levels, the game steadily ramps up speed and obstacle density, demanding sharper reactions and tighter fuel management as progress continues.

The experience is enhanced by a memorable soundtrack from Rob Hubbard, which adds atmosphere and momentum to the journey. Unusual, challenging, and full of character, Up Up and Away remains a niche but fondly remembered title in the Commodore 64 catalogue.

Originally developed by Gottlieb and ported to the Commodore 64 by Parker Brothers in 1983, Q*Bert is a landmark arcade game that blends fast reactions with puzzle-like precision. You guide the instantly recognisable orange hero across a pyramid of cubes, aiming to change every tile to the correct colour.

The challenge comes from timing and spatial awareness. Each hop alters the cube beneath you, but enemies, flying discs, and awkward jump angles constantly threaten to knock you off course. As stages progress, new hazards are introduced, turning simple movement into a tense test of nerve and planning.

The isometric perspective gives the game its distinctive pseudo-3D look, making depth and direction part of the challenge. On the Commodore 64, the conversion stays faithful to the arcade original, with bright colours, smooth animation, and the same addictive difficulty curve.

Q*Bert remains one of the most enduring arcade experiences of the early 1980s. Its simple goal, instantly readable design, and escalating pressure ensure it’s still just as compelling today as it was in the arcades.

Released in 1987 by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Kobyashi Naru is a science-fiction themed adventure that takes its inspiration from the famous no-win test of Star Trek lore. Designed by Clive Wilson and Les Hogarth, the game challenges players to prove their worth by surviving a sequence of cerebral trials rather than relying on action or reflexes.

Gameplay is divided into three distinct sections—Knowledge, Wisdom, and Understanding—each presenting puzzles that test logic, observation, and reasoning. Instead of a traditional text parser, the game uses an icon-based interface, allowing players to interact with objects and environments in a more visual and accessible way for the time.

The challenge is deliberately unforgiving. Incorrect decisions can lead to sudden failure, and progress often demands experimentation and lateral thinking. This difficulty split opinion on release, but it also gave the game a reputation as a demanding experience aimed squarely at players who enjoyed tough mental challenges.

As part of Mastertronic’s budget range, Kobyashi Naru offered something different from the usual arcade fare. While never a mainstream hit, it remains a curious and memorable entry in the Commodore 64’s interactive fiction catalogue.

Players choose from five different characters, each with their own strengths and abilities, and set out to investigate mysterious visions that threaten the harmony of their society. Exploration takes place across a large, interconnected world of platforms, villages, and natural environments, encouraging curiosity and careful observation.

Progress depends on communication, puzzle-solving, and understanding the world and its inhabitants, making every interaction meaningful.

The game was praised for its atmospheric visuals and depth, as well as its open-ended structure that allows players to approach challenges in different ways. Its calm tone and emphasis on empathy and intelligence set it apart from most contemporaries on the Commodore 64.

2OG2tPx5gnU.title: Amiga X-Copy Explained | The Legendary Disk Copier Every Amiga Owner Remembers
2OG2tPx5gnU.description:
🕹️ Amiga X-Copy explained — the legendary Commodore Amiga disk copier that became part of floppy disk culture.

X-Copy, developed by Cachet Software in the late 1980s, became one of the most recognisable disk-copying utilities ever created for the Commodore Amiga. Originally coded by Frank Neuhaus and Hans Georg Berg, X-Copy allowed Amiga users to duplicate floppy disks at sector level, including disks that used non-standard formats or stronger protection methods.

Its raw copying modes, verification system, formatting tools, boot-sector checks and support for protected disks made it a powerful utility for backups, preservation and software sharing throughout the Amiga era. But X-Copy was not remembered only because it worked.

Its bold interface, moving progress bar and unforgettable “BOING!” sound effect turned disk copying into something that felt completely Amiga. For many users, the sound and screen are burned into memory as much as the games themselves.

Later versions added support for hardware such as the Cyclone interface, helping users make faster and more reliable disk transfers. Officially, X-Copy was promoted as a legitimate backup utility. In reality, it also became central to the wider Amiga software-sharing scene of the late 1980s and early 1990s.

Today, X-Copy remains a retro computing legend — a symbol of floppy disks, backup tools, Amiga utilities, bedroom computing, preservation, and that unmistakable sound every Amiga owner remembers.

Released in 1985 by Odin Computer Graphics for the Commodore 64, Nodes of Yesod is a side-scrolling platform adventure set on a mysterious lunar landscape. Players take control of astronaut Charlemagne “Charlie” Fotheringham-Grunes, sent to investigate strange signals coming from a towering black monolith buried deep beneath the Moon’s surface.

Gameplay focuses on careful exploration and puzzle-solving as Charlie navigates interconnected caverns filled with hazards, enemies, and hidden routes. The main objective is to locate and collect eight coloured crystals known as alchiems, each required to progress deeper into the underground maze.

A defining feature is the ability to capture and release lunar moles, which can burrow through walls to open new paths and uncover secrets. This mechanic adds a strong strategic layer, forcing players to think ahead rather than rely purely on reflexes. Red astronaut-like enemies known as muggers increase the tension by stealing collected alchiems on contact, making safe traversal just as important as discovery.

The game’s structure and pacing draw comparisons with Ultimate’s Underwurlde, combining deliberate movement with a strong sense of atmosphere. On the Commodore 64, Nodes of Yesod delivers moody visuals and a distinct sci-fi tone that sets it apart from more traditional platform games of the era.

Widely praised for its originality and design, Nodes of Yesod is now regarded as a standout title in the C64 library. Its influence can be seen in later exploration-driven games, and it was followed by a same-year sequel, The Arc of Yesod. Today, it remains a memorable example of intelligent platform design from the mid-1980s.

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/tooth-invaders/

Released in 1982 by Commodore International for the Commodore 64, Tooth Invaders is an educational action game created in collaboration with the American Dental Association and Camelot Marketing Group. Developed as part of National Dental Month, the game set out to teach good dental hygiene through fast-paced, arcade-style gameplay.

Players take control of Plaqueman, tasked with cleaning a mouth containing eight teeth by removing plaque and stopping the notorious plaque germ D.K. Using a toothbrush, toothpaste, and dental floss, players must carefully navigate between teeth, clean surfaces thoroughly, and avoid direct contact with D.K., which costs a life.

Each tooth must be fully cleaned to prevent decay, and once completed it becomes immune to further plaque. Successfully cleaning a tooth also creates a brief opportunity to defeat D.K. for bonus points, adding a risk-versus-reward element to the gameplay. The game ends if all lives are lost or if four teeth decay completely.

Tooth Invaders stands out as an early example of “edutainment” done right, blending a clear educational goal with engaging mechanics. Its cultural impact has even earned it a place in the National Museum of Dentistry, where it’s remembered as a creative and memorable way of teaching healthy habits through gaming.

Originally released in arcades in 1983 by Sega, Congo Bongo is an isometric platform game that puts you in the role of a wronged safari explorer seeking revenge on the mischievous ape Bongo. After your camp is destroyed, the chase takes you through a series of hazard-filled environments viewed from a distinctive angled perspective.

Gameplay revolves around timing and positioning as you climb cliffs while dodging coconuts, cross swamps by hopping between hippos and lily pads, and avoid aggressive wildlife along the way. The isometric viewpoint adds depth and challenge, requiring careful judgement of jumps and movement.

The Commodore 64 saw two notable versions. The early 1983 release included only the first two stages, trimmed back to suit hardware limits. A later 1985 European release by U.S. Gold restored all four arcade levels with improved visuals and sound, delivering a more complete home conversion.

Often compared to Sega’s Zaxxon and Nintendo’s Donkey Kong, Congo Bongo stands as an early example of isometric design on home computers. While opinions were mixed at the time, it remains a memorable arcade port and a snapshot of experimentation during the early 1980s.

The C64 version preserves the fast pace and competitive spirit of the arcade, with support for up to four players turning it into a tense party favourite. Clear visuals and responsive controls keep the focus firmly on skill and reflexes, making every fraction of a second count.

Track & Field remains one of the most iconic sports games of the 8-bit era, remembered for wrecked joysticks, heated rivalries, and its pure test of physical timing and coordination.

Released in 1992 by LucasArts for the Commodore Amiga, Monkey Island 2: LeChuck’s Revenge continues the legendary adventures of Guybrush Threepwood in one of the most celebrated sequels in gaming history. Picking up after the events of The Secret of Monkey Island, you set off on a globe-trotting quest to uncover the mythical treasure of Big Whoop, all while dealing with pirates, curses, and unfinished business with LeChuck.

Built using the SCUMM engine, the game refines the point-and-click formula with deeper puzzles, sharper writing, and a much larger world to explore. You travel between multiple islands, combining inventory items, outwitting rivals, and engaging in some of the most memorable dialogue ever written for an adventure game.

The Amiga version shines with richly detailed hand-painted visuals and smooth presentation, while the innovative iMUSE system dynamically adjusts the music to match on-screen action, creating a seamless and immersive atmosphere. Every location feels alive, supported by a soundtrack that reacts intelligently as scenes unfold.

Despite spanning multiple floppy disks, the game is carefully structured to reduce disk swapping, keeping the experience flowing naturally. Later CD32 releases even added voice acting, further enhancing its cinematic feel.

Today, Monkey Island 2: LeChuck’s Revenge is widely regarded as one of the greatest adventure games of all time, praised for its storytelling, puzzle design, humour, and lasting influence on the genre.

Released in 1990 by Teque Software and published by Domark under the Tengen label for the Commodore 64, Badlands is an overhead racing game that blends high-speed competition with vehicular combat. Inspired by Atari’s Super Sprint series, it adds a distinctive post-apocalyptic twist to the arcade racing formula.

Gameplay features three armed vehicles battling for position over four-lap races across eight hazardous tracks. Viewed from a top-down perspective, each race demands sharp steering, careful braking, and constant awareness of rivals and environmental dangers.

During races, players can collect wrenches that are exchanged between events for upgrades such as improved speed, acceleration, and enhanced weapon systems. These progression mechanics add a strategic layer, rewarding consistent performance and smart investment.

Tracks are packed with hazards including mines, retractable barriers, and tight corners, forcing players to balance aggression with precision. Combat and racing are tightly intertwined, making every lap unpredictable and intense.

Despite hardware limitations, the C64 version delivers a faithful and enjoyable conversion, with clear visuals and effective sound design that support the fast-paced action. Its solid handling and competitive structure keep races engaging from start to finish.

Remembered for its distinctive mix of driving and destruction, Badlands remains a standout title in the Commodore 64 racing catalogue. Today, it’s celebrated as a cult favourite that delivers arcade-style thrills with strategic depth.

Released in 1988 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64 and re-released by Encore in 1989, Mike Read’s Computer Pop Quiz brings the popular BBC Radio 1 quiz show to home computers, hosted by Mike Read and packed with music trivia from the 1950s through the 1980s.

The game recreates a full TV-style quiz format, guiding players through multiple themed rounds that test knowledge of artists, songs, dates, and pop culture history.

Round One challenges players to select questions from a jukebox, while later rounds introduce clue-based star guessing, category choices, and year-identification challenges.

The fast-paced Quickfire Round adds pressure with timed questions and penalties for wrong answers, rewarding speed and accuracy under pressure.

A final jukebox segment offers one last chance to boost your score, keeping tension high right to the end.

Players can compete solo or against a friend, choosing music categories and animated team-mates that add personality and charm to each match.

The presentation is enhanced by lively graphics and strong audio, with music and sound effects by Mark Cooksey supporting the upbeat quiz-show atmosphere.

With design by Ian Upton and Nick Acton, graphics by David Percival, and programming by Richard Underhill, the game delivers a polished and authentic TV adaptation.

Blending nostalgia, music knowledge, and competitive fun, it remains one of the most distinctive quiz titles on the Commodore 64.

Today, it is remembered as a lively celebration of British pop culture and a favourite among retro trivia fans.

Released in 1986 by Domark and developed by Ernieware, Split Personalities is a clever and addictive sliding puzzle game that tasks you with rebuilding the faces of famous figures piece by piece. Played on a 5×5 grid, the goal is to restore each portrait before the clock runs out.

Using a flashing cursor, you slide individual pieces into position while referencing a miniature preview of the completed image, which also highlights the active tile. The puzzles feature recognisable personalities including Ronald Reagan, Margaret Thatcher, Marilyn Monroe, and Mick Jagger, adding a playful hook to the brain-teasing challenge.

As you progress, the game introduces hazards such as gaps that swallow pieces, bombs that must be pushed off-screen to avoid losing lives, and bonus objects that reward precise movement. These twists elevate the puzzles beyond simple tile-sliding and demand forward planning as well as speed.

Well received on release, Split Personalities stood out on the C64 for its smart design and compulsive gameplay. Today it remains a memorable example of how a simple concept, executed well, can deliver lasting appeal.

4iOuSVWC_FA.title: Was 1987 the C64’s Greatest Year? 42 Zzap!64 Award Winners Revisited
4iOuSVWC_FA.description:
🕹️ Every Commodore 64 game that won a Zzap!64 Gold Medal, Sizzler or Silver Medal in 1987 — all 42 award games revisited month by month.

After the award-packed runs of 1985 and 1986, you might expect 1987 to be another constant stream of Zzap!64 Gold Medals and Sizzlers. But 1987 is where things get strange. The Gold Medals almost disappear for months, some issues feel much quieter, and by June even Zzap!64’s own readers were asking: “Gold Medals, Gone?”

In this video, I go month by month through Zzap!64’s 1987 Commodore 64 awards, covering every Gold Medal, every Sizzler, and the two unusual Silver Medal entries that make this year slightly messier than usual.

That means classics and cult favourites like The Bard’s Tale, Gauntlet, Gunship, Wizball, Head Over Heels, Defender of the Crown, The Last Ninja, California Games, Bubble Bobble, International Karate Plus, Maniac Mansion, Buggy Boy, Shoot ’Em Up Construction Kit, Nebulus and many more.

There are also a few oddities along the way: SEUCK gets a Gold Medal with no overall percentage, Computer Scrabble De Luxe gets a Sizzler with no printed overall score, and Arcade Classics and Revenge of the Mutant Camels II bring Silver Medals into the mix.

1987 might not be as consistent as 1986, but weak? Not a chance.  The C64 still delivered RPGs, arcade conversions, text adventures, strategy games, simulations, fighting games, puzzle games, construction kits, and a few games that still stand tall today.

So were these really the best Commodore 64 games of 1987? Was Wizball robbed of a Gold Medal? Did Head Over Heels deserve to end the drought? Was Nebulus the right final Gold Medal of the year?

Released in 1990 by Crionics, Neverwhere is widely regarded as the group’s first true masterpiece and a demo that left a lasting impression on anyone who saw it at the time. It’s the kind of production that begged to be shown off to friends, pushing the Amiga as a visual and musical showpiece rather than just a games machine.

The demo features rich 3D vector routines, classic bobs, and a memorable flyby sequence over Horsens, all tightly paced to ProTracker music that many will instantly recognise from the Kefrens Jukebox demo. The balance between effects, flow, and soundtrack gives Neverwhere a confident, polished feel that stood out in the early 1990s scene.

Originally released on a single disk at the Horsens Copyparty 1990, the production credits reflect a strong collaborative effort. Programming was handled by Murphy, Deftronic, The Spy, Grumble, and Saxs, with fonts by Deftronic and Merlin, logo work by Zycho, graphics by Madonna Freak, and music by Blazer and SLL.

Today, Neverwhere is remembered as a defining early Crionics release and a perfect snapshot of what made Amiga demos so exciting at the dawn of the 1990s—technical flair, memorable music, and effects that felt genuinely impressive at the time.

Praised for its smooth scrolling, precise collision detection, and tactical depth, Delta remains one of the most respected shooters on the Commodore 64. Its difficulty, audio design, and polished gameplay have secured its reputation as a defining title in the genre.

Released in 1987 by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Kikstart II is the sequel to the hugely popular motorcycle trials racer, developed by Mr. Chip Software. It builds directly on the original’s foundations while adding deeper mechanics and one of the most influential features of its era — a full track construction set.

The game includes 24 challenging pre-designed courses packed with ramps, gates, fences, mud pits, and precision jumps that demand careful throttle control and balance. Players can race against the clock or go head-to-head in split-screen two-player mode, where mastering momentum and timing is key to victory.

Kikstart II’s standout feature is its track editor, which allows players to design, save, and replay custom courses. This dramatically extends replay value and turns the game into a creative sandbox, encouraging experimentation and competitive custom challenges long after the built-in tracks are mastered.

Visually, the game delivers smooth scrolling, clear course layouts, and functional sprite work, while sound effects keep things minimal and focused. What truly defines Kikstart II is its razor-sharp control and addictive gameplay loop, especially in multiplayer, where it becomes fiercely competitive.

Widely regarded as one of the finest racing games on the Commodore 64, Kikstart II remains a genre-defining classic and a benchmark for physics-based gameplay and user-created content on 8-bit systems.

Released in 1985 by Mr. Micro Ltd. and published by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Willow Pattern is an atmospheric action-maze game inspired by the famous Chinese porcelain design of the same name. Known in some regions as The Willow Pattern Adventure, the game blends exploration, timing, and tension with a distinctive oriental visual style.

Players control Chang, a humble clerk navigating a multi-screen garden maze filled with danger. The objective is to locate the key, rescue Princess Koong-Shee, and escape by boat, all while avoiding relentless samurai enemies who hurl swords that can be dodged, collected, and reused as weapons. Resource management and positioning are crucial to survival.

Gameplay alternates between overhead maze exploration and focused action sequences. One of the most memorable sections is the bridge-jump sequence, where Chang must leap across stepping stones as giant hands reach up from the water below, adding pressure and variety to the pacing.

On the Commodore 64, Willow Pattern stands out for its colourful presentation and strong visual identity. The oriental-influenced music adds atmosphere and dynamically speeds up when Chang is armed, reinforcing moments of danger and urgency despite some rough sprite animation.

While its difficulty and limited weapon supply can make progress frustrating, Willow Pattern remains a distinctive and memorable budget-era release. Today, it’s fondly remembered for its striking theme, unusual mechanics, and its place among the more visually creative action-maze games on the C64.

Released in 1987 by Rainbow Arts and developed by Time Warp, The Great Giana Sisters is one of the most famous and talked-about platform games on the Commodore 64. Players guide Giana through a surreal dream world packed with hazards, enemies, and precision jumps, all in a quest to reach a giant diamond and wake from her dream.

The gameplay is classic side-scrolling platform action spread across 33 increasingly demanding levels. Giana can jump on enemies, collect gems, and use power-ups that grant new abilities such as projectile attacks or temporarily disabling foes. Tight controls and fast-paced level design demand accuracy, timing, and memorisation to progress.

On the C64, the game stood out for its smooth scrolling and colourful visuals, pushing the hardware impressively hard. Chris Hülsbeck’s soundtrack became legendary, with its energetic and memorable tunes playing a huge role in the game’s enduring reputation.

While The Great Giana Sisters was praised on release, its strong resemblance to Super Mario Bros. led to legal pressure from Nintendo, resulting in the game being withdrawn from sale in the UK. That controversy only increased its fame, cementing its status as a cult classic. Today, it’s remembered as one of the most iconic platformers of the 8-bit era and a defining title in Commodore 64 history.

All events can be played competitively by two human players, making Knight Games particularly well-suited to head-to-head sessions. Its variety of disciplines and focus on skill-based play make it a memorable example of mid-1980s arcade-style competition on the Commodore 64.

5tpXo_IEU_U.description:
🧛‍♀️🕹️ The Astonishing Adventures of Mr. Weems and the She Vampires (1987) – Commodore 64
🌐 Full game info, manual & more:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/mr-weems-and-the-she-vampires/

Released in 1987 by Piranha, The Astonishing Adventures of Mr. Weems and the She Vampires is a bizarre Gauntlet-style Commodore 64 game from RamJam Corporation involving vampires, garlic and a bespectacled hero who looks considerably more suited to doing your accounts than clearing out a vampire-infested mansion.

You control Mr. Weems as he fights his way through six levels packed with She Vampires, bats and other nasties. His main weapon is a garlic gun, while keys are needed to open locked doors and make further progress through the mansion.

Simply reaching the end isn't enough. Across the first five levels Weems must track down five essential objects — a stake, mallet, mega-garlic, mirror and crucifix — because he'll need the entire collection when he eventually reaches the lair of the Great She Vampire.

There are also garlic pills which temporarily make Weems immune to attack, giving him a brief advantage when the mansion starts filling up with enemies.

📰 The C64 version certainly didn't impress Zzap!64, which awarded the game just 19%. By 1987 there were already plenty of Gauntlet-inspired games around, and Mr. Weems was criticised heavily for offering very little that hadn't been seen before.

The game was developed by RamJam Corporation and published by Piranha, the short-lived Macmillan software label responsible for games including The Trap Door, Through the Trap Door, The Colour of Magic and Flunky.

It was also released for the ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC and later appeared under the much shorter title She Vampires.

Whatever you think of the game itself, there's certainly no shortage of personality in the idea. A bloke called Mr. Weems wandering around a mansion firing garlic at female vampires isn't a premise you're likely to confuse with too many other Commodore 64 games.

🕹️ It Came from the Desert (1989) – Commodore Amiga Cinematic Horror Adventure
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/it-came-from-the-desert/

Released in 1989 by Cinemaware for the Commodore Amiga, It Came from the Desert is a cinematic action-adventure inspired by 1950s B-movie monster films, most notably Them!. Players take on the role of Dr. Greg Bradley, a geologist investigating a mysterious meteor crash near the desert town of Lizard Breath, only to uncover a terrifying mutant ant invasion.

Gameplay blends exploration, investigation, puzzle-solving, and tense action sequences within a strict real-time structure. Over the course of just 15 in-game days, players must gather clues, question townsfolk, explore underground tunnels, and fend off giant ants in order to prevent an impending catastrophe.

A dynamic day-and-night cycle drives the narrative forward, with events unfolding whether the player is ready or not. The Amiga version stands out for its detailed artwork, atmospheric sound design, and cinematic presentation, alongside varied mini-games that reinforce the sense of urgency and storytelling.

Praised for its originality and presentation, It Came from the Desert became one of Cinemaware’s most distinctive titles. Its mix of genres, time pressure, and loving homage to classic monster movies has secured its reputation as a cult favourite among Amiga fans.

💬 Did you uncover the truth in time, or did the ants overrun Lizard Breath?

69A09BuTcCM.title: Thundercats – Lion-O Takes on Mumm-Ra in Elite’s C64 Action Game
69A09BuTcCM.description:
🕹️ ThunderCats (1987) – Commodore 64 Licensed Action Adventure from the TV Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/thundercats/

Released in 1987 by Elite Systems, ThunderCats brings the hit animated series to the Commodore 64, casting you as Lion-O on a mission to reclaim the Eye of Thundera from the evil Mumm-Ra. The game translates the show’s fantasy setting into a side-scrolling action adventure built around urgency and exploration.

Each level represents a different elemental environment, with strict time limits pushing you forward as enemies and hazards close in. Combat is straightforward, but survival depends on learning layouts, managing momentum, and reacting quickly before time runs out.

Progression is tied to rescuing fellow ThunderCats, including Tygra, Panthro, and WilyKit, who play a role in advancing the quest. While the mechanics remain simple, the game leans heavily into atmosphere, using bold colours and moody music to capture the tone of the TV series.

Often debated but fondly remembered, ThunderCats stands as a classic example of 8-bit licensed gaming. For fans of the show, it remains a nostalgic slice of Saturday-morning cartoon action on the C64.

69sB6pCe-jo.title: Smash T.V. – Cash, Prizes and a Deadly Twin-Stick Game Show | C64
69sB6pCe-jo.description:
🕹️ Smash T.V. (1991) – Commodore 64 Arcade Arena Shooter Chaos
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/smash-tv/

Released in 1991 by Ocean Software and developed by Probe Software, Smash T.V. brings the explosive Williams arcade hit to the Commodore 64. Set in a dystopian future where ultra-violent game shows rule television, you step into a deadly arena battling for cash, prizes, and survival.

The action is relentless. Enemies pour in from all directions across compact, multi-directional arenas, demanding constant movement and sharp reactions. While the C64 lacks dual-stick controls, the conversion smartly adapts movement and firing to joystick directions, delivering fast, playable combat that keeps the pressure high.

Pickups such as cash, televisions, and toasters litter the arena, rewarding aggressive play and risk-taking. Despite 8-bit limitations, the game impresses with large sprites, smooth scrolling, and satisfying explosions that capture the arcade’s intensity.

Driven by Jonathan Dunn’s punchy soundtrack, Smash T.V. stands as a standout arcade conversion and a technical achievement on the Commodore 64. It remains a favourite for fans of pure, uncompromising action.

💬 How far did you make it before the arena finally took you down?

6AXyZPb9_Xk.title: Henry’s House – Tiny C64 Platforming Inside One Very Dangerous Home
6AXyZPb9_Xk.description:
🕹️ Henry’s House (1984) – Commodore 64 Single-Screen Platform Adventure Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/henrys-house/

Released in 1984 by English Software and developed by Chris Murray for the Commodore 64, Henry’s House is a charming single-screen platform game that transforms everyday household spaces into imaginative obstacle courses. Players take control of Little Henry as he explores the rooms of his home, collecting items and avoiding quirky domestic hazards.

Gameplay revolves around clearing each room by gathering all scattered objects, which causes a key to appear. Once collected, the key unlocks the exit and allows progression to the next area. With no time limit in place, players are encouraged to move carefully, study enemy patterns, and plan safe routes through each level.

Across eight distinct rooms, Henry must dodge moving toothbrushes, toasters, coffee machines, and other animated appliances that threaten to knock him off course. Precise jumping and smart positioning are essential, as even small mistakes can send players back to the start of a room.

Visually, the game delivers colourful, playful graphics and clearly defined environments that make each screen easy to read. Responsive controls and accurate collision detection contribute to a smooth and satisfying platforming experience, especially for players who enjoy methodical, puzzle-like challenges.

Although the game loops back to the beginning after completing all rooms, its addictive design and light-hearted presentation have helped it endure as a fondly remembered C64 favourite. Today, Henry’s House remains a delightful example of early British platform game creativity.

6clC36Rc5XA.title: Rampage – Three Monsters, One Goal: Flatten the City | C64
6clC36Rc5XA.description:
🕹️ Rampage (1987) – Commodore 64 Arcade Monster City Smash-Up
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/rampage/

Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Rampage is the home computer adaptation of Bally Midway’s hugely popular arcade destruction game. Developed by Monarch Development and published by Activision, it delivers chaotic monster mayhem straight to the 8-bit era.

You take control of one of three unfortunate humans transformed into towering monsters: George the giant ape, Lizzie the colossal reptile, or Ralph the werewolf-like brute. The goal is gloriously simple—smash buildings, eat civilians, and survive relentless attacks from military forces as cities crumble beneath you.

Each city brings escalating pressure as enemies become tougher and damage mounts, forcing you to balance destruction with survival. The C64 version supports up to three players, making it perfect for shared chaos, whether you’re working together or racing to cause the most destruction.

Despite hardware limitations, Rampage on the Commodore 64 stays true to the arcade’s spirit with smooth animation, responsive controls, and addictive gameplay. It remains a standout example of how larger-than-life arcade experiences could thrive on home computers.

6dfAyKnP_Uo.title: Thing on a Spring – The C64 Platformer with a Legendary Rob Hubbard SID Tune
6dfAyKnP_Uo.description:
🕹️ Thing on a Spring (1985) – Commodore 64 Platform Puzzle Toy Factory Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/thing-on-a-spring/

Released in 1985 by Micro Projects and published by Gremlin Graphics, Thing on a Spring is a distinctive side-scrolling platformer that immediately stands out on the Commodore 64. You control Thing, a spring-based character sent into a chaotic toy factory to recover stolen puzzle pieces while surviving a maze of hazards.

Movement is the heart of the game. Thing’s ability to bounce to extreme heights transforms every screen into a timing and positioning puzzle, forcing you to think carefully about momentum, landing points, and enemy patterns rather than relying on simple jumps.

Each factory section introduces new dangers such as conveyor belts, collapsing platforms, and aggressive toy enemies. Alongside this, you must collect all nine puzzle pieces while keeping an eye on the oil meter, which drains through enemy contact and environmental traps, adding constant pressure to every decision.

The presentation elevates the experience further. Mark Rogers’ colourful graphics give the factory a playful yet threatening feel, while Rob Hubbard’s energetic SID soundtrack drives the action and tension forward. Critics at the time praised its originality, with ZZap!64 awarding an impressive 93%.

Today, Thing on a Spring is remembered as one of the most inventive platform games on the C64, blending precision platforming with puzzle-solving in a way that still feels fresh decades later.
