🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/ant-attack/

Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64 by Quicksilva, following its original 1983 Spectrum debut by Sandy White, Ant Attack is a pioneering isometric adventure that introduced true three-dimensional movement to home computer gaming.

Set in the surreal walled city of Antescher, inspired by the artwork of M. C. Escher, players choose to control either a boy or a girl on a dangerous rescue mission.

The objective is to navigate the maze-like city, avoid towering hostile ants, and locate your captured partner before time runs out.

Movement allows players to travel forward, backward, sideways, and vertically, creating a genuine sense of height and depth rarely seen at the time.

Ants can be temporarily stunned by jumping on them or by using limited grenades, though careless use can put both characters at risk.

Once the captive is found, players must carefully guide them to safety, with the rescued character following at a slight delay that demands precise navigation.

Each successful rescue increases the difficulty and relocates the hostage, keeping tension high with every new attempt.

The Commodore 64 conversion, programmed by Paul Fik and Mevlut Dinc, successfully translated the game’s ambitious design to Commodore hardware.

Praised for its clarity and speed, the port retained the eerie atmosphere and experimental spirit of the original.

Today, Ant Attack is remembered as a landmark title that helped shape early isometric and immersive game design.

CNUCOvjxd3o.title: Immerse Yourself In The Retro Vibes Of Crionics - Hardwired | Stunning Commodore Amiga Music (1991)
CNUCOvjxd3o.description:
♫ Hardwired (1991) – Commodore Amiga Demo Scene Sci-Fi & Tech Showcase
🌐 Visit the Cheeky Commodore Gamer website for retro gaming features, videos & archives:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk

Released in 1991, Hardwired is a landmark Amiga demo that saw the Silents and Crionics joining forces on a bold, cinematic production. The demo opens aboard a spacecraft drifting through time and space, where the ship’s computer awakens its captain to warn of a possible intruder—before the alien presence reveals itself from the shadows and the demo explodes into life.

What follows is a rich sequence of technical showcases that defined the era. The demo features shaded bobs, bouncing B-splines, glenz vectors that morph into evolving shapes, elastic vector spines, ray-traced toilets, twist scrollers, and flowing sin-dot animations, all carefully paced to maintain momentum and atmosphere.

One of the standout moments is Crionics’ famous “box to logo” routine, where a spinning 3D cube spills individual pixels that reform into a logo elsewhere on the screen. This sequence echoes their earlier Pictrans routine from the Crionics Megademo, later transforming into rotating 3D vectors including cubes, spacecraft, and spiky abstract forms.

Equally memorable are the bouncing 3D bobs interacting with a sagging chessboard surface, convincingly demonstrating gravity and inertia, before a robotic hand literally wipes the screen clean to transition into the next section. With music by Jesper Kyd and contributions from multiple top-tier coders and artists, Hardwired stands as a defining example of how far Amiga coders were pushing the hardware in 1991.

💬 Was Hardwired your first real glimpse of how cinematic and technical Amiga demos could be?

Gameplay revolves around a complex survival simulation rarely seen at the time. The isometric presentation reinforces the sense of isolation, with bleak alien landscapes and threatening wildlife creating constant tension. Sound design and ambient effects further heighten the atmosphere, making exploration feel dangerous and unpredictable rather than heroic.

Notorious for its steep learning curve, Robinson’s Requiem rewards patience and persistence. Today, it holds cult classic status on the Amiga, remembered for pushing survival mechanics far beyond conventional RPG design and delivering an experience that still feels uncompromising and unique.

Released in 1987 by Hewson Consultants and developed by John M. Phillips, Nebulus is a standout platform-puzzle game that pushed the Commodore 64 in bold new directions. Also known as Tower Toppler in the U.S., it introduced a striking visual concept that made it instantly recognisable.

Players control Pogo, a small green alien sent to the planet Nebulus to dismantle a series of towering structures. Each level tasks you with climbing a cylindrical tower while avoiding enemies, navigating platforms, and dealing with hazards that demand careful timing and positioning.

The game’s defining feature is its rotating tower effect. As Pogo moves left or right, the tower appears to spin in 3D, creating a constantly shifting sense of perspective that adds both challenge and tension. A single misstep can send you plunging into the water below, costing a precious life.

Between towers, players enter a submarine bonus stage, collecting fish to earn extra time for the next ascent. The presentation was widely praised on release, from its crisp graphics and smooth scrolling to Martin Galway’s energetic soundtrack, which perfectly matches the game’s pace.

Nebulus received critical acclaim, including a Gold Medal from Zzap!64, and remains one of the Commodore 64’s most admired technical achievements. Today, it’s remembered as a true classic that combined originality, skill-based gameplay, and memorable audiovisual design.

Players take control of Zak McKracken, a tabloid journalist who stumbles upon a bizarre alien conspiracy aimed at dulling human intelligence using mind-control devices. The story spans multiple real-world and off-world locations, including San Francisco, Egypt, Peru, and Mars, with players switching between characters to solve puzzles using shared logic but separate inventories.

On the Commodore 64, the game uses a colourful pixel-art style within a 16-colour palette, paired with minimal sound effects that keep focus on exploration and problem-solving. While more limited than later versions, the C64 release retains the game’s wit, inventive puzzles, and memorable scenarios that reward experimentation and careful observation.

Zak McKracken remains a cult favourite among adventure fans, praised for its originality, humour, and ambition. It stands as an important stepping stone in the evolution of story-driven games and a defining title of late-era Commodore 64 adventures.

Released in 1985 by Ocean Software and developed by Denton Designs, Frankie Goes to Hollywood is one of the most unconventional and ambitious games ever created for the Commodore 64. Inspired directly by the music, imagery, and themes of the band, it drops you into the bizarre town of Mundanesville on a symbolic journey toward the mythical Pleasuredome.

Rather than following a single genre, the game blends exploration, action, puzzles, and narrative experimentation. You play as an anonymous everyman, raising four core personality stats — Sex, War, Love, and Faith — by collecting key items and completing more than 60 wildly varied mini-games. These range from arcade-style challenges and logic puzzles to a full murder mystery subplot that adds an unexpectedly dark investigative edge.

Progression is non-linear and often cryptic, encouraging experimentation and curiosity rather than brute force. Every discovery nudges your character closer to enlightenment, making the experience feel more like an interactive art piece than a traditional videogame.

On the Commodore 64, the surreal visuals are matched by Fred Gray’s powerful SID soundtrack, which reinterprets elements of Frankie Goes to Hollywood’s music in striking 8-bit form. Celebrated for pushing creative boundaries, the game was later ranked number one in Commodore Force’s Top 100 C64 Games list and remains a landmark in interactive storytelling.

Players take on the role of vampire Jerry Dandridge, stalking the rooms of his mansion in search of victims while racing against the coming sunrise.

Gameplay focuses on room-to-room exploration, draining victims to maintain health while avoiding supernatural hazards such as crucifixes, snakes, and grasping zombie hands. Careful timing and movement are essential, as players must always ensure they can return to their coffin before daylight to recover and continue the night’s hunt.

While the core loop can feel repetitive over time and lacks a defined ending, the game’s unusual perspective and theme give it a distinctive personality.

Fright Night remains a memorable licensed title on the Amiga, blending horror imagery with straightforward arcade action and standing out as an unconventional entry in the platform’s library.

Released in 1987 by Taito and ported to the Commodore 64 by Imagine Software, Arkanoid is one of the most iconic block-breaking games of the 1980s. Players control the paddle-shaped spaceship Vaus, bouncing an energy ball to smash through colourful brick formations and clear each stage without letting the ball fall.

Gameplay is built around precision, timing, and fast reactions, with increasingly complex layouts and enemy hazards appearing as the game progresses. The introduction of power-ups such as multi-ball, laser paddles, extended bats, and speed modifiers adds strategic depth and keeps every stage feeling fresh and unpredictable.

Progression depends on mastering ball control, anticipating rebounds, and making smart use of collected upgrades. Later levels demand near-perfect positioning and concentration, rewarding skilled players with high scores and extended survival.

The Commodore 64 version closely follows the original arcade release, delivering vibrant visuals and smooth animation that capture the feel of the coin-op experience. Its atmosphere is elevated by Martin Galway’s energetic soundtrack, which remains one of the most recognisable pieces of C64 game music.

Widely praised for its addictive design and responsive controls, Arkanoid earned strong reviews and became a defining title of the block-breaker genre on home computers. Today, it stands as a timeless classic that still offers compelling pick-up-and-play fun for retro fans.

Originally created for the BBC Micro in 1983, it was later ported to multiple platforms and became a familiar sight in UK schools throughout the 1980s and 1990s.

Players embark on a text-driven quest to rescue six missing children from the clutches of an evil witch. Progress is made by navigating locations, answering questions, and solving logic-based puzzles using one-word typed responses, encouraging problem-solving, reading comprehension, and memory skills.

The Commodore 64 version preserves the simplicity and structure of the original, with minimal graphics and sound used effectively to support the atmosphere. Despite its educational purpose, the game is remembered for its unsettling tone, particularly the sudden appearances of the witch, which left a lasting impression on many players.

Granny’s Garden remains one of the most iconic examples of educational software on home computers. For many, it served as an early introduction to interactive storytelling and computer-based learning, securing its place as a nostalgic classic of the classroom computing era.

Gameplay unfolds across horizontally scrolling stages packed with enemy formations, terrain hazards, and screen-filling bosses. A defining feature is Nemesis’s revolutionary power-up system, where collected capsules activate upgrades along a selectable meter, including speed boosts, missiles, double shots, lasers, and defensive shields. The Commodore 64 version was coded by Simon Pick, with graphics by Bob Stevenson, and is widely praised for capturing the feel of the arcade original despite hardware constraints. Smooth scrolling, precise controls, and well-judged difficulty helped deliver an authentic and challenging shooter experience on 8-bit hardware.

Nemesis remains a landmark shoot ’em up, influential for its flexible power-up design and intense gameplay flow. Its impact can be seen across countless shooters that followed, cementing its reputation as one of Konami’s most important and enduring arcade conversions.

Released in 1991 by DMA Design and published by Psygnosis for the Commodore Amiga, Lemmings is a landmark puzzle-strategy game built around a deceptively simple idea. A group of lemmings march blindly forward, and it’s your job to guide as many as possible safely to the exit using a limited set of skills.

Gameplay revolves around assigning roles such as digger, builder, blocker, and climber to individual lemmings in real time. Each level becomes a carefully balanced logic puzzle where timing, placement, and forward planning are essential to success. One wrong decision can doom the entire group.

With over 100 levels included, the difficulty steadily ramps up, introducing new hazards and tighter constraints that demand increasingly creative solutions. The intuitive interface and expressive animations make the game easy to understand, while the puzzle design provides long-lasting depth and challenge.

On the Amiga, Lemmings stands out for its smooth performance, clear visuals, and memorable presentation. The charming character animations and distinctive sound effects helped give the game a strong personality, making failure just as entertaining as success.

Today, Lemmings is regarded as one of the most influential games of all time. Its massive commercial success led to numerous sequels and spin-offs, and it remains a defining title of the Amiga era and a cornerstone of puzzle game design.

dDpqixaUnvY.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/the-sentinel/

Released in 1986 by Firebird Software and developed by Geoff Crammond, The Sentinel is a groundbreaking puzzle strategy game that pushed the Commodore 64 into entirely new territory. It was one of the first home computer games to use solid-filled 3D graphics, delivering a surreal and unsettling experience unlike anything else at the time.

Players control a synthoid exploring abstract, chessboard-like landscapes rendered in a striking pseudo-3D perspective. The objective is to climb the terrain by absorbing energy from trees, rocks, and other objects, creating new synthoids and strategically relocating across the landscape until the Sentinel itself can be absorbed.

Tension comes from the Sentinel’s constant surveillance. If it spots the player, it begins draining energy, forcing careful planning, positioning, and timing. Energy management is central to survival, with every move carrying risk and long-term consequences.

With 10,000 unique levels generated from a compact rule set, The Sentinel offers near-endless challenge and replayability. Its minimalist soundscape and stark visuals enhance the eerie atmosphere, cementing its reputation as one of the most intellectually demanding and influential puzzle games on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1985 by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64, Mail Order Monsters is an innovative action-strategy game designed by Paul Reiche III, Evan Robinson, and Nicky Robinson. The game places creativity at the centre of its design, allowing players to construct and customise their own combat creatures, known as morphs, before sending them into brutal arena battles.

Gameplay revolves around three distinct modes that cater to different skill levels. Free Trial mode introduces pre-built morphs and basic combat mechanics, while Rental mode gives players a limited budget of psychons to assemble a creature for a single fight. Tournament mode offers the deepest experience, challenging players to build, upgrade, and evolve their morph across multiple battles while managing resources and long-term strategy.

Combat takes place in a variety of arena formats, including Destruction, Capture the Flag, and The Horde, each demanding different tactics and loadouts. Players can choose from a wide range of morph types, such as towering Tyros, fast-moving Arachnids, and resilient Amoeboids, each with unique strengths and weaknesses.

Customisation is the game’s defining feature, with players able to purchase weapons, armour, tentacles, jetpacks, and special abilities to shape their ideal fighting monster. Every design choice affects movement, attack options, and survivability, encouraging experimentation and replayability.

Mail Order Monsters earned a lasting cult following thanks to its depth, originality, and player-driven creativity. Today, it’s widely regarded as a forward-thinking classic and an early forerunner to modern creature-building and competitive battler games on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1983 by Argus Press Software Ltd and developed by P. Rawling, Bismark is a strategic naval warfare game that challenges players to outthink rather than outgun their enemy. Also known as Strategy II, it places careful planning and intelligence gathering at the heart of the experience.

You command a fleet of twelve Allied ships tasked with locating and sinking the German battleship Bismarck before time runs out. The action unfolds on a 20×15 grid representing the North Atlantic, where every movement must be considered as you patrol sea lanes, avoid threats, and close in on your target.

Rather than fast-paced action, Bismark focuses on tactical decision-making and resource management. Players must interpret limited information, position ships effectively, and anticipate the Bismarck’s movements, creating constant tension as the clock ticks down.

The game formed part of Argus Press’s Strategy 1 series, designed to bring accessible but demanding strategy titles to home computers. Its later inclusion in the 30 Games compilation introduced it to a wider audience and helped secure its place in early Commodore 64 history.

Today, Bismark is remembered as a thoughtful and challenging strategy game that rewards patience and planning, standing as a reminder of how engaging early computer-based war games could be.

Released in 1984 by Llamasoft and developed by Jeff Minter, Sheep in Space is a horizontally scrolling shoot-’em-up that puts a surreal twist on classic arcade action. Players control a genetically engineered combat sheep defending a planetary colony from waves of invading droids.

Inspired by Defender, the game spans 48 levels, each requiring the destruction of 16 enemies before progressing. Alongside a standard blaster and shield, the sheep can perform a “DJump,” instantly warping to the nearest hostile for rapid attacks and emergency escapes. A distinctive survival mechanic adds pressure, as the sheep must regularly land on grassy areas to feed when hunger levels drop.

Managing energy is critical, as becoming famished weakens the player, while overeating leads to an explosive end. This balance between combat and survival creates a rhythm that keeps players constantly engaged. The visuals combine high-resolution and bitmap graphics, giving the game a distinctive look, while the soundtrack by James Lisney reinforces the otherworldly tone.

Although opinions were divided on release, Sheep in Space has since earned cult status among Commodore 64 fans. Its unusual mechanics and unmistakable Llamasoft identity make it a memorable entry in the C64 shoot-’em-up library.

Released in 1985 by Lucasfilm Games, Koronis Rift is a pioneering 3D action-strategy game that pushed the Commodore 64 into bold new territory. Set in the year 2049, players take on the role of a rover pilot exploring the dangerous Koronis Rift on an alien world, tasked with uncovering the remains of an ancient civilisation hidden deep within hostile terrain.

Gameplay blends real-time exploration with careful planning. Players must descend into twenty increasingly dangerous rifts, locating long-lost alien hulks and salvaging powerful modules to upgrade the rover. Each module serves a specific function, from improved shields and weapons to navigation and mapping tools, making preparation just as important as piloting skill.

A core mechanic is the colour-coded module system, which determines compatibility and effectiveness against enemy saucers guarding the hulks. With limited space to carry equipment, players are forced to make tactical choices, adapting their loadout to survive each mission and uncover deeper secrets.

Koronis Rift is especially remembered for its fractal-generated landscapes, building on technology first seen in Rescue on Fractalus!. The rolling terrain created a genuine sense of scale and immersion, while Douglas Crockford’s atmospheric sound design heightened the tension of exploration. Widely praised for its originality and depth, Koronis Rift remains one of the most ambitious and influential science-fiction games on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1990 by Rainbow Arts for the Commodore 64, Curse of Ra is a distinctive top-down puzzle game set deep within an ancient Egyptian pyramid. Players control a scarab beetle navigating fixed-screen chambers, tasked with clearing every stone from the board by matching pairs of identical symbols aligned horizontally or vertically.

The puzzle design gradually increases in complexity, introducing immovable blocks, teleporters, slippery tiles, and other hazards that require careful planning rather than quick reflexes. Each room becomes a test of logic and foresight, rewarding players who think several moves ahead.

The game offers two clearly defined modes. Logic Mode features over 100 untimed levels focused purely on problem-solving, while Arcade Mode introduces time limits across 75 stages, alongside collectible coins that can be spent on power-ups between rounds. This dual structure caters to both relaxed puzzle fans and players seeking a faster-paced challenge.

A standout feature is the built-in level editor, allowing players to design and share their own custom puzzles. Combined with detailed graphics by Arnold Franz Sakowski and atmospheric music by Rudolf Stember, Curse of Ra remains one of the most inventive and memorable puzzle titles on the Commodore 64.

Praised for its technical polish and pure arcade thrills, Lotus Turbo Challenge 2 is widely regarded as one of the finest racing games on the Amiga. Its accessible controls and relentless pace have secured it a lasting place among retro racing favourites.

Released in 1986 by Lucasfilm Games and published by Activision for the Commodore 64, Labyrinth: The Computer Game is a graphic adventure inspired by Jim Henson’s fantasy film. Players are dropped into a sprawling maze filled with traps, riddles, and strange characters, racing against time to confront Jareth and escape.

The adventure unfolds under a strict 13-hour real-time limit, adding tension and urgency to every decision. Gameplay begins with a text-based sequence before shifting into a graphical exploration format, featuring side-scrolling corridors, interactive environments, and a radar bar that maps each area.

A standout feature is the innovative “word wheel” interface, which replaces traditional text parsers with rotating menus of verbs and nouns. This system streamlines command input, reduces frustration, and makes experimentation more accessible for players new to adventure games.

Visually, Labyrinth delivers detailed environments and expressive animations that were highly regarded at the time. Its design philosophy and interface ideas helped shape future Lucasfilm titles, directly influencing the development of the SCUMM engine used in later classics.

Despite criticism for long loading times and a slower pace, the game is now recognised as a pioneering entry in the genre. Today, it stands as an important milestone in adventure gaming and a key part of Lucasfilm Games’ early legacy.

Building on the success of the original Hunchback, this sequel expands the formula into a series of varied, skill-based challenge stages rather than a single looping screen. It was designed specifically to showcase the strengths of the C64.

You once again control Quasimodo as he navigates swinging ropes, collapsing platforms, arrow traps, and precision jumps across multiple distinct events. Each stage introduces new mechanics, demanding fast reactions, sharp timing, and strong memorisation.

Visually, the game delivers clean sprite work, smooth scrolling, and clearly readable hazards — essential for high-speed arcade gameplay and competitive score-chasing.

On the Commodore 64, Hunchback II is widely regarded as a more ambitious and technically confident sequel, cementing its place as a classic of mid-80s British arcade conversions and a firm favourite among retro enthusiasts.

Released in 1991 for the Commodore 64, American 3D Pool is an ambitious cue sports game developed by Zeppelin Games that attempted something rarely seen on 8-bit hardware: a first-person, pseudo-3D pool simulation. Instead of the usual overhead view, the game places players right at table level, emphasising depth, angles, and shot precision.

Gameplay revolves around realistic aiming, power control, and judging perspective. The 3D-style camera changes how shots are lined up, forcing players to think carefully about spin, force, and positioning rather than relying on simple top-down geometry. This approach added a surprising amount of strategy and skill to each frame of play.

Technically, American 3D Pool pushes the Commodore 64 hard, using clever shading and perspective tricks to create the illusion of depth on an 8-bit system. While performance is naturally limited by the hardware, the table, balls, and collision physics feel convincing for the era, with simple but effective sound effects reinforcing each shot.

Although niche, American 3D Pool is remembered as a bold and experimental title that stood apart from other sports games on the C64. Its immersive presentation and technical ambition helped pave the way for more realistic cue sports simulations in later generations.

EeNXSvcKuD4.title: Did 1988 Change Zzap!64 Forever? 55 C64 & Amiga Award Winners
EeNXSvcKuD4.description:
🕹️ Every Commodore 64 and Amiga game that received a Zzap!64 Gold Medal, Sizzler, Silver Medal or 16-bit Sizzler during 1988 — all 55 award-winning entries revisited month by month.

After the strange scoring droughts of 1987, Zzap!64 returned in 1988 with considerably more awards, several enormous review scores and a magazine that was beginning to change.

The Commodore 64 was still producing major releases, but the Amiga was no longer sitting quietly in the background. The 16-bit coverage was growing, Jaz Rignall departed after 39 issues, and by the end of the year Zzap!64 seemed to be covering two different generations of Commodore gaming at once.

In this video, I go through every qualifying award from January to the Christmas Special, including all the Gold Medals, standard Sizzlers, budget Silver Medals, 16-bit Sizzlers and the year’s single 16-bit Gold Medal.

That means Commodore 64 classics and cult favourites including Combat School, Driller, Tetris, Hunter’s Moon, Platoon, Project Stealth Fighter, Cybernoid, Impossible Mission II, The Great Giana Sisters, Barbarian II, Hawkeye, Last Ninja 2, Salamander, Wasteland, Katakis, Armalyte, Bombuzal and many more.

The growing Amiga coverage also brings in games including Time Bandit, Buggy Boy, Carrier Command, Starglider 2, StarRay, Ultima IV, Fish!, Corruption, Ingrid’s Back, Nebulus, Rocket Ranger, Cybernoid and Impossible Mission II.

There are some major questions along the way.

Was Hawkeye really worth 96%?
Should Bruce Lee have received a Gold Medal instead of Silver?
Did Last Ninja 2 deserve more than 94%?
Was The Great Giana Sisters fairly rewarded, or was it sailing slightly too close to Super Mario Bros?
And did the increasing Amiga coverage improve Zzap!64, or was the magazine beginning to drift away from the Commodore 64?

For me, 1988 is the crossover year.

The C64 was still receiving superb games from programmers who knew the hardware inside out, while the Amiga was beginning to show why so many players would eventually move across. Games such as Armalyte, Bombuzal, The Great Giana Sisters and Last Ninja 2 proved the breadbin was nowhere near finished, while Starglider 2 and Rocket Ranger offered a glimpse of where computer gaming was heading next.

Originally developed by Irem and released in arcades in 1984, Kung-Fu Master arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1985 via a conversion by Berkeley Softworks, with Chris Hawley handling the port. Published by U.S. Gold in Europe, it brought one of arcade gaming’s most influential action titles to home computers.

Players step into the role of Thomas, a martial arts expert fighting his way through the five floors of the Devil’s Temple to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend, Sylvia. Each level throws relentless waves of enemies into the action, from knife throwers and grippers to powerful end-of-floor bosses that test timing and positioning.

The gameplay is fast, direct, and demanding, relying on punches, kicks, jumps, and crouches to survive the constant pressure. Despite the Commodore 64’s technical limits, the conversion delivers colourful visuals and a tense background soundtrack that maintain the urgency of the arcade experience.

As one of the earliest and most influential examples of the beat-’em-up genre, Kung-Fu Master helped define side-scrolling action games that followed. Its legacy is still felt today, and it remains a cornerstone title for fans of classic arcade combat.

💬 How far did you make it up the Devil’s Temple before the enemies overwhelmed you?

Released in 1985 by Konami for the Commodore 64, Hyper Sports is the sequel to the hugely popular Track & Field and delivers a fast-paced collection of Olympic-themed events straight from the arcade. You compete across a series of demanding challenges, pushing for qualifying scores just to stay in the competition.

The game features a varied lineup of events including swimming, skeet shooting, vaulting, archery, triple jump, and weightlifting, each with its own timing-based mechanics. Success depends on precision, rhythm, and endurance, with difficulty ramping up sharply as you progress through the tournament.

On the C64, Hyper Sports stands out as a strong arcade conversion, offering smooth movement, responsive controls, and clear event visuals that keep the action readable even under pressure. Every event tests a different skill, keeping the experience tense and competitive throughout.

The atmosphere is lifted even further by Martin Galway’s iconic SID soundtrack, featuring an energetic take on “Chariots of Fire” that perfectly matches the game’s sporting intensity. While not every arcade feature made it across, the overall package remains compelling.

Today, Hyper Sports is remembered as one of the defining multi-event sports games on the Commodore 64, celebrated for its challenge, presentation, and enduring arcade spirit.

Combat centres around a mix of close-range and ranged weapons, including knives, firearms, and grenades, which must be collected and used carefully. Enemies are persistent, and success often comes down to learning patterns and managing limited space rather than brute force alone.

While the presentation and controls were criticised at the time for feeling stiff and slow, COBRA still captures the raw attitude of its source material. Today, it stands as a familiar example of 1980s movie licensing on the Commodore 64, remembered more for its atmosphere and theme than refined mechanics.

eKrtrWzuEXQ.title: M.U.L.E. – Compete for Wealth, Cooperate to Save the Colony | C64

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/mule/

Released in 1983 by Ozark Softscape and published by Electronic Arts, M.U.L.E. is a landmark multiplayer strategy game designed by Danielle Bunten (credited as Dan Bunten). Set on the fictional planet Irata, players become rival colonists competing to build a thriving economy through careful planning, negotiation, and cooperation.

Gameplay is split between two contrasting phases. In the real-time auction, players bid aggressively for plots of land, while the turn-based phase focuses on managing resources using M.U.L.E.s to produce food, energy, smithore, and crystite. Balancing production with market demand is essential, especially as unexpected events such as pirate raids and meteor showers disrupt even the best-laid plans.

Supporting up to four players, M.U.L.E. shines as a social experience, encouraging deals, rivalries, and shifting alliances. Success depends not only on strategy, but on reading opponents and adapting to an ever-changing economy.

Praised for its originality and depth, M.U.L.E. remains one of the most influential strategy games ever made. Its innovative design and multiplayer focus continue to be celebrated as a defining moment in Commodore 64 gaming history.

💬 Were you the generous trader, or the ruthless tycoon who cornered the market?

Players guide Bruce Lee through a series of 20 single-screen rooms, collecting lanterns to unlock new areas on the path to confronting an evil wizard. Each room is carefully designed, combining vertical movement, environmental hazards, and enemy encounters that demand timing and control rather than brute force.

Bruce is constantly pursued by two iconic foes: the agile Ninja and the powerful Green Yamo, a sumo wrestler. Combat revolves around punches and flying kicks, while players must also contend with electrified walls, collapsing floors, and explosive traps that punish careless movement.

The game also includes a two-player mode, allowing one player to control Yamo, adding a competitive edge and extra replay value. With responsive joystick controls, smart level design, and a strong sense of balance between action and strategy, Bruce Lee earned its reputation as one of the Commodore 64’s standout titles.

EpkUyLF-VsQ.description:
🕹️ 25 of the hardest Commodore 64 games ever made — brutal C64 classics that tested your patience, joystick, memory and sanity.

This video dives into some of the most difficult games ever released on the Commodore 64: the ones that did not just challenge you, but punished every mistake. From pixel-perfect platformers and relentless shoot ’em ups to awkward controls, strict time limits, unforgiving level design and almost no mercy, these are the C64 games that pushed players to their absolute limit.

Featured in this countdown are notoriously difficult Commodore 64 games such as The Last V8, Airwolf, The Human Race, China Miner, Cauldron, Monty on the Run, Raid Over Moscow, Booty, Uridium, Spindizzy, Spelunker, Manic Miner, Jet Set Willy, IO, Shadow of the Beast, RoboCop, Cybernoid, Army Moves, Ghosts ’n Goblins, Green Beret, Cauldron II, Ninja Spirit, Cobra and more.

Back in the 8-bit era, difficulty was often part of the experience. There were no generous checkpoints, no endless continues, no quick saves, and very little forgiveness. Progress came through repetition, memorisation, timing, stubbornness, and the occasional urge to launch a joystick at the wall.

Some of these games were brilliantly designed challenges. Others were difficult for less flattering reasons. But all of them became part of the Commodore 64 experience, whether you loved them, hated them, or never made it past the first few screens.

So were these the hardest C64 games ever made? Or did I miss the one that ruined your childhood?

The operation unfolds across three carefully linked phases. First, you position snipers across the street to silently remove threats without endangering civilians. Hostages blends strategy, stealth, and action in a way that was ambitious for its time. Every mistake carries consequences, and success depends on patience, observation, and controlled execution rather than fast reflexes alone.

On the Amiga, the game delivers strong atmosphere and mounting tension through its sound design and methodical pacing. Despite some stiffness in movement, Hostages is remembered as a bold and influential title that helped shape the future of tactical and squad-based shooters.

EtAWlL343Lo.title: Toy Bizarre – The Activision C64 Platformer Set in a Toy Factory Gone Mad
EtAWlL343Lo.description:
🕹️ Toy Bizarre (1984) – Commodore 64 Platform Arcade Factory Challenge
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/toy-bizarre/

Released in 1984 by Activision for the Commodore 64, Toy Bizarre is a platform-based arcade game set inside a chaotic toy factory brought to life after hours. Designed by Mark Turmell, the game casts players as a lone night watchman tasked with stopping malfunctioning toys before the factory descends into complete disorder.

Gameplay centres on navigating multi-level platforms while managing factory systems in real time. Players must shut off valves to stop new toys being released, use pistons to deactivate roaming toys, and carefully time jumps to stun enemies temporarily. Each screen demands planning and awareness, as poorly managed valves can quickly overwhelm the factory floor.

A unique time-based structure divides the game into hourly shifts, with difficulty steadily increasing as the night progresses. The balance between movement, enemy control, and system management gives Toy Bizarre a distinctive rhythm that rewards calm decision-making over reckless play.

On the Commodore 64, the game delivers colourful sprites and fluid animation that clearly communicate the factory’s moving parts. The presentation draws inspiration from early arcade platformers while carving out its own identity through mechanical interactions and escalating tension.

Toy Bizarre may appear simple at first glance, but its clever design and addictive gameplay loop have secured it a lasting reputation among retro fans. Today, it stands as a memorable example of Activision’s early creativity on the C64 and a platformer that rewards skillful control under pressure.

Released in 1983 for the Commodore 64, GORF is a home conversion of the 1981 arcade hit originally developed by Dave Nutting Associates and produced by Midway, with its name standing for Galactic Orbiting Robot Force.

Players pilot a starship in a series of fixed-screen shooting missions, combining fast reflexes with tactical positioning in the lower portion of the screen.

The game features four distinct mission styles inspired by classics such as Space Invaders, Galaxian, and Phoenix, creating a varied and constantly evolving arcade experience.

A unique gameplay mechanic allows the quark laser to cancel existing shots when fired again, adding an extra layer of strategy to defensive play.

Stages range from classic alien formations to hyperspace warp sequences and intense boss encounters, keeping each round fresh and challenging.

The Commodore 64 version is especially notable for supporting speech synthesis via the Magic Voice or Votrax module, making it the only home port to feature in-game voice effects.

This rare audio feature, combined with escalating difficulty and player rank promotions, gives GORF a distinctive personality on the platform.

While visually simple, the game’s strong pacing, mechanical depth, and arcade accuracy helped it stand out among early 8-bit shooters.

Today, GORF is remembered as a beloved multi-stage shooter that blends familiar arcade traditions with innovative twists on the Commodore 64.

EuiU6Tc_RN0.title: These Arcade Games Felt Amazing… Until They Came Home | C64 & Amiga Ports
EuiU6Tc_RN0.description:
🕹️ Classic arcade games reviewed against their Commodore 64 and Amiga home ports — from Out Run and R-Type to Golden Axe, Double Dragon, Space Harrier and more.

Arcade games in the 1980s and early 1990s were built to impress: big cabinets, bold graphics, fast action, custom hardware, loud sound and that magical feeling of putting 10p or 20p into a machine that looked miles ahead of anything at home.

But when those arcade games came home to the Commodore 64 and Amiga, the experience often changed. This video looks at some of my favourite arcade games from the 80s and early 90s, comparing the original arcade versions with their C64 and Amiga ports.

Featured games include Dragon’s Lair, Out Run, After Burner, Space Harrier, R-Type, Golden Axe, Double Dragon, Rolling Thunder, Street Fighter and Splatterhouse.

Some home versions tried to recreate the arcade spectacle as closely as possible. Others had to take a completely different approach to make the game work on 8-bit and 16-bit home computer hardware.  Sometimes that meant a surprisingly playable version. Sometimes it meant missing speed, smaller sprites, weaker sound, changed level structure, awkward controls, or a conversion that could never really match the machine in the arcade.

Across the Commodore 64 and Amiga, we look at how speed, visuals, sound, controls and gameplay changed between arcade and home versions — and why some ports still hold up better than others today.

This is not just about which version looked best. It is about what survived the journey home, what was lost, and which arcade ports still deserve respect.

Released in 1982 by Commodore for the Commodore 64, Visible Solar System is an early educational software title designed to function as a digital planetarium. It allows users to explore the layout of the solar system and observe planets and their moons from different perspectives.

The program presents a visual model of the solar system, featuring basic animation such as planetary rotation and orbital movement. Users can zoom in on major bodies including Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, gaining a closer look at their appearance and relative positions in space.

Rather than focusing on traditional gameplay, Visible Solar System emphasises visual exploration and curiosity-driven learning. It does not include quizzes, missions, or detailed scientific explanations, instead encouraging users to observe and interact with the simulation at their own pace.

While its graphics and presentation are simple by modern standards, they represented an impressive technical achievement for early home computers. The minimalist design, combined with the absence of sound, gives the program a calm and distinctive atmosphere.

Today, Visible Solar System is best viewed as a historical snapshot of early educational computing. It reflects how the Commodore 64 was used not only for games, but also as a tool for learning and discovery during the early 1980s.

Released in 1984 by Llamasoft and developed by Jeff Minter, Revenge of the Mutant Camels is a horizontally scrolling shoot ’em up that cranks the absurdity to full blast. A direct sequel to Attack of the Mutant Camels, the game puts players in control of a heavily armed camel battling through 42 waves of surreal and unpredictable enemies.

Gameplay is fast, frantic, and deliberately offbeat. Players fire basic blue shots while weaving through enemies that range from falling umbrellas and vending machines to flying toilets, all rendered in Minter’s unmistakable psychedelic style. Power-ups boost firepower, but danger also comes in the form of tokens that can poison the player or reverse controls, keeping every moment unpredictable.

A standout feature is the optional two-player mode, where a second player controls a bipedal goat riding atop the camel, doubling firepower and adding a unique cooperative twist rarely seen in shooters of the era. The constantly shifting visuals and escalating difficulty demand sharp reflexes and adaptability.

Challenging, bizarre, and packed with personality, Revenge of the Mutant Camels has earned cult-classic status on the Commodore 64, standing as a prime example of Jeff Minter’s uncompromisingly original approach to game design.

Released in 1987, developed by Beam Software and published by Melbourne House, Street Hassle is a side-scrolling beat ’em up that takes the usual street-fighting formula and makes it considerably stranger.

Your job is simple enough: walk through the city and deal with anybody foolish enough to get in your way. The opposition, however, is anything but ordinary. Alongside the expected street thugs you’ll encounter gorillas, towering basketball players, dogs, motorcyclists and elderly ladies armed with handbags.

Combat gives you a surprisingly varied selection of attacks, with punches, kicks and some decidedly unconventional moves available as you work your way through each stage. There’s also a two-player option, with players taking turns to tackle the streets.

Street Hassle was developed by Australian studio Beam Software and was also released under the names Bop ’N Rumble and Bad Street Brawler in other territories. Neil Brennan provides the C64 soundtrack, while the game’s exaggerated characters and bizarre opponents give it an identity very different from more serious beat ’em ups of the period.

It may not be the first C64 fighting game that springs to mind, but Street Hassle is certainly difficult to forget once you’ve seen a muscular bloke fighting gorillas and handbag-wielding pensioners in the middle of the street.

Released in 1992 by Delphine Software International for the Commodore Amiga, Flashback is a landmark cinematic platformer designed by Paul Cuisset. Blending rotoscoped animation, science-fiction storytelling, and methodical puzzle-platforming, it pushed narrative and technical boundaries on home computers.

Set in a distant future, players take control of Conrad B. Hart, an agent who awakens on Titan with no memory of his past. As he journeys through futuristic cities, dense jungles, and alien environments, Conrad must survive hostile forces while uncovering a hidden conspiracy involving shape-shifting invaders.

Gameplay combines precise movement, environmental puzzles, and tactical combat. Players must carefully time jumps, manage limited ammunition, and use tools like shields and weapons to overcome enemies. Progress often depends on observation, patience, and mastering the game’s deliberate pacing.

Visually, Flashback stands out for its smooth rotoscoped character animation and cinematic presentation. Detailed backgrounds, subtle lighting, and atmospheric sound design create a noir-inspired sci-fi tone that draws players deeply into its world. Voice samples and cutscenes further enhance the storytelling.

Widely praised on release, Flashback became one of the defining titles of the Amiga era. Its blend of technical excellence, emotional storytelling, and challenging gameplay secured its reputation as one of the greatest cinematic platformers ever made and a true classic of retro gaming.

Players take control of Trogg, a caveman armed not with clubs or spears, but a yo-yo, on a mission to retrieve three keys from each increasingly hazardous level.

Gameplay focuses on careful movement across ladders and platforms arranged in deliberately awkward layouts. Trogg’s yo-yo acts as both a weapon and a tool, used to dispatch enemies and interact with the environment, demanding precision and timing rather than speed alone.

Each level is packed with strange hazards, including static enemies such as Scrubbly, Poglet, and Hooter, alongside moving threats like balloons and flying daggers. Touching any obstacle results in instant death, and a strict time limit keeps pressure high. When time runs out, darkness gradually closes in, making navigation far more dangerous unless light bulbs are collected to extend visibility.

Frak! is best remembered for its originality and distinctive personality rather than mainstream success. Its mix of experimentation, challenge, and memorable design has earned it a lasting cult following among Commodore 64 fans and platform game enthusiasts.

After covering Zzap!64’s first year of Gold Medals and Sizzlers in 1985, we now move into 1986: Zzap’s first full calendar year, and one of the most varied years in Commodore 64 history.

From Uridium, Mercenary, Leaderboard and Ghosts ’n Goblins to World Games, The Sentinel, Thrust, Kikstart II, International Karate, Sanxion, Dan Dare, Spindizzy, Cauldron II, Alter Ego, Ultima IV, Green Beret, Ballblazer, Koronis Rift, The Eidolon, Revs and many more, this is Zzap!64’s 1986 C64 awards revisited.

Back in the 1980s, a Zzap!64 Sizzler or Gold Medal really mattered. These awards helped shape what Commodore 64 owners wanted to play, what got talked about in playgrounds, what sold in computer shops, and what still gets debated decades later.

Some of these 1986 awards still feel fully deserved today. Others feel generous, strange, controversial, or very tied to the standards and expectations of the time.

This is not just a normal “best C64 games” list. It is a full look back at what Zzap!64 considered the best Commodore 64 games of 1986 — including the Gold Medals, the Sizzlers, the obvious classics, and a few scores that still deserve a debate today.

fFaWqRkVCIU.title: North & South – The Amiga Civil War Game You Didn’t Know Came from a Belgian Comic
fFaWqRkVCIU.description:
🕹️ North & South (1989) – Commodore Amiga Strategy Action Civil War Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/north-south/

Released in 1989 by Infogrames for the Commodore Amiga, North & South is a distinctive blend of strategy and action inspired by the Belgian comic series Les Tuniques Bleues. It presents a lighthearted and humorous take on the American Civil War, combining tactical planning with fast-paced arcade-style challenges.

Gameplay is divided into two interconnected phases. On the strategic map, players move armies across the United States, capturing states, forts, and railway lines in order to weaken the opposition and secure vital resources. Careful positioning and timing play a major role in long-term success.

When opposing forces meet, the game shifts into real-time action sequences. These include battlefield skirmishes, fort assaults, and train-capture missions, each requiring quick reflexes and smart use of infantry, cavalry, and artillery units with distinct strengths and weaknesses.

Throughout the campaign, humorous animations and unexpected events reflect the game’s comic book roots, adding personality and charm to every encounter. This balance of light-hearted presentation and tactical depth gives North & South its unique identity.

Supporting both single-player and two-player modes, the game encourages competitive and cooperative play alike. Today, North & South is remembered as one of the Amiga’s most inventive strategy titles and a classic example of accessible, character-driven game design.

💬 Did you prefer dominating the map through strategy, or winning wars in the action sequences?

Players take control of the armoured Black Knight, battling through dangerous medieval environments packed with enemies and deadly traps.

Gameplay focuses on precise movement, careful timing, and fast reactions. Each screen presents new hazards, from hostile creatures to narrow platforms and sudden drops, forcing players to learn patterns and master positioning in order to survive. Progress depends heavily on skill and persistence.

The game’s level design encourages strategic play, rewarding patience and memorisation. Mistakes are costly, and success comes from learning enemy behaviour, judging jumps accurately, and choosing when to advance or retreat.

Visually, Black Knight makes strong use of the C64’s capabilities, featuring detailed character sprites and smoothly animated medieval settings. Atmospheric sound effects and music help reinforce the sense of danger and isolation as players push deeper into the quest.

As a classic example of 1980s arcade-style difficulty, Black Knight remains a memorable challenge for retro fans. It stands as a reminder of an era when games demanded mastery, endurance, and determination from anyone brave enough to see them through.

Released in 1990, Defenders of the Earth is a side-scrolling action platformer for the Commodore 64, developed by Enigma Variations and published by Hi-Tec Software. Based on the animated television series, the game brings together legendary heroes Flash Gordon, Mandrake the Magician, Lothar, and the Phantom as they attempt to rescue their kidnapped children from the clutches of Ming the Merciless.

Players mainly take control of Flash Gordon, fighting through Ming’s fortress across enemy-filled screens packed with traps and demanding platforming sections. Progress isn’t just about combat, as players must regularly call upon the other Defenders to overcome obstacles and solve environmental challenges.

Each hero has a specific ability that is essential for advancement. Mandrake can conjure bridges to cross gaps, Lothar can smash through solid barriers, and the Phantom can unlock sealed doors. Switching between these powers adds a puzzle-like layer to the action and encourages careful planning rather than constant forward momentum.

The game is visually faithful to the TV series, with recognisable characters and detailed backdrops, but it received mixed reviews on release. While presentation was often praised, criticism focused on repetitive gameplay and a punishing difficulty curve, with Zzap!64 awarding it a score of 43%. Today, it’s remembered as a tough licensed title that aimed high and remains an interesting curiosity in the Commodore 64 catalogue.

Released in 1984 by Software Projects, Thrusta is a demanding gravity-based space shooter inspired by arcade classics like Gravitar. You pilot a small spacecraft through tightly designed caverns, with smooth 360-degree scrolling that evokes the feel of vector-based games such as Asteroids.

The objective is deceptively simple: collect a bomb and deliver it to the target zone. In practice, every movement is affected by gravity, forcing you to carefully manage thrust, momentum, and fuel while avoiding walls, hazards, and tight passages. Precision control is essential, and even small mistakes can quickly end a run.

Thrusta builds constant tension through its physics-driven gameplay, rewarding patience, skill, and mastery rather than quick reflex shooting. Each level increases the challenge, pushing you to refine your control and plan every manoeuvre.

Widely praised for its design and difficulty, Thrusta earned strong critical acclaim and remains one of the Commodore 64’s most respected skill-based space games. Today, it stands as a standout example of how simple mechanics can deliver deep, satisfying gameplay.

Released in 1984 by Activision for the Commodore 64, Pitfall II: Lost Caverns is the acclaimed sequel to the original Pitfall!, developed by David Crane and designed around exploration and discovery rather than simple score chasing.

Players take control of Pitfall Harry as he ventures deep into the caverns of the Andes to rescue his niece Rhonda and her pet mountain lion, Quickclaw, while searching for the legendary Raj Diamond.

The game features a vast interconnected world of over 100 screens, encouraging free exploration through swimming tunnels, climbing ropes, riding balloons, and navigating hidden passages. Progress depends on careful observation and learning the map layout.

A major innovation is the checkpoint system, which allows players to restart from the last red cross reached after losing a life. This makes the adventure more forgiving and supports longer play sessions.

The dynamic soundtrack changes as players move through different areas and uncover secrets, adding atmosphere and a sense of progression rarely seen in early platform games.

Visually, the C64 version delivers clear environments, smooth movement, and well-designed hazards including scorpions, bats, frogs, and electric eels. The presentation supports both precision platforming and exploration.

Praised for its ambitious design and technical innovation, Pitfall II helped redefine what console-style platform adventures could achieve on home computers.

Today, it’s remembered as one of the finest exploration-based platformers on the Commodore 64 and a landmark title in Activision’s catalogue.

China Miner (1984), developed by Ian Gray and published by Interceptor Software, is a notoriously tough single-screen platform game for the Commodore 64.

Players control Wally, the sole keeper of the secret location of the Jade Mines of the Pong Dynasty, as he navigates 30 dangerous screens in search of vital objects and an exit key.

Each level requires you to collect essential items such as lanterns, pickaxes, and jade artefacts before unlocking the route forward, all while avoiding enemies, lasers, collapsing platforms, and deadly falls.

Touching an enemy costs a life and resets all collected objects, making precision, memory, and patience essential to progress.

The game’s unforgiving difficulty, flick-screen level design, and tightly timed jumps earned it a reputation as one of the C64’s most challenging platformers.

With atmospheric music by Chris Cox and classic early-80s Commodore visuals, China Miner remains a favourite among players who enjoy mastering tough, pattern-based gameplay.

Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Renegade is a home computer adaptation of Technōs Japan’s 1986 arcade hit, developed by Ocean Software under the Imagine label. The C64 version features programming by Max Taylor, graphics by Stephen Wahid and Jane Lowe, and a hard-hitting soundtrack by Fred Gray.

Players take on the role of a lone street fighter battling through five distinct stages to rescue a kidnapped girlfriend. Action unfolds across gritty locations such as subways, docks, and alleyways, with waves of enemies attacking from both sides. Combat allows for punches, kicks, jump attacks, and grabs, giving players a surprising amount of tactical freedom for the time.

The Commodore 64 conversion was widely praised for capturing the feel of the arcade original, delivering fluid animation and responsive movement. While the control scheme required use of the space bar for certain actions, many players appreciated the depth and challenge this added to the fighting system.

Renegade is now recognised as a foundational title in the beat-’em-up genre, directly influencing later classics such as Double Dragon. Its impact on side-scrolling fighting games secures its place as a key release in retro gaming history.

Players take on the role of Super Joe, a lone soldier battling through enemy territory with the mission to survive, push forward, and rescue captured hostages.

The gameplay is fast, direct, and relentless. Armed with a machine gun and limited grenades, players must clear waves of enemy soldiers, avoid ambushes from bunkers, and keep moving upward through hostile environments. On the Commodore 64, Commando delivers solid sprite work and confident vertical scrolling that keeps the action flowing smoothly. The real highlight is Rob Hubbard’s iconic soundtrack, which injects urgency and atmosphere into every firefight and remains one of the most celebrated pieces of C64 game music.

While its structure is simple, Commando is remembered for its intense arcade feel, tight controls, and unforgettable audio. It stands as a defining early example of the run-and-gun genre on home systems and a staple of many C64 collections.

Players take control of Donald Duck as he works a series of everyday jobs to earn money for building a playground for his nephews, Huey, Dewey, and Louie.

The gameplay is split into a collection of mini-games set across different workplaces, including a greengrocer’s shop, a toy store, a railroad switchboard, and an airport cargo terminal. Money earned from each job is carefully managed and spent on playground equipment such as swings and slides, which are then placed piece by piece to complete the final goal. The structure encourages basic arithmetic, budgeting, and time management while keeping the experience accessible and rewarding for younger players.

On the Commodore 64, the game features colourful character sprites and clear, friendly visuals that make each task easy to understand. The pacing is relaxed but purposeful, reinforcing learning through repetition rather than difficulty spikes.

Donald Duck’s Playground remains fondly remembered as an early example of character-led educational gaming, combining Disney charm with thoughtful design. Today, it stands as a nostalgic reminder of Sierra’s early versatility and the era when learning games shared shelf space with arcade classics.

Released in 1985 by Martech for the Commodore 64, Crazy Comets is a fast-paced multidirectional shooter inspired by Gottlieb’s arcade hit Mad Planets. Players are tasked with defending a vulnerable planet from waves of unpredictable comets and space debris.

You control a rotating spaceship positioned at the centre of the screen, firing in all directions to intercept incoming threats. Each stage increases in speed and intensity, demanding sharper reflexes and tighter control as the screen fills with hostile objects.

The minimalist design keeps the focus firmly on pure arcade action. With no distractions, success depends entirely on positioning, timing, and managing multiple attack angles at once. The steadily rising difficulty ensures constant pressure throughout every session.

One of the game’s defining features is its iconic soundtrack by Rob Hubbard. The energetic SID composition drives the pace of play and adds excitement to every encounter, helping elevate Crazy Comets beyond a simple shooter.

Blending tight controls, escalating challenge, and legendary music, Crazy Comets became a favourite among C64 arcade fans. Today, it’s remembered as one of the finest fixed-screen shooters of the 8-bit era.

Released in 1991, Hunter was developed by Paul Holmes and published by Activision, delivering a level of freedom rarely seen in games of its era. Designed for the Amiga and Atari ST, it places players in control of a lone soldier dropped into a vast archipelago under enemy control, with no fixed path to success.

The game’s defining feature is its open-ended structure. Players can explore freely on foot or by swimming, and can commandeer a wide range of vehicles including cars, tanks, helicopters, boats, and even surfboards. Missions can be tackled in multiple ways, rewarding experimentation, planning, and improvisation rather than rigid solutions.

Hunter’s world feels alive and reactive. Buildings can be entered, civilians and enemies move independently, and player actions can influence future encounters. This dynamic design creates a strong sense of immersion and scale, especially impressive given the hardware limitations of the time.

Often cited as a precursor to modern open-world games, Hunter remains a landmark achievement in early 3D game design. Today, it’s remembered as a bold and influential title that helped shape the future of sandbox-style gameplay.

You can choose to play as the barbarian or Princess Mariana, each fighting their way through three hostile environments: a volcanic wasteland, a twisting cave network, and the infamous Dungeon of Drax itself. Combat remains the core focus, featuring brutal encounters with multiple enemy types and the return of the series’ signature decapitations when strikes are perfectly timed. Environmental hazards such as lava pits and deadly drops add constant pressure, forcing careful movement as well as sharp reactions.

Known for its large, detailed sprites and atmospheric sound effects, Barbarian II divided opinion on release but has since earned its place as a bold and memorable sequel. Today it stands as a distinctive blend of beat ’em up action and exploratory design on the C64.

Gameplay centres on piloting a skimmer through vast hostile cities, battling robotic defenders while exploring complex urban environments. Progress depends on locating and assembling reactor cooling rods, managing limited fuel and ammunition, and making smart use of tools such as infrared vision, scanners, and flares to survive the planet’s dangers.

What truly set Tau Ceti apart was its technical ambition. The game features solid 3D environments with shadow effects and a dynamic day-night cycle, creating a strong sense of scale and atmosphere that was astonishing on 8-bit hardware. These visuals, combined with strategic resource management and puzzle-like objectives, deliver a tense and immersive experience.

Critically acclaimed on release, Tau Ceti is widely regarded as one of the Commodore 64’s most innovative titles. Its blend of action, strategy, and technical wizardry helped shape future space and simulation games, securing its reputation as a true 8-bit classic.

fu52vUOmIbY.title: Tilt – The Codemasters C64 Puzzle That Made You Move the Entire Maze

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Released in 1990 by Codemasters, Tilt is a distinctive action-puzzle game for the Commodore 64 that puts physics and precision front and centre. Players guide a marble through a series of maze-like levels by tilting the entire playfield, aiming to reach the exit without smashing into obstacles or running out of energy.

Rather than moving the marble directly, the screen itself is rotated to influence momentum. As levels progress, the challenge increases with tighter layouts, gates, traps, and changes to the marble’s size, all of which demand careful control and forward planning rather than brute force reactions.

Technically, Tilt is an impressive showcase for the C64. The marble physics feel convincing, movement is smooth, and the controls are responsive, making success feel earned rather than random. The experience is backed by a fitting soundtrack composed by Steve Barrett, which complements the calm-but-tense puzzle action.

The game is also remembered for its quirky publishing history. The cover artwork features Roger Frames from Commodore Format, and when Tilt appeared on the magazine’s issue 48 cover tape, the printed instructions mistakenly belonged to a completely different game with the same name, leaving many players baffled on first load. Today, Tilt stands out as a clever, skill-based puzzle title that still feels fresh and inventive.

Released in 1985 by Hungarian studio Andromeda Software and published by Ariolasoft for the Commodore 64, Scarabaeus is a pioneering first-person 3D maze adventure set deep within a mysterious Egyptian tomb. Known as Invaders of the Lost Tomb in North America, the game blends exploration, puzzle-solving, and survival into a tense and atmospheric experience.

The adventure unfolds across three distinct stages. Players first navigate a sprawling maze to capture wandering ghosts, each revealing a hieroglyphic symbol. These symbols become essential clues in the second phase, where logic puzzles involving alcoves, medicinal vials, and zombie traps must be solved through careful deduction.

In the final stage, knowledge gathered earlier is put to the test as players confront zombies and solve a central puzzle to access the inner sanctum and recover the sacred jewel. Success depends on observation, memory, and understanding how each element connects across the game’s structure.

Scarabaeus was technically impressive on the C64, featuring smooth first-person scrolling and an eerie audio design that switches between haunting music and the explorer’s breathing. The sense of isolation and danger gives the tomb a powerful atmosphere rarely seen at the time.

Today, Scarabaeus is regarded as a landmark Commodore 64 title. Praised for its ambition and originality, it earned a Sizzler award and a 96% rating from Zzap!64, securing its place as one of the most innovative adventure games of the 8-bit era.

Released in 1993 by the Norwegian demo group Spaceballs, 9 Fingers is a two-disk Amiga production built around techno music tightly synchronised to on-screen visuals. While not chasing raw technical extremes, the demo focuses on presentation, timing, and atmosphere, delivering a confident and entertaining audiovisual experience.

Much of the demo relies on low-resolution digitised graphics, a deliberate choice that allowed the creators to squeeze in extended video sequences, lively visual edits, and a strong soundtrack without overwhelming the hardware. The result feels cohesive and energetic, with visuals and music working in lockstep rather than competing for attention.

The scope of the production suggests a hands-on approach, with Spaceballs likely combining self-shot footage and sourced material before digitising and assembling everything into a flowing, music-driven sequence. It’s a reminder of how inventive demo makers had to be when balancing ambition against tight memory and disk limits.

Formed in 1988 by Dark Helmet, Spaceballs grew from a solo project into a recognised Amiga demo group with roots in Halden, Norway. Early members such as Lone Starr helped shape the group’s identity, which leaned toward polished presentation and memorable music-led demos.

Today, 9 Fingers is remembered as a classic example of early-1990s Amiga demo culture, where rhythm, editing, and creativity mattered just as much as technical wizardry.

Released in 1993 by Blue Byte for the Commodore Amiga, The Settlers is a landmark city-building and real-time strategy game designed by Volker Wertich. Set in a richly detailed medieval world, the game challenges players to balance economic growth with territorial expansion in order to build a thriving settlement.

Gameplay revolves around managing complex supply chains, with resources such as wood, stone, and food feeding into interconnected production systems. Every settler performs a specific role, from woodcutters and miners to bakers and soldiers, making careful planning and logistics essential to long-term success.

Progression is driven by smart infrastructure design, efficient road networks, and the steady development of military strength. As settlements grow, players must optimise workflows, expand into new territories, and defend their borders against increasingly capable opponents.

The game features a 30-mission campaign that gradually introduces advanced mechanics and tougher AI rivals, alongside a free-play mode that supports two-player split-screen multiplayer. Its intuitive point-and-click interface, charming visuals, and ambient sound design create a deeply immersive and accessible strategy experience.

Widely praised for its depth and originality, The Settlers carved out its own identity alongside titles such as SimCity and Populous. Its success on the Amiga launched a long-running franchise and secured its reputation as one of the most influential strategy games of the 1990s.

g6UIT7E97Jc.title: Dragon’s Lair – How Did a LaserDisc Arcade Game End Up on the C64?

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/dragons-lair/

Released in 1986 by Software Projects for the Commodore 64, Dragon’s Lair is a home computer adaptation of Don Bluth’s groundbreaking laserdisc arcade phenomenon.

Players guide the heroic knight Dirk the Daring through a series of deadly traps and timing-based challenges as he attempts to rescue Princess Daphne from the evil dragon Singe.

Rather than using full-motion video, the C64 version reimagines the cinematic adventure through hand-drawn sprites, animated sequences, and carefully timed gameplay events. This approach allowed the game to function within the system’s technical limits.

The game was developed by John Darnell and Steve Birtles, with graphics by Nicole Baikaloff and music composed by Colin Porch. It also features the distinctive “Dragonload” tape-loading system, which enabled its large, multi-stage structure.

Gameplay focuses on memorisation, quick reactions, and pattern recognition, requiring players to learn the correct inputs for each sequence in order to progress.

Visually, the adaptation preserves much of the original’s fantasy atmosphere, while the soundtrack and sound effects help reinforce its storybook tone.

Although demanding and sometimes unforgiving, Dragon’s Lair on the Commodore 64 stands as a testament to 8-bit ingenuity. It demonstrates how ambitious arcade experiences could be reshaped for home computers.

Today, it’s remembered as one of the most technically impressive and historically significant arcade conversions on the platform.

Released in 1985 by Firebird Software and developed by Shahid Ahmad, CHIMERA is an atmospheric isometric action-adventure that places survival and problem-solving at its core. Set aboard a mysterious alien spacecraft orbiting Earth, the stakes are immediate: disable the ship’s weapons and trigger its self-destruct before the planet is destroyed.

Players control a lone robot navigating a maze of 64 interconnected rooms, each presented in a classic isometric view. Progress depends on careful exploration, avoiding environmental hazards such as electrical barriers, and solving puzzles that gradually reveal how the ship functions.

A key twist is survival management. Food and water steadily deplete, forcing players to plan routes efficiently and prioritise resources alongside puzzle objectives. Items must be gathered and combined to assemble warheads, which are then placed in specific blue rooms to initiate the self-destruct sequence, before racing to the green escape room.

The game’s tension is amplified by its stark presentation and unsettling audio design, including a memorable digitised scream that heightens the sense of danger. While often compared to Knight Lore due to its perspective, CHIMERA stands apart through its harsher survival mechanics and sci-fi setting.

Today, CHIMERA is remembered as a challenging and inventive entry in the Commodore 64 library, rewarding patience, mapping skills, and strategic thinking in equal measure.

Released in October 1992 at the Digital Symposium demo party, Jesus on E’s is one of the most iconic and talked-about techno demos ever created for the Commodore Amiga. Produced by LSD, with music by Echo (Graham Gray, also known as SpoonWizard) and graphics by Shag Ratt!, it quickly earned legendary status within the demo scene.

The demo is driven by an intense, continuously evolving soundtrack that blends techno, rave, hardcore, dance, and old-school styles into a single extended mix. Packed with memorable samples and relentless energy, the music carries the experience across its full runtime, demanding to be watched from start to finish.

Visually, Jesus on E’s complements its soundtrack with bold, fast-moving graphics and a raw demo scene aesthetic that perfectly matches the music’s urgency and attitude. The sheer scale of the production is even more impressive when you remember that the entire experience originally fit onto just two 3.5-inch floppy disks.

More than three decades on, Jesus on E’s remains a defining Amiga demo, still captivating viewers today and standing as a high point of early-90s demo scene creativity and ambition.

Released in 1986 by Ocean Software and developed by Denton Designs, The Great Escape is an isometric action-adventure for the Commodore 64 inspired by the classic 1963 war film. Players take on the role of a prisoner of war held in a heavily guarded German camp during World War II, with one goal in mind: escape without raising suspicion.

The game centres around a strict daily routine. Roll calls, exercise periods, and mealtimes must all be attended, and ignoring camp rules quickly draws the attention of guards. Within these constraints, players must carefully plan their breakout, balancing obedience with secret preparation.

Multiple escape routes are available, including digging tunnels, forging documents, bribing guards, or navigating underground drains. Each method requires patience, exploration, and clever use of limited resources, creating a constant sense of tension and risk.

Presented in an isometric 2.5D perspective, the camp is laid out as a living, breathing environment filled with guards, fellow prisoners, and hidden opportunities. While the Commodore 64 version made some compromises, The Great Escape remains respected for its ambitious design and innovative approach to stealth and strategy. Today, it’s remembered as one of the most distinctive adventure games of its era.

Released in 1987 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore 64, Maniac Mansion is a landmark graphic adventure that redefined how games told stories. Built on the newly created SCUMM engine, it introduced a point-and-click interface that made interaction more intuitive and opened the door to deeper, more expressive game narratives.

Players control Dave Miller and choose two friends from a cast of six unique characters, each with different abilities, as they infiltrate the bizarre mansion of Dr. Fred Edison to rescue Dave’s kidnapped girlfriend, Sandy Pantz. The non-linear design allows multiple solutions to puzzles, encouraging experimentation and replayability as different character combinations unlock new paths and outcomes.

The Commodore 64 version delivers colourful visuals, atmospheric music, and animated cutscenes that push the story forward, helping the mansion feel alive and unpredictable. Its humour, strange characters, and occasional danger create a tone that balances comedy with tension, something rarely seen at the time.

Widely praised for its innovation, Maniac Mansion laid the foundations for countless adventure games that followed. Decades later, it remains a defining title of the genre and a beloved classic in the Commodore 64 library.

Blending fast-paced arcade combat with strategic mission design, the game features large scrolling maps, detailed mission briefings, hostage rescues, and multiple objectives that must be completed in sequence.

Players must carefully manage fuel, ammunition, and armour while navigating hostile territory, balancing aggression with planning to survive each operation.

The distinctive isometric viewpoint delivers a strong pseudo-3D effect, allowing smooth movement across varied terrain and enhancing spatial awareness during combat.

On the Amiga, the game retains the depth and challenge of the original Sega Mega Drive version, standing out as one of the strongest home computer conversions of the era.

Its mix of real-time action and tactical decision-making helped redefine helicopter combat games and laid the foundations for a hugely successful Strike series.

Visually sharp and mechanically rewarding, Desert Strike remains a benchmark for mission-based action games on the platform.

The Last V8 (1985) is a futuristic, post-apocalyptic racing game for the Commodore 64, developed by David Darling, with graphics by Jim Wilson and music by Rob Hubbard.

Released under Mastertronic’s MAD label, you pilot a radiation-shielded V8 through a nuclear wasteland, balancing speed, fuel, and shield power in a race for survival.

Gameplay features a split-screen display with action view and dashboard, precise steering, and a steep difficulty curve. The famous “V8, return to base immediately” intro sets the tone.

Rob Hubbard’s soundtrack is a highlight, despite a small sync glitch later fixed in the HVSC archive. Visually, the game delivers striking post-apocalyptic imagery.

Despite its flaws, The Last V8 remains a cult classic, remembered for its atmosphere, soundtrack, and brutal challenge.
