Released in 1991 by Coktel Vision, Gobliiins is a point-and-click puzzle adventure for the Commodore Amiga that blends surreal humour with inventive problem-solving. Players are tasked with curing King Angoulafre of madness after he falls victim to a voodoo curse, guided by a trio of mischievous goblins sent on a bizarre rescue mission.

The game’s core mechanic revolves around controlling three characters at once, each with a distinct role. Oups handles object interaction, Ignatius casts unpredictable spells, and Asgard relies on brute strength to manipulate the environment. Solving each of the game’s 22 single-screen puzzles requires careful coordination, experimentation, and sometimes intentionally wrong choices to discover the right solution.

Mistakes come at a cost, as the goblins share a single energy bar that drains when actions backfire. This adds tension to the puzzle-solving, forcing players to think ahead rather than click blindly through each scene.

Visually, Gobliiins is instantly recognisable thanks to Pierre Gilhodes’ expressive hand-drawn artwork and exaggerated character animations. While the sound design is understated, the game’s humour, visual storytelling, and creative puzzle design have secured it a lasting reputation as one of the Amiga’s most memorable adventure titles.

Set in the brutal cyber-future of 2105, it transforms competitive sport into a fast, violent spectacle where precision, tactics, and aggression are equally important.

You control a team of nine cybernetic athletes in a high-speed arena sport that blends handball-style scoring with the physical intensity of ice hockey. Matches are frantic and unforgiving, with players smashing into opponents, stealing the ball, and triggering devastating power-ups that can swing momentum in seconds. Success depends not just on reflexes, but on team management, upgrades, and knowing when to play dirty.

The Amiga version is widely regarded as definitive, delivering smooth scrolling, sharp visuals, and an intense sense of speed. The atmosphere is elevated by Nation 12’s driving soundtrack, which perfectly matches the game’s cold, industrial tone. Multiplayer is where Speedball 2 truly shines, offering fiercely competitive matches that remain addictive decades later.

Critically acclaimed on release, Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe became a defining title for the Commodore Amiga and a benchmark for futuristic sports games. It remains a cult classic and a standout example of The Bitmap Brothers’ distinctive design philosophy.

Released in 1986 by Hewson Consultants for the Commodore 64, Southern Belle is a pioneering train simulation programmed by Mike Male and Bob Hillyer during the height of the 8-bit era. It stands out as one of the earliest serious attempts to recreate the operation of a real steam locomotive on a home computer.

Players take on the demanding roles of both driver and fireman aboard a King Arthur class steam passenger locomotive, tasked with completing the famous journey from London Victoria to Brighton. Success depends on carefully managing speed, coal, water levels and braking while keeping to a strict timetable and avoiding derailment.

The game uses a first-person, vector-style presentation and focuses on measured control rather than arcade reflexes. Multiple levels of complexity allow players to observe automated runs or take full command of the locomotive, balancing realism with accessibility on limited C64 hardware.

With its emphasis on operational detail and patience, Southern Belle carved out a unique niche among Commodore 64 simulations. It demonstrated that complex real-world systems could be convincingly represented on 8-bit machines and remains a respected milestone in retro simulation history today.

Released in 1985 by Beam Software for the Commodore 64, The Way of the Exploding Fist is a landmark martial arts fighting game that helped define the genre on home computers. Inspired by the arcade hit Karate Champ, it introduced a more measured, skill-based approach to one-on-one combat, placing emphasis on timing, spacing, and precise control.

Players compete in karate matches where victory is achieved by scoring two full points, represented by yin-yang symbols. The control system offers 18 distinct moves, including punches, kicks, blocks, and acrobatic somersaults, all executed through deliberate joystick movements. As the game progresses, opponents become faster and more disciplined, testing both reflexes and technique across a range of atmospheric locations.

A memorable highlight is the bonus stage, where players attempt to defeat a charging bull with a single perfectly timed strike—a direct nod to martial arts legend Mas Oyama. This sequence, along with the game’s calm but tense pacing, reinforces its focus on mastery rather than button-mashing.

The experience is elevated by Neil Brennan’s evocative soundtrack, which adds mood and gravitas to each encounter. A huge commercial and critical success, the game topped UK sales charts and earned a 93% “Sizzler” award from Zzap!64. Today, The Way of the Exploding Fist is widely regarded as one of the most influential fighting games on the Commodore 64.

Gameplay is built around hexagonal battlefields where careful positioning, resource management, and spellcasting are essential for success. Players summon mythical creatures, deploy armies, and unleash powerful magic in order to weaken enemy forces and secure control of each island.

Progression relies on long-term planning and adaptive tactics, as every decision affects future encounters. Choosing when to attack, defend, or invest in magical abilities can determine the outcome of extended campaigns, rewarding thoughtful and patient play.

Visually, Celtic Legends delivers detailed fantasy environments and well-animated units that bring its myth-inspired setting to life. Subtle sound effects and atmospheric music further enhance the sense of immersion and strategic tension.

Praised for its depth and addictive gameplay, the game earned strong reviews, including a 91% score from Amiga Action. With support for two-player battles alongside its extensive single-player campaign, Celtic Legends remains a standout strategy title and a beloved cult favourite among Amiga enthusiasts.

Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64, Batman: The Caped Crusader is an inventive action-adventure developed by Special FX Software and published by Ocean Software. Rather than following a conventional layout, the game presents its world like a living comic book, with each new area revealed as a fresh panel complete with captions and dramatic transitions.

The game is split into two self-contained episodes. “A Bird in the Hand” pits Batman against the Penguin, while “A Fete Worse Than Death” focuses on the Joker. Both episodes mix side-scrolling combat with exploration and environmental interaction, requiring you to think as much as you fight.

Batman’s moveset includes punches, kicks, and his iconic Batarang, but progress often depends on using the surroundings to your advantage. Solving light puzzles, timing actions correctly, and understanding each location’s layout are just as important as defeating enemies.

Visually, the comic-panel presentation gives the game a strong identity, making it feel like you’re playing through the pages of a graphic novel. Atmospheric sound effects and a fitting musical score reinforce the darker tone of Gotham and its villains.

Critically well received on release, Batman: The Caped Crusader was praised for its originality and faithful interpretation of the character, earning high scores from magazines of the time and securing its place as one of the most distinctive licensed games on the Commodore 64.

R-Type is the 1988 Commodore 64 port of Irem’s legendary arcade “force-ship” shooter, published by Electric Dreams / Rainbow Arts and coded by Manfred Trenz.

In the game, you pilot the iconic R-9 “Arrowhead” spacecraft through eight intense horizontally-scrolling stages, battling the alien Bydo Empire, navigating hazardous terrain, and facing massive biomechanical bosses.

Your arsenal includes rapid-fire shots, a powerful chargeable wave cannon, and the game’s signature feature — the indestructible “Force” orb. Attach it, detach it, or deploy it freely to act as both shield and weapon platform.

The C64 conversion delivers fast gameplay and smooth scrolling, outperforming many other 8-bit shooters of its era. Atmospheric visuals, detailed sci-fi environments, and an outstanding soundtrack by Chris Hülsbeck and Ramiro Vaca add to the experience.

Remarkably, the port was reportedly developed in just a few weeks, yet it remains one of the finest technical showcases on the Commodore 64. R-Type proved what the hardware was capable of and continues to be celebrated as a benchmark arcade conversion.

Today, it stands as a true classic — combining demanding gameplay, iconic design, and lasting sci-fi atmosphere.

Released in 1984 by Sega and ported to the Commodore 64 by Synapse Software, with European distribution by US Gold, Zaxxon brings one of the most innovative arcade shooters of the early 1980s to home computers. Players pilot a futuristic spacecraft on a dangerous assault through a heavily fortified enemy fortress.

The game’s defining feature is its isometric perspective, which creates a pseudo-3D battlefield unlike most traditional vertical or horizontal shooters. Players must constantly manage altitude and positioning, weaving between walls, fuel tanks, gun turrets, and enemy fire while maintaining forward momentum.

Progression depends on precise control, spatial awareness, and careful resource management. Fuel must be conserved, shots timed accurately, and key targets destroyed in order to reach the later stages and complete each mission successfully.

Visually, the Commodore 64 version delivers atmospheric environments and strong depth illusion that closely reflect the arcade original. The distinctive viewpoint, combined with challenging level layouts, gives Zaxxon its unmistakable identity and demanding learning curve.

Widely praised for its faithful conversion and technical achievement, Zaxxon remains one of the most recognisable shooters on the C64. Although its perspective can be unforgiving at first, mastery brings immense satisfaction. Today, it stands as a landmark title that helped expand what arcade shooters could be on 8-bit systems.

You can choose to play as either Brad or Janet, with the goal of rescuing your partner after they’ve been turned to stone by the Medusa machine. A strict one-item carry limit forces players to plan routes and actions carefully.

The game captures the atmosphere of the stage show through its visuals and music, featuring adapted tunes such as “The Time Warp.” While technically simple, The Rocky Horror Show is fondly remembered for its faithfulness to the source material and its unmistakable sense of style, making it a nostalgic curiosity for fans of the musical and retro adventure games alike.

Released in 1987 by Electric Dreams Software for the Commodore 64, Big Trouble in Little China is a side-scrolling beat ’em up developed by Software Studios and based on John Carpenter’s cult action-fantasy film.

Players switch between three heroes — Jack Burton, Wang Chi, and Egg Shen — as they battle through Chinatown’s criminal underworld to rescue two kidnapped girls. Each character brings unique abilities, from Jack’s firearm to Wang’s fragile swords and Shen’s growing magic attacks.

Combat takes place against waves of enemies attacking from both directions, requiring careful positioning and weapon management. Picking the right character and knowing when to use special abilities is key to surviving the later stages.

Visually, the game features large character sprites and atmospheric urban backdrops that push the limits of 1987 C64 hardware. The presentation is supported by sparse but effective sound effects, including digitised punches and minimal musical stabs.

One unusual feature is the game’s right-to-left “reverse” scrolling, which sets it apart from most beat ’em ups of the era. Combined with its weapon system, this gives the gameplay a distinctive feel.

While often criticised for its high difficulty, Big Trouble in Little China remains a memorable licensed title. It reflects Electric Dreams’ strong output in movie adaptations and continues to attract fans of classic C64 action games.

Today, it’s remembered as a tough but atmospheric beat ’em up that captures much of the film’s personality in 8-bit form.

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Released in 1990 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore Amiga, Loom is a beautifully crafted graphic adventure led by Brian Moriarty, set in a mysterious fantasy world ruled by the ancient Guild of Weavers.

Players follow young Bobbin Threadbare on a personal and emotional journey to uncover the secrets of the Great Loom and rescue his disappearing guild.

Instead of traditional inventory puzzles, the game introduces a unique spell-casting system based on musical drafts played on a magical distaff, allowing players to reshape the world through sound.

These musical spells can open paths, transform objects, reverse effects, and solve environmental puzzles through experimentation and logic.

True to Lucasfilm’s design philosophy, Loom removes player death and dead ends, encouraging relaxed exploration and story-driven discovery.

Visually, the game features striking high-resolution artwork with distinctive EGA and VGA dithering that gives Fantasia a painterly, dreamlike quality.

The haunting soundtrack is based on Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake, arranged for the Amiga by George “The Fat Man” Sanger, creating a powerful emotional atmosphere.

An extended audio prologue further deepens immersion, helping establish the game’s tone and mythology from the very beginning.

With its minimalist interface, elegant puzzles, and musical magic system, Loom remains one of the most creative adventure games ever made.

Today, it is celebrated as a timeless classic and a defining achievement of the golden age of adventure gaming.

You take control of Blade or Striker, two hard-hitting vigilantes on a mission to rescue “President Ronnie” from the ruthless Dragon Ninja clan.

The action unfolds across six side-scrolling stages packed with gangs, ambushes, and end-of-level bosses, including a memorable crossover appearance from Data East’s Karnov. Combat focuses on punches, kicks, and timing, with weapons such as nunchaku and knives adding extra punch when picked up.

The C64 conversion, developed by David Collier with graphics by Stephen Wahid and John Palmer, does a solid job of translating the arcade experience. Large character sprites and recognisable environments give the game real presence, while Jonathan Dunn’s music helps drive the action forward.

Although animation smoothness and sound were sometimes criticised, Bad Dudes vs. DragonNinja remains a fondly remembered beat ’em up. Its challenge, personality, and unmistakable 1980s arcade attitude have secured it a lasting place in Commodore 64 history.

The action is fast and unforgiving, with health constantly draining as you battle through room after room in search of food, keys, and the all-important exit. Cooperation is at the heart of the experience, especially in two-player mode, where sharing resources and covering each other becomes essential as the difficulty ramps up.

While the C64 hardware required some compromises, the game captures the spirit of the arcade original with chunky sprites, colourful dungeons, and nonstop pressure. The sense of urgency and constant enemy spawns keep every run tense and addictive.

Gauntlet remains a landmark title, not just for its action, but for popularising cooperative dungeon crawling. Decades on, it’s still remembered as a defining experience of mid-80s arcade and home computer gaming.

Released in 1987 by Gigglywurx and published by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, BMX Kidz is a fast-paced side-scrolling racing game inspired by the BMX craze of the 1980s.

Players race against five computer-controlled opponents across a series of challenging tracks, performing wheelies, jumps, and stunts in order to maintain speed and gain an advantage.

A key gameplay element is energy and bike management. Crashes and failed tricks drain stamina and damage the bike, while collecting soda cans restores energy and replacement spokes keep performance at its peak.

The game uses a distinctive 2.5D perspective that creates a strong sense of depth and motion, helping it stand out among other racing titles of the era.

Progression depends on mastering the game’s slippery physics, timing jumps accurately, and choosing when to risk stunts for extra speed.

Visually, BMX Kidz delivers crisp character sprites and smoothly scrolling tracks that convey speed and momentum effectively.

The experience is elevated by Rob Hubbard’s energetic SID soundtrack, featuring memorable tunes and sampled voice effects, with additional hi-score music by Jori Olkkonen.

Balancing arcade challenge with trick-based gameplay, BMX Kidz became a standout sports title on the Commodore 64.

Today, it’s remembered as a nostalgic favourite and one of the most recognisable BMX games of the 8-bit era.

Released in 1986 by Chris Gray Enterprises and published by Mindscape and U.S. Gold, Infiltrator is a unique combat flight simulation and stealth action game for the Commodore 64.

Players step into the role of Johnny “Jimbo Baby” McGibbits, piloting the advanced Gizmo DHX-3 helicopter to infiltrate enemy territory and stop the plans of the mysterious Mad Leader.

Each mission is divided into two phases: an aerial combat section and a ground-based infiltration segment. During flight missions, players navigate hostile airspace, identify friendly aircraft, and deploy missiles while using whisper mode for stealth.

Ground missions focus on careful planning and disguise, requiring players to use fake documents, gas grenades, security cards, and explosives to bypass guards and complete objectives without raising alarms.

This blend of flight simulation and espionage gameplay was highly innovative for its time, offering a level of depth and variety rarely seen on 8-bit systems. Success depends on both reflexes and tactical decision-making.

Visually, the game delivers detailed cockpit displays, readable terrain, and clear mission interfaces that support its hybrid design. The presentation reinforces the feeling of taking part in a high-risk covert operation.

Praised for its ambition and originality, Infiltrator earned a strong reputation among Commodore 64 players and helped influence later stealth-action titles.

Today, it’s remembered as one of the platform’s most distinctive and inventive action simulations.

A major highlight is the title theme composed by Martin Galway, who adapted the film’s iconic melody into a memorable SID soundtrack.

The music and visuals together create an immersive mood that elevates the adventure beyond typical licensed titles of the era.

Critically well received on release, the game earned praise for its detailed presentation and strong audio design.

Released at The Gathering in 1993, Desert Dream by Kefrens is one of the most celebrated Amiga demos of all time, storming the competition and securing first place in the Amiga compo. It’s a production that perfectly captures the confidence and polish of the early-90s demo scene at its peak.

From the moment it starts, Desert Dream delivers a flowing sequence of striking visuals paired with a stunning soundtrack, blending atmosphere, colour, and movement into something that feels effortlessly cinematic. And yes—this is the demo with the flying watermelons, a playful touch that somehow fits perfectly within the otherwise slick presentation.

The demo is packed with memorable moments and clever design choices, including a hidden Easter egg accessible by booting from disk two and pressing the left mouse button, right mouse button, and joystick button together on a blank screen. It’s details like this that helped cement the demo’s legendary status among Amiga fans.

Created by a strong team of artists and musicians, Desert Dream remains a defining example of what the Amiga demo scene could achieve when visuals, music, and timing came together in perfect balance. Even today, it’s still essential viewing for anyone exploring classic Amiga demos.

Originally developed by Ron Haliburton and released by Midway in 1981, Omega Race arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1982 as a remarkably faithful home conversion of the arcade original. It delivers fast, precision-based shooting action built around clean vector-style visuals and tight arena combat.

Players pilot an Omegan Fighter within a rectangular arena, rotating and thrusting freely in any direction while battling hostile droid ships and avoiding deadly mines. Movement has a deliberate, momentum-driven feel similar to Asteroids, demanding careful control and spatial awareness at all times.

The arena itself adds to the challenge, with invisible force-field walls that punish reckless movement and force players to master positioning and timing. Success depends on understanding enemy patterns, conserving momentum, and keeping full control of the ship under pressure.

The Commodore 64 version captures the spirit of the arcade machine with striking monochrome vector graphics and responsive controls. While the coloured overlays of the original cabinet are absent, the gameplay remains intense, focused, and highly addictive. Omega Race stands as Midway’s only vector-based arcade title and is still celebrated today as a pure early-80s arcade design that translates beautifully to home computers.

Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Herbert’s Dummy Run is a 2D arcade-adventure developed by David Perry and published by Mikro-Gen. The fourth entry in the Wally Week series shifts the spotlight away from Wally himself and places players in control of his adventurous infant son, Herbert.

Set inside a vast multi-floor department store, the game tasks players with guiding Herbert through more than 25 interconnected rooms after becoming separated from his parents. Progress depends on exploration, careful timing, and logical problem-solving as players collect and use items to overcome obstacles before the store closes at 5:30 PM.

A standout feature is the inclusion of clever mini-games that parody classic arcade hits such as Breakout, Space Invaders, and Duck Shoot. These sequences are woven directly into the puzzles, adding variety and a playful sense of humour to the overall experience.

The game’s atmosphere is enhanced by its musical theme, using “Baby Face” by Harry Warren and Benny Davis, which reinforces the light-hearted tone. While it didn’t reach the same legendary status as earlier Wally Week titles, Herbert’s Dummy Run remains fondly remembered for its inventive design, charming presentation, and unusual premise.

Designed by Archer Maclean, with a legendary soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, IK+ refined and expanded the original International Karate formula into a faster, deeper, and far more distinctive experience.

The game’s standout feature is its unique three-player combat system, where fighters battle simultaneously on a single screen. Matches are scored through well-timed punches, kicks, sweeps, and acrobatic flips, rewarding precision and positioning rather than button mashing. Controls are tight and responsive, making every exchange feel deliberate and skill-based.

Between bouts, IK+ introduces bonus rounds such as deflecting bouncing balls, adding variety and extra challenge. Smooth animation, humorous background details, and expressive character movement give the game a lively personality that still holds up decades later.

International Karate + became a defining title of the Commodore 64 era. Its blend of competitive depth, technical polish, and unforgettable music secured its place as one of the system’s most enduring and influential fighting games.

Released in 1988 by Hewson Consultants and programmed for the Commodore 64 by Nick Jones (based on Raffaele Cecco’s original design), Cybernoid: The Fighting Machine is a futuristic shoot ’em up in which players pilot a highly armed combat craft to reclaim stolen Federation cargo from deadly pirate strongholds. 

Divided into three flip-screen levels rather than smooth scrolling, the game demands tactical navigation and weapons selection as you confront gun turrets, homing missiles and hostile pirate vessels. Power-ups and built-in ship weapons — including shields, impact mines, bounce bombs and homing seekers — must be used thoughtfully to survive each screen and collect treasure before time runs out.

The Commodore 64 version is especially revered for its colourful graphics that pushed the 8-bit system’s palette, and its atmospheric SID soundtrack composed by Jeroen Tel, giving it a distinctive audio-visual identity among classic C64 shooters. 

While its difficulty curve is challenging and often unforgiving, Cybernoid’s blend of arcade shooting and puzzle-like screen design helped it stand out in the crowded late-1980s home computer market. Today it remains a respected favourite in the retro gaming community and a benchmark for Commodore 64 action titles.

Mr. Robot and His Robot Factory (1983), developed by Ron Rosen and published by Datamost, is a classic platform game that was later ported to the Commodore 64.

Players guide a humanoid robot through 22 built-in factory screens, collecting white power pills while navigating ladders, conveyor belts, escalators, traps, and roaming fireball enemies.

Each stage begins with a limited energy meter that constantly drains, creating urgency and forcing players to plan their movements carefully.

Touching hazards or falling too far costs a life, while collecting a pulsing white ring grants temporary invulnerability and allows enemies to be destroyed.

One of the game’s standout features is its built-in level editor, known as the “Robot Factory,” which lets players design, save, and load up to 26 custom levels — greatly extending replay value.

Visually, the game features crisp sprites and clear platform layouts typical of early 1980s home computer titles, while the sound design supports the fast-paced gameplay.

Thanks to its creative level editor and clever stage design, Mr. Robot and His Robot Factory remains a favourite among retro fans and is remembered as an early example of platforming mixed with user creativity.

Released in 1992 by Digital Illusions for the Commodore Amiga, Pinball Dreams is a landmark pinball simulation and one of the earliest titles from the studio that would later become DICE. It set a new standard for realism, presentation, and table design on home computers.

The game features four expertly crafted tables, each with its own theme and rule set. Ignition is built around space travel and rocket launches, Steel Wheel takes inspiration from the Old West with steam trains and frontier imagery, Beat Box reflects the music industry with charts and touring bands, while Nightmare delivers a dark graveyard setting filled with supernatural elements.

Gameplay focuses on precise flipper control, table knowledge, and chaining bonuses through skilful shots. Each table introduces unique mechanics and scoring strategies, encouraging players to learn layouts thoroughly and aim for high-risk, high-reward play.

Pinball Dreams stands out for its smooth ball physics, detailed visuals, and atmospheric sound design, all of which combine to create an authentic pinball experience on the Amiga. The attention to detail and strong table variety gave it long-lasting replay value.

Today, Pinball Dreams is widely regarded as one of the greatest pinball games ever released on the Amiga. Its success led to acclaimed follow-ups such as Pinball Fantasies and Pinball Illusions, firmly establishing Digital Illusions as masters of the genre.

Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Rocket Ball is a futuristic sports-action game developed by IJK Software and coded by John S. Sinclair. Set in the then-future year of 2010, the game imagines a world where international disputes are settled through a violent, high-energy arena sport.

The action blends elements of roller derby and American football. Teams of five skaters battle it out in a circular arena, aiming to score by launching a heavy metal ball into a cone-shaped goal while physically overpowering their opponents. Elbows, knees, and fists are all fair game as chaos unfolds at high speed.

Players must skate quickly, collect the ball, and time their shots carefully while defending against relentless attacks. Four teams are available — Houston, Tokyo, Moscow, and Madrid — each with different strengths, adding variety and tactical choice to matches that last a tense ten minutes.

Rocket Ball is instantly memorable for its anarchic tone and aggressive gameplay, summed up perfectly by its slogan: “The rules are, there are no rules.” The soundtrack enhances the drama by mixing classical music with contemporary themes, including Bach’s Prelude and Fugue No. 6 and Gonna Fly Now from Rocky.

Today, Rocket Ball is remembered as a bold and unconventional Commodore 64 title. Its imaginative premise, physical gameplay, and strong multiplayer appeal have earned it cult status among retro sports and action fans.

iFDaeYjZnsc.title: Zeewolf – Was This the Amiga’s Best 3D Combat Game?
iFDaeYjZnsc.description:
🕹️ Zeewolf (1994) – Commodore Amiga 3D Helicopter Combat
🌐 Full game information, manual & more:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/zeewolf/

Released for the Commodore Amiga in 1994, Zeewolf is a 3D helicopter combat game created by Binary Asylum. Combining fast shoot-em-up action with tactical missions, hostage rescues and vehicle transportation, it became one of the Amiga’s most distinctive military action games.

My first experience with Zeewolf came from the Amiga Format cover-disk demo. I couldn’t afford the full game at the time, and none of my mates had a dodgy copy I could put through X-Copy, so I played that demo to death. I knew every target, building and stretch of water, but revisiting the complete game revealed how little of Zeewolf I had actually seen.

Across 32 missions, players pilot the heavily armed Zeewolf helicopter over islands, military bases and open water. Objectives include attacking enemy installations, rescuing prisoners, escorting aircraft and transporting friendly Buffalo tanks into battle.

Zeewolf is often compared with Virus and Desert Strike. It shares the floating 3D landscape of Virus and the military mission structure of Desert Strike, but places greater emphasis on controlling the helicopter, choosing an attack route and approaching enemy positions from the right direction.

The polygon graphics may look basic today, but the moving shadows, water impacts, burning aircraft and smooth low-level flying gave the game a convincing sense of height and movement. Hostage rescues could become especially tense, with one misplaced shot capable of ruining an otherwise successful operation.

The controls require patience, particularly when using the more precise mouse option, but Zeewolf becomes increasingly rewarding once the helicopter starts to feel familiar. The scanner can occasionally retain destroyed targets, while the severe slowdown on a standard Amiga A500 or A600 remains the game’s largest weakness. An Amiga 1200 or faster emulated system provides a considerably smoother experience.

Despite those rough edges, Zeewolf remains an absorbing mixture of Amiga shoot-em-up action and tactical gameplay. Its missions become difficult as hell later on, but learning how to fly, conserve ammunition and approach each target gives successful operations a real sense of achievement.

Zeewolf 2: Wild Justice followed in 1995 and improved several areas, but the original remains a memorable Amiga game—and one I mistakenly thought I knew from playing a single magazine demo hundreds of times.

While the visuals are understated, they effectively convey mood and isolation, supported by subtle music that complements each period. Time Tunnel is widely regarded as a hidden gem on the Commodore 64, praised for its inventive structure, clever puzzles, and memorable sense of discovery.

Released in 1985 by Simon Pick and published by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Mad Nurse is a distinctive platform arcade game set inside a chaotic hospital maternity ward. Players take on the role of a nurse tasked with rescuing wandering babies before they meet a variety of dangerous hazards.

Each level presents a multi-storey hospital layout filled with elevators, platforms, and environmental threats such as electrical sockets, medicine bottles, and open shafts. The challenge escalates as more babies appear simultaneously, requiring quick reactions and careful route planning to return them safely to their cribs.

A key gameplay mechanic is the nurse’s limited supply of stun gas, which temporarily freezes all babies in place and offers a brief moment to regain control. Using it too often, however, comes at a cost, reinforcing the game’s risk-versus-reward structure. The game ends if three babies are harmed, resulting in instant dismissal.

While its subject matter caused controversy at the time, Mad Nurse is remembered today for its unusual premise, demanding gameplay, and uncompromising difficulty. It remains one of the more talked-about and unconventional platform games on the Commodore 64.

💬 Could you keep every baby safe, or did the hospital descend into chaos?

Praised for its large sprites and moody sound design, Predator succeeds in capturing the atmosphere of the movie, even as difficulty and controls divided opinion. Today, it remains a memorable and demanding movie adaptation on the C64, especially for fans of the film.

This balance of arcade responsiveness and tactical control helped it stand out against rivals.

Critically acclaimed on release, Emlyn Hughes International Soccer earned a 90% score from Zzap!64 and has since become a benchmark for retro football games. Today, it’s remembered as a defining C64 sports title with depth, longevity, and a fiercely loyal fanbase.

Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64, Samurai Warrior: The Battles of Usagi Yojimbo is an action-adventure developed by Beam Software and published by Firebird, based on Stan Sakai’s acclaimed comic series. Players step into the sandals of Miyamoto Usagi, a wandering rabbit samurai navigating a dangerous world shaped as much by ethics as by steel.

Gameplay unfolds in a side-scrolling format, blending sword combat with exploration and interaction. Usagi faces bandits, ninjas, and deceptive enemies who may appear as harmless villagers or monks, requiring constant vigilance and careful judgment during encounters.

A defining feature is the game’s karma system. Honorable actions raise Usagi’s standing, while attacking innocents or acting dishonorably reduces it. Let karma fall too low and Usagi is forced into seppuku, bringing the journey to an abrupt end. Between battles, players can gamble at inns for money and purchase food to restore health, adding a strategic layer to survival.

With atmospheric music composed by Neil Brennan and a thoughtful adaptation of the source material, Samurai Warrior stands out for its blend of action, philosophy, and role-playing elements. It remains a distinctive and respected title in the Commodore 64 library, especially among fans of the Usagi Yojimbo universe.

Released in 1987 by Ocean Software and developed by Sensible Software, Wizball is a horizontal-scrolling shoot ’em up that completely rethinks the genre. Designed by Chris Yates and Jon Hare, with a standout soundtrack by Martin Galway, it combines fast action with inventive mechanics and a bold visual identity.

You control Wiz, a wizard transformed into a bouncing green ball, travelling through a drained, monochrome world. Defeated enemies release colour droplets, and by collecting and mixing primary colours you gradually restore the landscape, unlocking new areas and abilities as colour returns to the screen.

The Commodore 64 version is especially celebrated for its fluid animation and imaginative level design. A unique control system lets you manage both Wiz and his feline companion, Catellite, adding tactical depth alongside the constant action. Galway’s music drives the pace and atmosphere throughout.

Wizball was a critical triumph, earning a 96% score in Zzap!64 and later being voted one of the greatest C64 games ever made. Today, it’s rightly remembered as a landmark title that pushed the shoot ’em up genre in a bold new direction.

Released in 1994 by Creative Reality for the Commodore Amiga, DreamWeb is a dark cyberpunk adventure that pushes the genre into far more mature territory. You play as Ryan, a troubled bartender haunted by violent dreams of a parallel dimension known as the Dreamweb, where a mysterious monk reveals that Ryan is the “Deliverer” chosen to eliminate seven individuals threatening the balance between worlds.

Gameplay is presented from a top-down perspective with static screens, using a contextual verb menu to examine environments, collect items, and interrogate NPCs. Progression is driven by investigation and dialogue, with the story unfolding in a largely linear fashion that emphasises atmosphere and narrative over traditional puzzle complexity.

DreamWeb stands out for its uncompromising themes, including psychological trauma, violence, and adult subject matter rarely seen in adventure games of the era. The gritty pixel art and detailed city locations create a bleak, oppressive future, while the haunting soundtrack reinforces the game’s uneasy tone throughout.

Although it never achieved mainstream success, DreamWeb has earned cult status among Amiga fans. Its distinctive cyberpunk aesthetic and mature storytelling make it one of the most memorable and unusual point-and-click adventures of the 16-bit era.

Released in 1992 by Infogrames for the Commodore Amiga, Alcatraz is a fast-paced action-shooter developed by 221B Software Developments that blends side-scrolling combat with first-person stealth gameplay.

Players take on the role of a U.S. Navy SEAL sent to storm Alcatraz prison, destroy hidden weapons caches, and capture the criminal mastermind controlling the operation.

The game is divided into multiple levels that alternate between outdoor run-and-gun sections and indoor infiltration missions. Outdoor stages feature heavy firepower such as flamethrowers, machine guns, and grenades, while indoor sections focus on radar-guided navigation and precision shooting.

This dual-perspective design creates constant variety, requiring players to adapt their tactics between fast reflex-based combat and careful stealth-based movement.

Alcatraz supports both single-player and two-player split-screen cooperative play, allowing friends to tackle missions together and coordinate their strategies.

Visually, the game delivers smooth animations, detailed environments, and strong visual effects that were widely praised in contemporary Amiga magazines.

The experience is enhanced by Ray Norrish’s memorable soundtrack, which adds tension and atmosphere to both combat and stealth sections.

Building on the foundations laid by Infogrames’ earlier title Hostages, Alcatraz refined the stealth-action formula and helped establish the studio’s reputation for cinematic action games.

Today, it’s remembered as one of the Amiga’s standout action titles of the early 1990s and a strong example of hybrid game design.

Released in 1982 by HAL Laboratory and published by Commodore, LeMans is one of the earliest racing games available for the Commodore 64 and a showcase of forward-thinking arcade design. Presented from a bird’s-eye view, the game challenges players to overtake traffic at speed while managing risk and precision under constant pressure.

The goal is simple but demanding: pass as many cars as possible within a 60-second time limit. Overtaking ten cars cleanly earns a 1,000-point bonus, while reaching 20,000 points extends the race by another minute. Crashes force a pit stop on the left side of the track, resetting your overtake count and costing valuable seconds.

LeMans keeps things fresh with changing conditions, including icy roads that affect handling, night stages lit only by headlights, and the notorious LeMans Esses that test steering control. Originally designed for paddle controllers, the game offers smooth, responsive input that rewards careful driving and rhythm.

As a Commodore 64 launch-era title and an early release from HAL Laboratory, LeMans holds an important place in gaming history. Its focused gameplay loop and escalating challenge still make it an engaging experience for fans of early arcade-style racers today.

Each level represents a distinct era, with gameplay mechanics and environments changing dramatically as you advance. Those who managed to push beyond the early challenges were rewarded with one of the more inventive and distinctive platformers on the Commodore 64. Released in 1982 by Commodore and developed by HAL Laboratory, Jupiter Lander is one of the earliest arcade-style titles available for the Commodore 64. As a launch-era game, it played a key role in demonstrating the system’s technical potential and introducing players to physics-based gameplay on home computers.

The objective is simple but demanding. Players pilot a spacecraft descending toward the surface of Jupiter, carefully managing thrust to counter gravity and line up with one of three landing platforms, each offering different levels of difficulty. Safe landings reward points and replenish fuel, while hard impacts or collisions with the terrain result in instant failure.

Fuel management is central to the challenge. Every burst of thrust must be carefully judged, as running out of fuel brings the mission to an abrupt end. Precision, timing, and restraint are essential, turning each descent into a tense balancing act between control and momentum.

Inspired by Atari’s Lunar Lander, Jupiter Lander builds on that foundation with platform-specific refinements and a clean presentation that suits the Commodore 64’s hardware. Its minimalist visuals and focused design keep attention firmly on skill and technique. Today, it’s remembered as an important early C64 title and a foundational example of space-landing gameplay.

Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, B.C. II: Grog’s Revenge is an action-adventure sequel developed by Sydney Development and published by Sierra On-Line. Continuing the comic-inspired world of B.C.’s Quest for Tires, the game once again follows Thor, the stone-age caveman on his stone unicycle, as he sets off in search of the “Meaning of Life.”

Gameplay alternates between two distinct styles. Mountain sections require careful balance and timing as Thor navigates narrow paths, avoids rocks and holes, and collects clams used as currency to pay tolls. Cave sections shift the pace, limiting visibility to a narrow beam of light and demanding precise movement to avoid hazards while gathering more clams.

Adding constant tension is the ever-present threat of Grog. His thunderous roar can knock Thor from his unicycle at any moment, abruptly ending the journey and reinforcing the game’s risk-reward balance. Progress depends on steady nerves, pattern recognition, and learning when to push forward or slow down.

With expressive animations and a light-hearted tone drawn from Johnny Hart’s original comic strip, B.C. II: Grog’s Revenge delivers a playful yet challenging experience. It remains a fondly remembered title for its humour, distinctive mechanics, and unique place in the Commodore 64 library.

💬 Did you master the caves, or did Grog always get the last laugh?

Originally developed by Konami and released in arcades in 1984, Mikie arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1986 via Imagine Software, bringing its unusual school-based action to home computers. Instead of battling aliens or monsters, players take control of Mikie, a lovestruck student determined to deliver a heartfelt letter to his girlfriend.

Gameplay unfolds across a series of school locations including classrooms, locker rooms, the cafeteria, dance studio, and the playground. Mikie must collect scattered hearts to complete his message, all while avoiding or dealing with teachers, janitors, and other authority figures who are determined to stop his romantic mission.

Each room presents its own hazards and opportunities, encouraging careful movement, timing, and quick thinking. Doors can be opened to reveal surprises, items can be collected for points, and some staff members can be temporarily neutralised, adding a light strategic layer to the action.

The Commodore 64 version is particularly remembered for its soundtrack by Martin Galway, featuring chiptune interpretations of A Hard Day’s Night and Twist and Shout. Combined with its playful premise and varied environments, Mikie stands out as a memorable blend of stealth, action, and humour.

Today, Mikie is fondly remembered as one of the more distinctive arcade conversions on the C64, offering a refreshingly different take on classic arcade gameplay.

jCeyn8T4_do.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/platoon/

Released in 1987 by Ocean Software and published by Data East for the Commodore 64, Platoon is an ambitious action-adventure game based on Oliver Stone’s acclaimed Vietnam War film. Rather than focusing on a single gameplay style, the game attempts to capture the chaos and intensity of combat through multiple distinct scenarios.

The experience is split across four varied segments. Jungle Trek plays as a side-scrolling shooter through hostile terrain filled with traps and enemy patrols. Tunnel Exploration shifts to a tense first-person perspective as you navigate claustrophobic underground passages. Night Ambush uses a fixed-screen viewpoint with limited visibility, forcing careful positioning and awareness, while the Final Assault presents an isometric shooter climax inside an enemy bunker.

A unique morale system underpins the gameplay, dropping if civilians are harmed or objectives are failed, which directly impacts progression. This adds a layer of responsibility and strategy rarely seen in action games of the period. The visuals and sound design reinforce the oppressive atmosphere, aiming for tension rather than arcade spectacle.

Platoon stands out as one of the more thoughtful movie adaptations on the Commodore 64. Its varied structure and thematic ambition have earned it a lasting reputation as a bold and memorable title in late-1980s action gaming.

Released in 1982 by Synapse Software, Fort Apocalypse is a demanding multi-directional scrolling shooter for the Commodore 64. Developed by Steve Hales and ported by Joe Vierra, the game drops players into a vast underground fortress with a single goal: rescue prisoners and dismantle enemy installations while surviving relentless opposition.

Players pilot a highly manoeuvrable rocket copter through sprawling caverns, contending with tight passages, gun turrets, and hostile forces attacking from all directions. Movement and combat require precision, as weapon controls change depending on the helicopter’s orientation, forcing players to think carefully about positioning and timing.

A standout feature is the Navatron system, which provides a radar-style preview of upcoming threats beyond the visible screen. This adds a strategic layer rarely seen at the time, allowing players to plan routes and prepare for ambushes before entering dangerous areas.

Praised for its smooth four-way scrolling and intense difficulty, Fort Apocalypse quickly earned a reputation as one of the Commodore 64’s most impressive early action games. Its blend of twitch skill, situational awareness, and strategic planning has secured its place as a true 8-bit classic.

Released in 1984 by Crystal Computing and developed by Design Design, Halls of the Things is a tense action-adventure that drops you into a mysterious seven-floor tower packed with danger. Programmed by Neil Mottershead, Simon Brattel, and Martin S. Horsley, the game quickly built a reputation for depth, atmosphere, and replay value.

You explore each floor from a top-down perspective, navigating intricate mazes in search of seven magical rings hidden throughout the tower. Once collected, you must locate a magical key deep within the dungeon to unlock the drawbridge and escape alive.

What truly sets the game apart is its randomly generated maze layout, ensuring every run feels different. You’re armed with a mix of sword combat, arrows, fireballs, and lightning spells, all while facing “Things” — enemies that roam the halls and can disguise themselves as harmless objects to catch you off guard.

Critically praised on release, with Sinclair User awarding 9/10 and Zzap!64 scoring it 88%, Halls of the Things became one of the standout dungeon adventures of the era. Later re-released by Firebird and followed by Return of the Things, it remains a defining example of early procedural design on the Commodore 64.

Though often viewed as a modest budget release, The Wombles remains a nostalgic example of British licensed gaming on the Commodore 64 — quirky, charming, and a true time capsule of early 1990s home computing.

Released in 1991 by Audiogenic for the Commodore 64, Exile is a groundbreaking sci-fi action-adventure developed by Peter Irvin and Jeremy Smith. Originally created for the BBC Micro and Acorn Electron, the C64 version preserves the game’s most ambitious ideas, delivering a remarkably deep experience for an 8-bit system.

You play as Mike Finn, a lone pilot sent to the hostile planet Phoebus to rescue a lost research team and stop the rogue scientist Triax. The game blends platforming, exploration, shooting, and puzzle-solving within a vast, interconnected world that can be tackled in multiple ways.

What truly sets Exile apart is its advanced physics and simulation systems. Gravity, inertia, heat, pressure, and enemy behaviour all interact dynamically, meaning the environment constantly responds to your actions. Solutions are rarely scripted, encouraging experimentation and emergent gameplay long before it became a common design philosophy.

On the Commodore 64, Exile delivers smooth performance, intelligent enemy AI, and a surprisingly rich world packed with secrets. The visuals are minimal but purposeful, and the eerie sound design reinforces the isolation and tension of the alien landscape.

Exile is widely regarded as a cult classic and a technical masterpiece. Its influence can be seen in later open-ended and physics-driven games, earning it a reputation as one of the most ambitious and forward-thinking titles ever released on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1983 by Timeworks Inc. for the Commodore 64 and developed by Patrick Quinn, Cave of the Word Wizard is an inventive educational action game that blends platforming with spelling challenges. Designed as an early example of “edutainment,” it combines learning and gameplay using pioneering speech synthesis technology.

Players choose between two characters, Mark or Becky, and explore a multi-level cave in search of four hidden crystals. The underground environment is filled with hazards such as pits, falling rocks, snakes, and scorpions, requiring careful movement and accurate jumping to survive. Each mistake costs one of the player’s limited bandages.

At regular intervals, the mysterious Word Wizard appears to test the player’s spelling skills. Using the keyboard, players must correctly type displayed words to earn rewards. Successful answers restore bandages and trigger encouraging voice feedback, while mistakes result in scolding responses and reduced visibility from a weakening flashlight.

Progress depends on balancing action and education. Players must manage health, light levels, and vocabulary performance while navigating increasingly dangerous cave layouts. The game ends when bandages run out, the flashlight is depleted, or all crystals are collected and the exit is reached.

Visually simple but creatively designed, the game stands out for its ambitious use of speech synthesis and its seamless integration of learning into an arcade-style format. For many players, it provided both entertainment and practical spelling practice in the early home computing era.

Today, Cave of the Word Wizard is remembered as a standout educational title on the Commodore 64, showcasing how early developers experimented with combining fun and learning in meaningful ways.

Released in 1983 by Jeff Minter’s Llamasoft, Attack of the Mutant Camels is a horizontally scrolling shooter that perfectly sums up Minter’s distinctive style. You pilot a small jet fighter defending Earth from waves of giant mutant camels, grotesquely transformed by hostile aliens and marching relentlessly toward your base.

The action is fast and unforgiving. Each camel takes multiple hits to bring down and fires back with streams of deadly projectiles, forcing you to balance aggression with precise movement. Clear a wave and you’re thrown into a hyperspace sequence, dodging high-speed missiles before the next assault begins.

What sets the game apart is its unmistakable presentation. Psychedelic visuals, intense pacing, and an absurd premise combine to create an experience that feels chaotic, funny, and surprisingly tense all at once. It’s instantly recognisable as a Llamasoft production.

Attack of the Mutant Camels earned cult status over the years and even featured in the Smithsonian Institution’s The Art of Video Games exhibition in 2011. Today, it stands as one of the most iconic and unconventional shooters on the Commodore 64.

Gameplay centres on a one-on-one strip poker match, with Maria initially dressed in a Santa Claus outfit to fit the Christmas theme. Critically acclaimed and hugely successful, Last Ninja 2 became one of the best-selling C64 games of all time and is widely regarded as the high point of the series, cementing its status as a true 8-bit classic.

Released in 1983 by Terminal Software for the Commodore 64, Super Gridder is a minimalist arcade-style puzzle game developed and programmed by R. W. Stevens. Also published by Microdigital Ltd., it delivers a deceptively simple concept built around precision, timing, and risk management.

Gameplay takes place on a single 8×8 grid where players control a character tracing the grid’s boundaries. Successfully enclosing a square fills it in, pushing you closer to completion, but danger lurks within the grid itself. Scorpions roam the interior, and a single touch costs a life, forcing careful planning and steady movement.

The challenge comes from balancing speed and accuracy under constant time pressure. Complete the grid before the timer expires to earn bonus points, but rush too much and mistakes can quickly end a run. Every movement matters, turning simple line-drawing into a tense arcade puzzle.

On the Commodore 64, Super Gridder keeps presentation deliberately modest. Clean graphics and straightforward sound effects maintain focus on gameplay, creating a tightly controlled experience that rewards concentration rather than spectacle.

Though often overlooked, Super Gridder has earned a quiet appreciation among retro fans for its clever design and pure arcade challenge. Today, it stands as a strong example of early C64 puzzle games that proved engaging gameplay didn’t need complexity to be effective.

Released in 1985 by Ozark Softscape and published by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64, Heart of Africa is a deep strategy adventure that builds on the foundations of The Seven Cities of Gold. Set in 1890, the game places players in the role of an ambitious explorer searching for the lost tomb of Pharaoh Ahnk Ahnk somewhere in the vast African continent.

Beginning at a port near Cairo with limited supplies, players must carefully plan expeditions across deserts, mountains, rivers, and jungles. Success depends on managing resources, trading goods, and building relationships with indigenous tribes to gather vital clues, maps, and equipment needed to continue the journey.

Progression is driven by exploration, diplomacy, and information gathering. Interactions can involve negotiation, gift-giving, trade, or intimidation, with each approach affecting future encounters. A detailed diary, world map, and inventory system help players track discoveries and organise their expedition.

The game’s top-down scrolling map presents a living, dynamic world that rewards curiosity and persistence. Changing terrain, unpredictable events, and shifting political relationships ensure that no two journeys unfold in exactly the same way.

Notable for its educational elements and emphasis on geography and culture, Heart of Africa also offers strong replay value through its randomly generated tomb location. While occasionally criticised for its pacing, it remains a respected classic, praised for its ambition, storytelling, and thoughtful design. Today, it stands as one of the Commodore 64’s most distinctive exploration adventures.

Released in 1988 by Dynamix and published by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64, Caveman Ugh-Lympics is a tongue-in-cheek sports game that reimagines the Olympic Games through a prehistoric lens. Packed with slapstick humour and over-the-top animation, it turns athletic competition into pure caveman chaos.

The game features six distinct events, each with its own mechanics and timing challenges. From outrunning a rival while a saber-toothed tiger gives chase, to spinning and launching your partner in the absurd Matetoss, every event puts reflexes and precision to the test. Other contests include frantic fire-starting, brutal clubbing duels, dinosaur racing, and pole-vaulting over a very unimpressed Tyrannosaurus rex.

Large, expressive sprites and exaggerated animations give the game its unmistakable personality, while simple sound effects reinforce the lighthearted tone. Each event feels different, keeping the action fresh whether you’re playing solo or rotating through challenges with friends.

Caveman Ugh-Lympics truly shines as a multiplayer experience, supporting up to six players and making it a staple of party play on the C64. Today, it’s fondly remembered as a cult classic that perfectly blends humour, competition, and prehistoric nonsense.

Released in 1987 by Rainbow Arts for the Commodore 64, To Be on Top is an unusual music-themed action game that challenges players to create a chart-topping hit single.

Players roam a busy street, dodging pedestrians, traffic, and roller skaters while visiting locations such as their home, disco, recording studio, and TV station in search of musical inspiration.

Throughout the adventure, mini-games appear on television screens, allowing players to collect bass lines, melodies, accompaniments, and sequences. These elements are then combined using a synthesiser, along with one of sixteen drum patterns, to produce a finished demo track.

Success in the charts unlocks a live television performance, where audience applause determines whether your song reaches number one. This adds a unique performance element rarely seen in 8-bit games.

Visually, the game features colourful characters and lively urban environments that reflect its playful tone. The experience is enhanced by a memorable soundtrack composed by Chris Hülsbeck, showcasing the creative potential of the SID chip.

While unconventional in design, To Be on Top stands out as one of the most imaginative music-based games on the Commodore 64. Its blend of action, creativity, and simulation has earned it lasting appreciation among retro gaming fans.

Today, it’s remembered as a charming and experimental title that highlights Rainbow Arts’ willingness to push creative boundaries.

Released in 1984 by Brøderbund and designed by Will Wright, Raid on Bungeling Bay is a distinctive shoot ’em up that blends fast-paced action with strategic depth. Players pilot a helicopter launched from an aircraft carrier, striking at the Bungeling Empire by bombing factories scattered across multiple islands on a small planetoid.

Gameplay revolves around repeated attack runs against enemy infrastructure while defending the aircraft carrier, which serves as the player’s home base. As missions progress, resistance intensifies with gun turrets, fighter jets, guided missiles, and even a battleship hunting the player down. A hidden island provides a vital opportunity to rearm and refuel, rewarding exploration and careful planning.

What truly sets the game apart is its underlying simulation-style design. Factories evolve over time, developing new defences and technologies if left unchecked, while supply boats visibly move between islands, reinforcing their interdependence. Victory depends on striking quickly and decisively, preventing the Bungeling Empire from escalating its war machine to unstoppable levels.

Raid on Bungeling Bay is often seen as a fascinating precursor to Will Wright’s later work on SimCity. Its mix of action and emergent systems makes it one of the most inventive and thought-provoking shooters on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1986 by Domark for the Commodore 64, Friday the 13th: The Computer Game is a survival horror action-adventure inspired by the iconic slasher film series. Set at the ominous Camp Crystal Lake, players must hunt down and eliminate the masked killer, Jason Voorhees, before he wipes out the camp’s counselors.

Gameplay places you in control of multiple counselors, each with different strengths, as you explore cabins, paths, and interiors while scavenging weapons such as machetes and chainsaws. Survival depends on careful exploration, quick reactions, and protecting other counselors from sudden attacks. A key twist is Jason’s ability to disguise himself as ordinary characters, forcing players to identify him through observation and risky confrontation.

The game uses a pseudo-3D perspective to enhance tension and atmosphere, supported by a distinctive fear meter that rises as panic sets in. Sudden cutaway scenes depicting violent encounters mirror the tone of the films, making it one of the more shocking and atmospheric titles on the C64 at the time.

Although reviews were mixed, with criticism aimed at repetition and limited depth, the game’s ambition and horror focus helped it stand out. Today, Friday the 13th is remembered as a bold licensed experiment and a cult favourite among horror fans and retro gamers alike.

Released in 1985 by Odin Computer Graphics for the Commodore 64, Robin of the Wood is an atmospheric action-adventure maze game programmed by Marc Dawson, featuring graphics by Stuart Fotheringham and music by Fred Gray.

Players step into the role of Robin Hood, exploring the depths of Sherwood Forest in search of the legendary Silver Arrow, which has been seized by the Sheriff of Nottingham. Progress begins by collecting gold to purchase essential equipment, including swords and bows, from the mysterious forest Ent before venturing deeper into hostile territory.

The game unfolds across a vast 16×20 screen maze populated by Norman soldiers, wild boars, witches, a wise Hermit, and surprise encounters with high-ranking medieval figures. Navigation relies on careful exploration, memory, and timing, with screen-by-screen progression rewarding patient and methodical play.

Visually, the game delivers richly detailed 2D environments and smoothly animated sprites that bring the forest to life. Its haunting yet rhythmic SID soundtrack perfectly complements the eerie woodland atmosphere, enhancing immersion throughout the adventure.

Drawing inspiration from Ultimate’s Sabre Wulf, the game establishes its own identity through darker tone and deeper progression systems. Today, Robin of the Wood is remembered as a cult favourite and one of the most distinctive maze adventures on the Commodore 64.

Matches take place in a tournament setting where success depends on positioning, timing, and executing precise joystick combinations to perform throws and holds. The control system rewards planning and technique over fast reactions, making each bout feel tactical and deliberate rather than frantic.

Uchi Mata features more than 400 frames of animation, resulting in fluid and convincing character movement. Players can attempt both legal and illegal judo techniques, with the powerful Uchi Mata throw capable of ending a match instantly. Risky moves come at a cost, however, as repeated fouls can lead to disqualification.

Large, well-animated sprites, detailed arenas, an on-screen referee, and an electronic scoreboard all contribute to the game’s strong simulation feel. These elements help Uchi Mata stand apart from other sports and fighting titles of the era.

Often seen as ahead of its time, Uchi Mata is remembered as a bold and innovative entry in the Commodore 64 library, offering a thoughtful and authentic take on martial arts competition.

kVHVYViVveo.title: Elite – The C64 Space Game That Made the Universe Feel Massive
kVHVYViVveo.description:
🕹️ Elite (1985) – Commodore 64 Space Trading & Combat Simulation Pioneer
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/elite/

Released in 1985 by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Elite is a landmark space trading and combat simulation developed by David Braben and Ian Bell. It introduced players to a vast, open-ended universe of 2,040 star systems, each defined by its own economy, political alignment, and opportunities for profit or danger.

Starting as a novice pilot with a basic ship, players are free to carve their own path toward the coveted Elite combat rating. Lawful trading, smuggling, piracy, bounty hunting, or a careful mix of all four are viable approaches, with player choice shaping every journey. The procedurally generated galaxy ensures a sense of scale and freedom that was unprecedented at the time.

Elite’s technical achievements on the Commodore 64 were extraordinary. Its 3D wireframe vector graphics created a convincing illusion of depth, allowing for space combat, hyperspace travel, and precision docking sequences despite the machine’s limited hardware. Mastery of controls and situational awareness were essential to survival.

Beyond mechanics, Elite offered rich world-building. The included novella The Dark Wheel by Robert Holdstock added narrative depth and mythology, giving context to the universe and reinforcing the sense that players were part of something far larger than a single mission or storyline.

Elite’s influence on game design cannot be overstated. It set the foundation for open-world space simulations and remains one of the most important and respected titles in the Commodore 64 library. Today, it stands as a defining moment in gaming history and a touchstone for the entire genre.

l15ptEz8kng.title: Was 1989 Zzap!64’s Wildest Year? 79 Awards Across 70 C64 & Amiga Games
l15ptEz8kng.description:
🕹️ Every Zzap!64 Gold Medal, Sizzler and Silver Medal awarded to Commodore 64 and Amiga games during 1989 — 79 awards across 70 games, revisited month by month.

Was 1989 Zzap!64’s wildest year? The Amiga was now firmly part of the magazine, C64 and Amiga versions were increasingly reviewed together, and both machines could receive their own overall percentage. The old “16-bit Sizzler” wording had gone too: a Sizzler was simply a Sizzler, whichever Commodore machine earned it.

Across 1989 we have 62 Sizzlers, nine Silver Medals and eight Gold Medals, covering some of the best and most debated C64 and Amiga games of the year.

On the Commodore 64 that includes Operation Wolf, Total Eclipse, MicroProse Soccer, Rocket Ranger, Batman: The Caped Crusader, Zamzara, Project Firestart, Rainbow Islands, Power Drift, The Untouchables, Turbo Out Run, Myth and Stunt Car Racer.

The Amiga brings Elite, Dungeon Master, Populous, R-Type, Kick Off, Blood Money, Federation of Free Traders, Xenon 2: Megablast, Batman: The Movie, North & South and Interphase.

And 1989 produced some Zzap!64 ratings that are still worth arguing about.

Rambo jumped from 65% to an astonishing 96% when it returned at budget price. Strider received 96% on the Amiga despite a much more mixed reception elsewhere. APB received an Amiga Sizzler at only 89%, while several direct comparisons saw the Commodore 64 outscore the Amiga, including LED Storm, Rocket Ranger, The New Zealand Story and Stunt Car Racer.

Budget Silver Medals were another major part of 1989. Pastfinder, Heavy Metal Paradroid, Tetris, Manic Miner, Ghosts ’N Goblins, Pitstop II and Wizball all returned at lower prices and picked up enormous new scores.

So did Zzap!64 get these awards right — or were some of those percentages getting a little generous?

Released in 1994 by Team17 for the Commodore Amiga, Arcade Pool is a polished top-down cue sports game that blends accessible arcade-style play with surprisingly deep and realistic simulation mechanics. It quickly became a favourite among Amiga owners looking for both competitive and casual multiplayer fun.

The game includes several popular pool variants, such as UK 8-ball, US 9-ball, and Killer, with options to compete against computer opponents or up to eight players in hot-seat multiplayer. Its intuitive aiming system and responsive controls make it easy to learn, while still rewarding precision and tactical thinking.

Arcade Pool stands out for its convincing ball physics, clean visual presentation, and smooth animation. Subtle touches such as custom player names, humorous in-game messages, and Team17’s trademark personality give the game added charm and replay value.

Rather than aiming for strict realism, the game strikes a careful balance between authenticity and fun. It delivers fast, flowing matches while preserving the strategic depth that makes cue sports so addictive.

Widely regarded as one of the finest pool games on any 16-bit system, Arcade Pool remains a benchmark for the genre. Today, it’s remembered as a timeless multiplayer classic and one of Team17’s most enduring Amiga successes.

Released in 1986 by Melbourne House and developed by Beam Software, Fist II: The Legend Continues takes the foundations of The Way of the Exploding Fist and expands them into a far more ambitious experience. Rather than a straight sequence of duels, you’re dropped into a sprawling island adventure where exploration and combat are equally important.

You travel across jungles, caves, villages, and ancient temples in search of sacred scrolls, with martial arts battles breaking out whenever rivals challenge your progress. Combat features a deep move set, rewarding timing and technique, while each opponent demands a slightly different approach to win.

Between fights, the game slows the pace deliberately, encouraging exploration, memory, and careful route planning. Progression comes not just from winning battles, but from meditation, learning new techniques, and collecting the scrolls needed to unlock the game’s true ending.

The Commodore 64 version creates a strong sense of atmosphere, with varied environments and a haunting soundtrack by Neil Brennan that gives each area its own identity. While some found the pacing slow and the combat repetitive over long sessions, the scope and ideas on display were unlike anything else in the genre at the time.

Today, Fist II is remembered as an ambitious and unconventional sequel, blending martial arts combat with open-ended exploration and earning a lasting reputation as one of the most distinctive fighting adventures on the C64.

Released in 1986 for the Commodore 64, Spy vs Spy III: Arctic Antics is the third entry in First Star Software’s classic series inspired by MAD Magazine’s iconic comic strip. This time, the Black Spy and White Spy trade tropical islands for the freezing Arctic, where survival is as important as sabotage.

The goal remains familiar: assemble a rocket by locating a Gyroscope, Fuel Canister, and Key Card before your rival does. The icy setting introduces new challenges, including managing body heat, navigating slippery terrain, and avoiding traps hidden beneath the snow. Players must balance exploration with constant interference from the opposing spy.

New tools and mechanics add extra depth and humour, such as snowball fights, snowshoes, ice picks, and the plunger detonator. Levels are presented as flip-screen environments with snowy exteriors and warmer interiors like igloos, which provide both shelter and tactical advantages.

With colourful visuals, a playful soundtrack by Nick Scarim, and support for both single-player and two-player split-screen action, Arctic Antics expands the Spy vs Spy formula in inventive ways. Though reviews were mixed at the time, it remains a nostalgic favourite for fans of the series and a memorable twist on classic cartoon espionage.

Released in 1987 by Players Software under the Interceptor Micros label, Joe Blade is a side-scrolling action platform game for the Commodore 64 developed by Colin Swinbourne. Players take on the role of Joe Blade, a lone commando sent deep into an enemy complex to rescue six kidnapped world leaders from the grip of the villainous Crax Bloodfinger.

The game unfolds across a maze of flip-screen rooms packed with guards, traps, and explosives. Armed with a machine gun and working against a strict time limit, players must carefully explore the complex, disable bombs, and locate hostages while conserving limited ammunition. Progress depends on learning the layout, planning efficient routes, and avoiding costly mistakes.

Each room presents its own hazards, encouraging methodical movement and memorisation rather than reckless action. The emphasis on exploration and timing gives Joe Blade a tense rhythm, where every wrong turn can waste precious seconds or resources.

On the Commodore 64, the game features distinctive sprite work and a bold visual style that helps it stand out among late-80s budget releases. The experience is driven by a memorable soundtrack from Gary Biasillo, whose music adds urgency and atmosphere to the mission.

Joe Blade was a major commercial success on release, reaching the top of the UK charts and proving that budget titles could deliver depth and excitement. Its popularity led to sequels and cemented its place as one of the most recognisable action games in the Commodore 64 library.

Originally developed by Sega AM2 for arcades in 1988, Power Drift roared onto the Commodore 64 in 1990 thanks to an ambitious conversion by Chris Butler, published by Activision. Against the odds, it delivers a bold, high-speed take on 3D arcade racing on 8-bit hardware.

You choose from a colourful roster of drivers and tackle five circuits, each made up of five increasingly demanding tracks. Races unfold across wild, roller-coaster-style courses packed with jumps, tight corners, and dramatic elevation changes, where mastering drifting and momentum is key to staying in the top three and qualifying for the next stage.

The C64 version is a technical showcase, using clever programming tricks to create a convincing sense of depth and speed. While backgrounds are simplified and corners can appear suddenly, the fast, responsive handling keeps the action flowing. David Lowe’s energetic soundtrack does a superb job of capturing the spirit of Sega’s arcade original.

Celebrated for pushing the Commodore 64 far beyond expectations, Power Drift remains one of the system’s most impressive racing games and a standout example of how arcade ambition could still shine on 8-bit hardware.

Building on the success of the original, the sequel delivers faster combat, tougher enemies, and more varied stage design.

The C64 version preserves the core arcade experience, featuring side-scrolling brawling action, cooperative two-player gameplay, and a wide range of martial arts techniques. Players can punch, kick, jump, and use weapons to fight their way through gangs of enemies and imposing boss characters.

Each stage introduces new environments and enemy types, gradually increasing the challenge. While occasional slowdown can occur during intense scenes, the smooth scrolling and colourful graphics help maintain the game’s fast-paced momentum.

The soundtrack, composed by Dave Lowe, adds energy and atmosphere to the action, reinforcing the dramatic tone of the revenge storyline. Although some weapons and enemy behaviours differ slightly from the arcade original, the overall experience remains faithful and highly playable.

Widely praised for its accessibility and replay value, Double Dragon II on the Commodore 64 stands as one of the platform’s strongest beat ’em ups. Today, it’s remembered as a benchmark title that demonstrated how close home computers could come to true arcade-quality action.

Players take command of a U.S. Navy Gato-class submarine, embarking on tense war patrols against Japanese shipping with survival depending on patience, planning, and precision.

Gameplay is split between strategic navigation and high-stakes combat. During patrols, players plot courses, manage fuel and systems, and decide when to engage or evade. Combat brings torpedo targeting, sonar interpretation, periscope tracking, and evasive manoeuvres as enemy escorts hunt you down. Weather conditions, day-night cycles, and detection mechanics all play a critical role in each encounter.

The simulation places strong emphasis on realism, featuring authentic instrumentation, damage modelling, and multiple difficulty levels that cater to both newcomers and experienced players. Success requires careful decision-making, resource management, and a steady nerve, reflecting the slow, methodical nature of real submarine warfare.

Praised for its depth and authenticity, Silent Service helped define the naval simulation genre on home computers. Today, it remains a respected and influential classic, remembered for bringing thoughtful, strategic gameplay to the Commodore 64.

Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Skool Daze is an open-world action-adventure developed by Microsphere and designed by David Reidy, with graphics by Keith Warrington. Players take control of Eric, a mischievous schoolboy on a mission to retrieve his disastrous report card from the headmaster’s safe before it’s sent home.

To succeed, Eric must explore a fully interactive school building, attending lessons, sneaking through corridors, and outwitting teachers. The safe’s combination is uncovered by firing a catapult at shields around the school, each linked to a letter held by a different member of staff. Timing, planning, and clever mischief are essential.

What sets Skool Daze apart is its pioneering sandbox design. Teachers and pupils follow their own routines, creating a living, unpredictable environment. Eric must balance rule-breaking with caution, as accumulating too many “lines” leads to expulsion and game over.

Blending stealth, strategy, and humour, Skool Daze became one of the most influential titles on the Commodore 64. Its open-ended structure and interactive world laid the groundwork for future sandbox games, and its success led to the sequel Back to Skool, expanding on the original’s ideas.
