You control a lone android dropped into a hostile, futuristic maze with one objective: eliminate five deadly Millitoids before time runs out.

Gameplay blends fast maze navigation with careful combat. The wrap-around arena design keeps enemies constantly in play, while hazards like landmines, indestructible robots, and hostile aliens force you to think several moves ahead. Ammunition is limited, so success depends on positioning, timing, and knowing when to engage or evade.

What truly sets Android 2 apart is its technical ambition. The scrolling, pseudo-3D maze was highly unusual for early 1980s home computers, giving the game a strong arcade feel and a real sense of depth and motion. The pressure of the countdown timer adds urgency to every decision.

Today, Android 2 is remembered as a forward-thinking early C64 title. Its mix of arcade inspiration, maze strategy, and technical flair earned it lasting respect and makes it a fascinating snapshot of innovation during the platform’s formative years.

Set in a colourful jungle environment, the game mixes arcade action with competitive scoring.

Players control Floyd as he leaps through the jungle, avoiding hazards such as alligators, elephants, and hostile pygmies. The goal is to rescue Janice, but competition is fierce, as rivals George and another Floyd are also racing to impress her. Simple, energetic, and unmistakably arcade-inspired, Floyd of the Jungle stands out as a rare and intriguing entry in Sid Meier’s catalogue and a memorable part of the Commodore 64 library.

Picking up after the rescue of the wizard Gimbal, Magic Knight is unexpectedly transported to the 25th century aboard the starship USS Pisces, far from his medieval roots.

The adventure blends fantasy and science fiction as players explore futuristic locations, interact with crew members and aliens, and work toward assembling the Golden Sundial to return home. Knight Tyme uses the Windimation system, a menu-driven interface that allows players to select actions and objects rather than type commands. This approach makes interaction clear and accessible while still offering layered puzzles, inventory management, and meaningful choices that affect progress.

On the Commodore 64, the game is enhanced by atmospheric graphics and a memorable soundtrack composed by David Whittaker, adding weight and mood to the sci-fi setting. Knight Tyme is remembered as an ambitious and creative adventure that helped push graphic storytelling forward on the C64.

Released in 1986 by Access Software, Leader Board is a landmark golf simulation that redefined realism in sports games on home computers. Originally developed for the Commodore 64 and later enhanced on the Amiga, the game introduced precision mechanics and presentation that set a new benchmark for virtual golf.

Gameplay is built around four full 18-hole courses, viewed from behind the golfer for a realistic perspective of the fairways and greens. Players control shot power and direction using a timing bar, with carefully timed inputs allowing shots to hook or slice. This added a layer of skill and finesse that rewarded practice and consistency rather than guesswork.

The Amiga version benefits from smoother animation and improved visuals, making courses feel more alive and immersive. Water hazards, bunkers, and varied terrain demand thoughtful club selection and strategic play, while subtle risk-and-reward decisions keep every hole engaging.

Highly praised on release by magazines such as Zzap!64 and Your Sinclair, Leader Board became one of the most influential sports games of its era. Its balance of accessibility and depth laid the groundwork for future golf simulations and secured its reputation as a true classic on both the Commodore 64 and Amiga.

Survival depends on observation, timing, and learning from mistakes, creating a challenging but deeply immersive experience.

A key gameplay feature is Lester’s energy gun, which can fire standard shots, generate protective shields, and unleash powerful charged blasts. Mastering these abilities is essential for overcoming enemies and solving environmental obstacles throughout the journey.

Visually, Another World stands out for its use of vector-style graphics and fluid animation, delivering expressive characters and cinematic scenes that were years ahead of their time. Subtle sound design and atmospheric music further enhance the sense of isolation and mystery.

Widely praised for its innovation and artistic ambition, Another World became one of the most influential games of the early 1990s. Its minimalist storytelling and emotional impact helped redefine interactive narrative and secured its status as a timeless classic in retro gaming history.

Julie Dunn’s cheerful SID soundtrack complements the colourful presentation and helps give the game its distinctive tone. A major commercial success, Finders Keepers laid the groundwork for the Magic Knight series and remains a fondly remembered Commodore 64 classic.

Released in 1990 by Gray Matter and published by Mindscape, Fiendish Freddy’s Big Top o’ Fun brings dark humour and arcade-style action to the Commodore 64. Originally a 16-bit title, the game was later converted to the C64 and became one of the showcase releases for the Commodore 64 Games System, highlighting what the platform could still achieve late in its life.

Players are tasked with saving a failing circus from demolition by successfully performing six dangerous circus acts. These include diving, juggling, trapeze, knife throwing, tightrope walking, and the human cannonball, each presented as a distinct mini-game with its own rules, timing, and skill demands.

Adding chaos to every performance is Fiendish Freddy himself, a malicious saboteur who interferes at the worst possible moments. His unpredictable antics turn otherwise straightforward acts into tense, reactive challenges that demand concentration and quick reactions.

On the Commodore 64, the game delivers strong visuals and expressive animations that retain the personality of the original version. The presentation is enhanced by lively music and exaggerated sound effects that reinforce the slapstick circus theme and keep the tone playful despite the rising difficulty.

Fiendish Freddy’s Big Top o’ Fun stands out as one of the most inventive late-era C64 releases, combining humour, variety, and arcade challenge into a single package. Today, it’s remembered as a bold and memorable circus-themed game that pushed the platform in unexpected directions.

Enemies range from ghosts to ghoulies, reinforcing the game’s uneasy tone. The lack of traditional goals or rewards heightens the sense of dread, making survival itself the only objective. This structure gives Frightmare a distinctive rhythm that sets it apart from more conventional platformers.

With atmospheric visuals and restrained sound design, Frightmare delivers an unsettling experience that lingers long after play. Though notoriously difficult and unconventional, it has earned a cult following for its originality and its bold interpretation of a nightmare brought to life on the C64.

Released in 1987 by Martech for the Commodore 64, Nemesis the Warlock is an action platform game based on the iconic 2000 AD comic series created by Pat Mills and Kevin O’Neill. Developed by Creative Reality, the game brings the dark sci-fi world of Nemesis to life in fast-paced 8-bit form.

Players take control of Nemesis, a powerful alien warrior armed with both a gun and a sword, battling through 30 single-screen levels packed with enemies and hazards. Progress depends on defeating a required number of Terminators on each stage, encouraging aggressive and tactical play.

One of the game’s most distinctive mechanics is the ability to pile up defeated enemies and use their bodies as makeshift platforms. This unusual feature adds a strategic layer to level navigation and sets Nemesis apart from traditional platformers of the era.

Visually, the game makes strong use of colour and fluid sprite animation to convey movement and impact. While backgrounds are relatively minimal, the clear presentation keeps the focus on intense action and precise positioning.

A major highlight is Rob Hubbard’s driving soundtrack, which reinforces the game’s dark atmosphere and relentless pace. His music remains one of the most memorable aspects of the C64 version.

Although sometimes criticised for repetitive structure, Nemesis the Warlock is widely praised for its polish and originality. Today, it stands as a cult classic and one of the finest comic-book adaptations on the Commodore 64.

MjVEFcdKWgI.title: Cosmic Convoy – The C64 Shooter Where Losing the Convoy Meant Everything

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Cosmic Convoy (1983), developed by Andy Walker and published by Taskset, is a horizontal shoot-’em-up for the Commodore 64 with a unique escort-based gameplay twist.

In the game, you pilot a squadron of three fighter ships tasked with protecting a convoy of relief freighters as they travel through the solar system “System Coman.”

Unlike many traditional shooters, Cosmic Convoy focuses on defence rather than pure attack. You must intercept incoming alien waves before they crash into the vulnerable convoy ships.

Movement is fully four-directional, with the screen scrolling only as your fighters move. A long-range radar display beneath the main play area shows convoy routes and approaching enemies, adding a strategic layer to the action.

You are given two squadrons in total, and the game ends if either all freighters are destroyed or your fighters are wiped out. Successfully reaching each planet earns medals and bonus points.

Graphically, the game reflects early-1980s C64 design with simple sprites, minimal backgrounds, and basic sound effects. However, the escort-mission structure and radar system give it a distinctive identity among early shooters.

While not one of the most famous C64 titles, Cosmic Convoy remains an interesting and worthwhile experience for fans of early 8-bit shoot-’em-ups and the Taskset catalogue.

Skull & Crossbones (1991), developed by Walking Circles and published by Domark / Tengen, is a pirate-themed side-scrolling beat ’em up for the Commodore 64.

Players choose between One Eye or Red Dog, two swashbuckling heroes on a mission to recover stolen treasure and rescue a kidnapped princess from an evil wizard.

The adventure takes you through ships, castles, caves, and other exotic locations, battling waves of enemies and powerful bosses along the way.

Between stages, collected loot can be traded to upgrade weapons such as cutlasses, knives, and flintlock pistols, adding a light role-playing element to progression.

The C64 conversion removes some arcade features, including true simultaneous co-op, replacing it with alternating turns. Controls are often criticised for feeling sluggish, with certain actions requiring awkward inputs.

One standout feature is the soundtrack by Matt Furniss, which delivers a memorable high-seas theme — though players must choose between music and sound effects.

While imperfect, Skull & Crossbones remains a notable example of an ambitious arcade port on the Commodore 64, earning cult status among fans of pirate-themed action games.

Players take control of Alphonse T. Nurd, a lab assistant who accidentally creates a duplicate of himself after activating a malfunctioning machine.

The objective is to reunite with this mischievous double by navigating five increasingly complex laboratory stages. Gameplay centres on puzzle-platform mechanics, requiring careful use of switches, elevators, and timing-based movement to progress through each room.

What sets Schizofrenia apart is the behaviour of the duplicate, which actively interferes with the player’s plans. This constant disruption forces strategic thinking and precise execution, as even small mistakes can undo progress. The tight controls and escalating difficulty demand patience and concentration.

While reviews at the time were mixed—some praising the originality and challenge, others criticising the steep learning curve—Schizofrenia has since earned a small but dedicated following. Its inventive premise and demanding design make it a distinctive entry in the Commodore 64’s puzzle platform catalogue.

Originally released in arcades by Capcom in 1987 and later ported to the Amiga in 1990 by U.S. Gold, Black Tiger delivers a fast-paced blend of action, exploration, and light RPG mechanics. Players step into the role of a barbarian warrior battling through a hostile fantasy world filled with monsters, traps, and hidden secrets.

Armed with a morning star and throwing daggers, the hero must fight through eight sprawling stages packed with enemies and powerful end-of-level bosses. Along the way, players collect the in-game currency Zenny, which can be spent on upgrades such as stronger weapons, armour, keys, and vital items purchased from mysterious wise men found throughout the levels.

The Amiga version features both horizontal and vertical scrolling, secret dungeons, and hidden treasure chests that reward careful exploration. While the port captures the structure and gameplay of the arcade original, it received mixed feedback at the time due to technical compromises, including uneven scrolling and a presentation that didn’t fully match Capcom’s coin-op standard.

Despite this, Black Tiger remains fondly remembered by Amiga fans for its addictive combat loop, progression system, and arcade heritage. Today, it stands as a solid example of late-80s arcade design making the jump to home computers.

Based on Adrian Edmondson’s book, it drops you into a house party with a single goal: cause as much chaos as possible and drive every guest away.

Played from an isometric perspective, the game revolves around exploring rooms, interacting with objects, and performing increasingly antisocial actions to rack up “bastard points.” You’ll need to juggle meters such as the Weeometer, Drunkometer, and Fartometer, balancing maximum disruption with personal survival.

Rather than traditional puzzles, progress comes from experimentation and timing, learning how different actions affect guests and the party atmosphere. Its humour leans heavily into satire, mocking social etiquette and pushing boundaries far beyond typical 8-bit adventures.

Divisive on release but unforgettable, How to Be a Complete Bastard earned cult status thanks to its originality and unapologetic tone. Today it stands as one of the boldest and strangest titles in the C64 library.

mWyXf7yKoLs.title: Ikari Warriors – Why Were There Two Different C64 Versions?
mWyXf7yKoLs.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/ikari-warriors/

Originally released in arcades in 1986 by SNK, Ikari Warriors became one of the defining run-and-gun shooters of the era, and its Commodore 64 history is notable for having two very different home conversions.

The first C64 version arrived in 1986 via Data East and Quicksilver Software, offering a single-player experience split into four phases. This early take delivers straightforward vertical shooting with basic visuals and limited enemy variety, capturing the core idea of the arcade but in a stripped-back form.

A later and far more ambitious 1988 release by Elite Systems refined the formula significantly. This version supports both solo play and two-player simultaneous action, with improved graphics, stronger sound, and more varied enemy behaviour. You fight your way through jungles, rivers, and fortified positions, using power-ups, tanks, and helicopters to survive the onslaught.

While neither C64 version could replicate the arcade’s distinctive rotary joystick controls, both adaptations helped bring Ikari Warriors’ intense combat to home systems. Today, the Elite version in particular is remembered as one of the stronger run-and-gun shooters on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1986 by Palace Software, The Sacred Armour of Antiriad is a landmark action-adventure on the Commodore 64, blending exploration, combat, and progression in a way that was ahead of its time. Set in a distant post-apocalyptic future, the game casts players as Tal, a lone warrior facing an alien threat that has devastated the world.

Progression is driven by exploration across interconnected environments, with access to new areas tied directly to abilities gained along the way. Central to this is the legendary Antiriad battlesuit, which grants Tal the power to fly, survive radiation zones, and engage enemies more effectively. Recovering and upgrading the suit transforms both movement and combat, encouraging careful backtracking and discovery.

Energy management plays a key role, as both Tal and the armour draw from limited reserves. Players must balance exploration, combat, and survival, adding a strategic edge to what might otherwise be straightforward action. Hostile creatures, environmental hazards, and maze-like level design demand patience and planning.

The Commodore 64 version is especially well regarded for its detailed sprites, fluid animation, and atmospheric presentation. Music by Richard Joseph enhances the sense of isolation and danger, reinforcing the game’s distinctive tone.

Today, The Sacred Armour of Antiriad is widely recognised as an early example of Metroidvania-style design and remains one of the most innovative action-adventure titles in the C64 library.

n11taRLnacg.title: Donkey Kong – Why Did the C64 Get TWO Different Official Arcade Conversions?
n11taRLnacg.description:
🕹️ Donkey Kong (1983 / 1986) – Commodore 64 Arcade Platforming Legend
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/donkey-kong/

Donkey Kong is one of the most iconic arcade games of all time, and on the Commodore 64 it arrived in two very different forms. The first port, released in 1983 by Atarisoft, aimed to replicate the arcade original as closely as possible, delivering familiar layouts, bold colours, and a faithful sense of challenge that many players still regard as the most authentic C64 version.

In 1986, Ocean Software released their own take on Donkey Kong, featuring more detailed graphics and enhanced sound. While visually more polished, this version takes a few liberties with the arcade feel, making it a fascinating comparison for long-time fans of the game.

In both releases, you control Jumpman as he climbs girders, ladders, and elevators to rescue Lady from the clutches of Donkey Kong. Across four classic stages — the Construction Zone, Cement Factory, Elevator Stage, and the Final Rescue — success depends on precise timing, smart movement, and learning enemy patterns under constant pressure.

Whether you prefer Atarisoft’s arcade-accurate approach or Ocean’s more refined presentation, Donkey Kong on the Commodore 64 remains a cornerstone of platform gaming history and a true test of skill that still holds up today.

💬 Which C64 version do you prefer — Atarisoft’s arcade faithfulness or Ocean’s enhanced take?

N202Hy1dvQI.title: Floor 13 – The Amiga Game That Put You in Charge of a Secret Government
N202Hy1dvQI.description:
🕹️ Floor 13 (1992) – Commodore Amiga Political Strategy Espionage Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/floor-13/

Released in 1992 by Virgin Interactive Entertainment and developed by PSI Software Designers, Floor 13 is a dark political strategy game for the Commodore Amiga that places players at the heart of a shadowy British government agency. Operating from the infamous secret 13th floor, you assume the role of Director General, tasked with keeping the government in power by any means necessary.

Gameplay is driven through a menu-based interface styled with a film noir presentation, blending espionage, bureaucracy, and moral compromise. Players issue orders to departments such as surveillance, propaganda, blackmail, and assassination in order to suppress scandals, manipulate public opinion, and neutralise threats to government stability. Every decision carries consequences, often with unpredictable outcomes.

Public approval is reviewed every 21 days, and failure to maintain sufficient popularity can result in dismissal, imprisonment, or assassination. The game’s scenarios are semi-randomised, ensuring no two playthroughs unfold the same way, while subplots involving secret societies and internal conspiracies add further depth and tension.

On the Amiga, Floor 13 stands out for its moody visuals, subdued colour palette, and atmospheric soundtrack, all of which reinforce its bleak and cynical tone. Rather than focusing on action, the experience is built around pressure, consequence, and the uncomfortable weight of authority.

Bold, controversial, and far ahead of its time, Floor 13 remains a cult classic celebrated for its satirical take on power and political manipulation. Today, it’s remembered as one of the most distinctive and daring strategy games ever released on the Commodore Amiga.

💬 Did you rule through subtle manipulation, or embrace ruthless control to stay in power?

Murder on the Mississippi is a classic detective adventure for the Commodore 64 that places players aboard the luxury paddle steamer Delta Princess. While enjoying a holiday cruise, renowned detective Sir Charles Foxworth and his loyal servant Regis stumble upon a grim discovery: the body of Raleigh Cartwright III. With the ship due to arrive in New Orleans in just three days, time is running out to catch the killer before they escape.

Gameplay blends exploration with investigation, using joystick-controlled movement and a context-sensitive command menu. Players walk the decks, inspect cabins, examine evidence, and interact with passengers and crew, all of whom may be suspects. Early progress depends on locating the body, after which characters become far more forthcoming with information.

The heart of the game lies in careful note-taking and deduction. Players must gather statements, share information between characters, and piece together contradictions and motives. When confident, an accusation can be made directly against a suspect, with the outcome depending entirely on how thoroughly the evidence has been collected.

Featuring multiple endings and varied outcomes, Murder on the Mississippi rewards methodical investigation and logical thinking. Its race-against-the-clock structure and narrative focus make it a memorable and tense adventure, standing out as one of the Commodore 64’s more engaging detective experiences.

Released in 1989, Turbo Out Run is a high-speed arcade racer developed by Sega AM2 and expertly converted to the Commodore 64 by Probe Software. Acting as a sequel to Out Run, the game sends players on a coast-to-coast race from New York City to Los Angeles, battling a rival Porsche 959 while dodging traffic and police along the way.

Gameplay builds on the original formula with the introduction of a turbo boost system, allowing brief bursts of extreme speed at critical moments. Across 16 stages, players can upgrade their Ferrari F40 every fourth level, choosing improvements such as engine power, turbo performance, and tyre grip to stay competitive as the difficulty ramps up.

The Commodore 64 version is widely praised for its sense of speed and smooth scrolling, delivering an impressive arcade-style experience on 8-bit hardware. The presentation is elevated further by Jeroen Tel’s outstanding SID soundtrack, with tracks like Rush A Difficulty and Keep Your Heart becoming firm favourites among C64 fans.

Critically acclaimed on release, Turbo Out Run earned some of the highest review scores of its era. Despite minor criticisms around car size and tape multiload interruptions, it remains one of the most celebrated racing games on the Commodore 64 and a benchmark for arcade conversions.

Released in 1987 by Electronic Arts, Skate or Die! is a landmark skateboarding game for the Commodore 64 and a defining slice of 1980s gaming culture. Notably, it was EA’s first internally developed title, helping establish the publisher’s early reputation for polished, personality-driven sports games.

The game offers five distinct skateboarding events, each focusing on a different skill set. Players can compete in Freestyle half-pipe trick sessions, test timing in the High Jump, race downhill at speed, battle opponents in Downhill Jam, or knock rivals off their boards in the chaotic Joust mode. This variety gives the game an arcade-style structure that keeps play sessions fast and competitive.

One of Skate or Die!’s standout features is its multiplayer support, allowing up to eight players to compete by rotating turns, making it a popular choice for social gaming. On the Commodore 64, the game was especially praised for its fluid animations and expressive character sprites, which captured the rebellious skate culture of the era.

The iconic title theme by Rob Hubbard is frequently cited as one of the C64’s most memorable pieces of music, featuring sampled guitar effects that pushed the hardware in new directions. While opinions on the controls and long-term depth were mixed, Skate or Die! left a lasting impact and helped pave the way for future skateboarding and extreme sports games.

Released in 1984 by Epyx for the Commodore 64, Pitstop II is a landmark racing game that redefined multiplayer competition on home computers. Designed by Dennis Caswell and Stephen Landrum, it famously introduced split-screen racing, allowing two players to compete head-to-head simultaneously—an innovation that set it apart from its contemporaries.

Players race across six international circuits, including Brands Hatch, Hockenheim, Sebring, and Watkins Glen, choosing from multiple difficulty levels and race lengths. On track, success depends on precision driving, careful braking, and learning each circuit’s flow as speeds and pressure increase.

What truly elevates Pitstop II is its strategic depth. Fuel consumption and tyre wear must be monitored closely, with pit stops playing a crucial role. Rather than being automated, players take direct control of the pit crew, manually changing tyres and refuelling as quickly as possible, turning every stop into a tense, skill-based mini-game.

Critically acclaimed on release, Pitstop II earned an 89% score from Zzap!64 and remains widely regarded as one of the finest racing games on the Commodore 64. Its blend of competitive multiplayer, strategy, and technical ambition has secured its place as a true C64 classic.

Players take on the role of Ben E. Factor, a former soldier turned hero, tasked with rescuing the kidnapped Merry Men across six moons of the planet Minniat.

The game spans 60 carefully designed levels that combine traditional platforming with strategic planning. Players must avoid enemies, activate switches, manipulate the environment, and escort vulnerable characters to safety, creating gameplay reminiscent of Lemmings but with direct, hands-on control.

Each Merry Man has unique behaviours and abilities that influence how puzzles are solved. Some require protection and guidance, while others must be “reformed” using special colouring machines before they can be rescued. These mechanics add variety and depth to every stage.

Benefactor features three difficulty settings, with higher modes carrying damage between levels, increasing tension and rewarding consistent performance. The CD32 edition further enhances the experience with improved audio and visual presentation.

Praised for its colourful graphics, imaginative level design, and atmospheric soundtrack, Benefactor remains one of the most charming puzzle-platformers on the Amiga. Today, it stands as a showcase of DICE’s early creativity and a beloved classic among retro gaming fans.

Released in 1987 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Head Over Heels is a landmark isometric action-adventure created by Jon Ritman and Bernie Drummond. Building on the ideas introduced in Batman, it pushed the genre forward with a clever dual-character system and a vast, interconnected world to explore.

You control two very different heroes. Head can leap higher and fire doughnuts to temporarily paralyse enemies, while Heels runs faster, climbs certain staircases, and carries objects. Progress depends on knowing when to switch between them, using their unique abilities to solve puzzles, avoid traps, and outsmart enemies across hundreds of rooms.

The game’s surreal environments, precise isometric design, and thoughtful room layouts reward patience and planning. On the C64, the colourful visuals and atmospheric soundtrack by Guy Stevens help give each area its own identity, drawing you deeper into its strange, offbeat universe.

Today, Head Over Heels is rightly regarded as one of the finest action-adventures on the Commodore 64. Its originality, scale, and elegant design have secured its status as an all-time classic that still stands up decades later.

Limited energy supplies, hostile environments, and malfunctioning machinery add constant pressure. Success depends on balancing speed with caution, learning the facility’s layout, and using each android effectively to reach the reactor core in time.

Praised for its scale and technical ambition, Countdown to Meltdown pushed the Commodore 64 well beyond typical expectations for early 3D games. Today, it stands as a landmark title, remembered for its complexity, challenge, and bold design philosophy.

Players take on the role of a daring explorer racing to rescue a captured woman from hostile cannibals. The adventure is split across four varied stages, each testing different skills. Released on the Commodore 64 in 1984, River Raid is a vertically scrolling shooter developed by Micro Projects Engineering and published by Activision. Originally designed by Carol Shaw for the Atari 2600, this C64 version brings the same intense aerial combat and precision gameplay to Commodore’s 8-bit hardware.

Players pilot the B-1 StratoWing Assault Jet along the perilous “River of No Return,” blasting enemy helicopters, jets, tankers, bridges, and fuel depots while navigating ever-narrowing river passages. Movement is restricted to horizontal control and speed adjustment, demanding sharp reflexes and careful positioning at all times.

A defining feature is fuel management. Supplies constantly drain as you fly, forcing players to skim over fuel depots to stay airborne. This simple mechanic adds strategic tension to the action, rewarding risk-taking and route planning alongside shooting accuracy.

Praised for its smooth scrolling, responsive controls, and endlessly replayable design, River Raid became one of the most recognisable shooters of the 8-bit era. On the Commodore 64, it stands as a benchmark for pure arcade-style gameplay and remains a timeless classic in the genre.

Released in 1987 by System 3 for the Commodore 64, The Last Ninja is a landmark action-adventure that pushed the machine to its limits. You play as Armakuni, the sole survivor of a destroyed ninja clan, on a quest for revenge against the evil shogun Kunitoki and the recovery of a sacred scroll.

The adventure unfolds across six large isometric levels, ranging from serene gardens to dangerous wastelands, underground dungeons, and Kunitoki’s heavily guarded palace. Movement is deliberate and precise, with narrow paths, traps, and environmental hazards demanding careful control and spatial awareness.

Combat is unusually deep for its time, allowing you to strike enemies at different body areas using a combination of direction and timing. A wide selection of ninja weapons—including the ninjato, nunchaku, staff, shuriken, and smoke bombs—adds tactical variety, while puzzles and hidden items encourage exploration and observation.

Visually, The Last Ninja stands out with high-resolution sprites, fluid animation, and a cinematic sense of presentation that few C64 games could match. Ben Daglish’s atmospheric soundtrack further elevates the experience, perfectly matching the game’s tone and locations.

Critically and commercially successful, The Last Ninja became one of the Commodore 64’s best-selling titles and spawned two sequels. Today, it’s remembered as a defining example of ambition, style, and technical excellence on 8-bit hardware.

Released in 1985 by Creative Sparks and developed by James Allen, Mad Doctor is a darkly inventive action-adventure for the Commodore 64 that blends horror themes with open-ended gameplay. Players step into the role of Professor Franz Johann Blockenspiel, an unhinged scientist determined to create life by assembling and reanimating a creature from stolen body parts.

Set in the eerie village of Struddleberg, the game unfolds across six interconnected areas including a castle, graveyard, forest, village districts, and Lightning Hill. Exploration is key, as players search for tools, ingredients, and body parts while navigating hostile villagers who become increasingly suspicious of your activities.

The game runs from a top-down, fixed-screen perspective and introduces survival elements such as hunger, thirst, and health management. A day-and-night cycle adds further tension, forcing players to carefully plan movements and actions to avoid capture or attack.

Mad Doctor also features an early command-based interaction system, allowing players to manipulate objects and characters in flexible ways. Multiple endings are possible depending on choices made, particularly during the final public unveiling of your creation.

Celebrated for its originality and unsettling atmosphere, Mad Doctor stands apart from typical C64 releases of the era. Today, it’s remembered as a cult classic that dared to experiment with narrative freedom, moral consequence, and horror-driven gameplay.

Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Army Moves is a tough scrolling action shooter developed by Dinamic Software and published by Imagine Software. As the first entry in the famous Moves trilogy, it tasks players with a dangerous military mission to recover stolen secret documents from heavily guarded enemy territory.

The game is split into two distinct gameplay phases across seven levels. The opening stages place you in control of a jeep and later a helicopter, navigating hostile landscapes packed with enemy vehicles, gun emplacements, and relentless fire. These sections demand sharp reflexes, precise positioning, and constant awareness as threats attack from all directions.

The final stages switch perspective to on-foot action, transforming the game into a tense platform shooter. Players must infiltrate enemy bases, dodge grenades, avoid traps, and carefully time jumps while pushing deeper into fortified areas. This shift in gameplay adds variety and keeps the challenge fresh right through to the end.

On the Commodore 64, Army Moves is remembered for its smooth scrolling, responsive controls, and uncompromising difficulty. Fred Gray’s soundtrack, featuring military-style themes such as Colonel Bogey, reinforces the game’s wartime atmosphere. While its brutal challenge divided opinion on release, Army Moves has since earned cult status as one of the C64’s most demanding and distinctive action titles.

Released in 1983 by Commodore International for the Commodore 64, International Soccer is a pioneering football game developed by Andrew Spencer. Known in some regions as Cup Final or Voetbal 64, it was one of the first soccer titles to present the action from a realistic side-on perspective, helping to shape the future of sports games on home computers.

Matches feature two teams of six players and can be played solo against the computer or head-to-head with a second player. Games are split into two 200-second halves, with no fouls or offside rules, keeping the focus firmly on fast, uninterrupted play. Players can choose from six kit colours and even switch to a grayscale mode designed for black-and-white televisions.

The gameplay is smooth and responsive, with flowing scrolling and intuitive controls that made it instantly accessible. Its emphasis on movement, passing, and positioning laid the groundwork for many football games that followed throughout the 1980s.

International Soccer was widely praised on release and earned a Certificate of Merit for Best Computer Sports Game at the 1984 Arkie Awards. Later re-released by CRL in 1988, it remains a landmark title and a fondly remembered classic in the Commodore 64’s sports library.

Released in 1985 by Firebird Software for the Commodore 64, Raging Beast—originally titled Olé!—is a lighthearted arcade-style game that puts a playful spin on the traditional bullfighting spectacle. Developed by François Lionet, with graphics by Frédéric Pinlet and music by Jim Cuomo, the game focuses on timing, nerve, and quick reactions rather than violence.

Players step into the arena as a torero, using a red cloak to lure and dodge a charging bull within a fixed-perspective playfield. Points are awarded for well-timed evasions, but progress depends on waiting for a ring to be thrown into the arena and successfully placing it onto the bull’s horns. A mistimed dodge sends the torero flying, and failing to recover quickly can end the round in spectacular fashion.

The tone is deliberately comical, with colourful visuals and exaggerated animations keeping things playful and accessible. The controls are simple and the objective clear, making it easy to pick up while still demanding precise movement as the bull’s aggression ramps up.

While not a technical showcase, Raging Beast stands out for its originality and humour, offering a distinctly different arcade experience that has earned it a fond place among Commodore 64 curiosities.

Released in 1984 by Taskset for the Commodore 64, Poster Paster is a quirky arcade-style platform game designed by Andy Walker, with music composed by Paul Hodgson. You play as Bill Stickers, a hard-working billboard poster racing against time to plaster advertisements across a series of increasingly hazardous cityscapes.

Each fixed-screen level challenges you to position ladders and apply poster sections in the correct order, all while dodging a cast of mischievous troublemakers including Gnurds, Wazzocks, and Brain Drains. Careful planning is essential, as poor ladder placement or mistimed movement can quickly bring your shift to a sticky end.

A unique twist comes in the form of the Paste Consistency Gauge, which forces you to manage how thick or thin your paste is before applying posters. Get it wrong and the poster won’t stick, adding an extra layer of strategy to what initially looks like simple arcade action.

With bold, multi-coloured visuals, a catchy if repetitive chiptune soundtrack, and tongue-in-cheek references to 1980s computer culture, Poster Paster stands out for its originality. While it never reached classic status, it remains a distinctive and memorable entry in the Commodore 64’s early arcade catalogue.

Released in 1993 by Electronic Arts for the Commodore Amiga, Space Hulk is a tense real-time tactical game set in the dark, brutal universe of Warhammer 40,000. Based on Games Workshop’s 1989 board game, it places players in command of elite Space Marine squads sent into derelict spacecraft infested with deadly Genestealers.

Gameplay blends first-person action with strategic squad management. Players control up to five Space Marines simultaneously, each viewed through their own 3D window, while coordinating movement, positioning, and firepower through narrow, claustrophobic corridors. Missions range from extermination and escort duties to data retrieval and object recovery.

A key feature is the innovative “freeze-time” system, which allows players to pause the action briefly to issue commands. This mechanic adds vital tactical depth, letting players react to sudden ambushes and carefully plan defensive formations under pressure.

Combat is unforgiving, with Genestealers attacking at high speed and overwhelming unprepared squads. Limited ammunition, slow movement, and restricted visibility force players to think ahead, manage resources, and use choke points effectively to survive.

Atmospherically, Space Hulk excels at building tension. Dark corridors, motion trackers, and constant audio cues create an experience often compared to the film Aliens. Combined with moody visuals and sound design, the game delivers one of the most suspenseful strategy experiences on the Amiga.

Critically praised for its immersive design and faithful adaptation of the tabletop game, Space Hulk became a defining Warhammer title in video game form. Today, it is remembered as a demanding but deeply rewarding classic that perfectly captures the terror and heroism of the 40K universe.

💬 Did you carefully fortify every corridor, or were your Marines overwhelmed by Genestealer swarms?

obHqQCQzB6o.title: Sanxion – The C64 Shooter That Showed the Battle from Two Angles at Once
obHqQCQzB6o.description:
🕹️ Sanxion (1986) – Commodore 64 Innovative Split-Screen Shoot ’Em Up
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/sanxion/

Released in 1986 for the Commodore 64, Sanxion was developed by Stavros Fasoulas and published by Thalamus as the company’s very first release. From the outset, it established Thalamus as a publisher willing to push technical and design boundaries, delivering a shoot-’em-up that felt fresh and ambitious.

Players pilot a futuristic aircraft through horizontally scrolling stages packed with enemies and hazards. Sanxion’s most distinctive feature is its split-screen presentation: the upper section shows an overhead tactical view, while the lower portion displays the traditional side-on action. This dual perspective allows players to anticipate threats ahead while reacting to immediate danger, adding an extra layer of strategy rarely seen in the genre.

Another standout mechanic is the adjustable scrolling speed. Movement accelerates as the player ship approaches the centre of the screen, forcing constant judgment calls between speed, control, and survival. This dynamic pacing keeps the action tense and unpredictable throughout each level.

Between stages, Sanxion offers non-lethal bonus rounds where floating letters can be shot or avoided for extra points, providing a brief change of pace. Visually, the game delivers smooth parallax scrolling, flicker-free sprites, and varied environments ranging from deserts to industrial zones and icy landscapes. Rob Hubbard’s soundtrack completes the package, with a memorable SID interpretation of Prokofiev’s Dance of the Knights greeting players on the loading screen.

Inventive, stylish, and technically impressive, Sanxion remains one of the most respected shoot-’em-ups on the Commodore 64 and a defining debut for Thalamus.

Released in 1984 by Activision and designed by David Crane for the Commodore 64, Pitfall! is one of the most influential platform adventures of the early home computer era. Players take control of Pitfall Harry, a fearless treasure hunter racing through a dangerous jungle to collect 32 hidden treasures within a strict 20-minute time limit.

Gameplay unfolds across 256 horizontally connected screens packed with hazards including bottomless pits, quicksand, rolling logs, fire, rattlesnakes, scorpions, and snapping crocodiles. Using precise jumping, ladder climbing, and vine swinging, players must carefully time every movement to survive and keep momentum.

Progression is driven by exploration, memory, and risk management. Treasures such as bags of money, gold and silver bars, and diamond rings boost the player’s score, while mistakes cost valuable points and time. Achieving the perfect score of 114,000 points requires flawless play and complete mastery of the jungle.

Visually simple yet highly readable, Pitfall! delivers smooth animation and instantly recognisable environments that prioritise gameplay clarity. Its tight controls and consistent level design make it both accessible to newcomers and brutally demanding for high-score chasers.

While the Commodore 64 version may not fully exploit the system’s technical capabilities, it remains a timeless classic thanks to its innovative structure and addictive challenge. Today, Pitfall! is remembered as a foundation of the platform genre and a defining title of 1980s gaming.

Released in 1993 by Team17 for the Commodore Amiga, Superfrog is a colourful side-scrolling platformer that became one of the defining titles of the platform’s golden era.

Players control a young prince transformed into a frog by an evil witch, setting out on a quest to rescue his kidnapped princess. The adventure spans six themed worlds, each packed with enemies, hazards, and hidden secrets.

Gameplay focuses on precise jumping, projectile attacks, and item collection, including wings for gliding and Lucozade for restoring health. A unique slot machine system allows players to gamble collected credits for bonuses, passwords, and extra lives.

One of the game’s standout features is the hidden “Project-F” bonus level, a side-scrolling shoot-’em-up tribute to Team17’s Project-X, adding variety and surprise to the adventure.

Visually, Superfrog is renowned for its vibrant colour palette, fluid animation, and smooth scrolling. These are complemented by an energetic soundtrack composed by Allister Brimble, which remains iconic among Amiga fans.

Developed during the peak of Amiga gaming, the title reflects Team17’s commitment to polish and creativity. Its combination of accessibility and depth helped it reach a wide audience.

Today, Superfrog is remembered as one of the finest platformers on the Commodore Amiga and a lasting symbol of the system’s creative high point.

Gameplay is fast and demanding, centred on precision flying and pattern recognition. Players blast through waves of enemies, deploy screen-clearing bombs, and make use of the game’s signature loop-the-loop manoeuvre to evade incoming fire. The Commodore 64 version does an admirable job of capturing the arcade original’s feel, with smooth vertical scrolling, responsive controls, and an atmospheric soundtrack by Mark Cooksey that drives the action forward. While collision detection can feel unforgiving at times, mastering enemy patterns becomes part of the challenge and long-term appeal.

A cornerstone of the shoot ’em up genre, 1942 remains a firm favourite on the C64, remembered for its intensity, iconic mechanics, and enduring arcade spirit.

Released in 1984 by Epyx, Summer Games is a landmark title that helped define the multi-event sports genre on the Commodore 64. Inspired by the unreleased Starpath game Sweat!, it became the first entry in Epyx’s celebrated Games series and set the template for everything that followed.

You compete across a range of Olympic-style events including the 100m sprint, pole vault, platform diving, gymnastics, freestyle swimming, and skeet shooting. Each discipline has its own rhythm and control style, rewarding timing, coordination, and practice rather than button-mashing.

The game supports up to eight players, each representing a chosen country, making it perfect for competitive multiplayer sessions. Events can be played individually, selected freely, or tackled as a full tournament with medals awarded for top performances.

A major step forward for Epyx, Summer Games was one of the first titles to feature a dedicated graphics designer, helping elevate presentation and polish. Today, it’s remembered as a genre-defining classic and a cornerstone of Commodore 64 sports gaming.

Originally developed by Atari Games and released on the Commodore 64 by Domark in 1992, Rampart delivers a distinctive blend of real-time strategy, action, and puzzle gameplay. Rather than traditional armies or units, the focus here is on building, repairing, and defending medieval castles under constant threat.

Gameplay is split into two intense phases. During the building phase, players use a limited supply of wall pieces to repair damage and expand their fortress layout, deciding how best to enclose space for cannons and protection. Once time runs out, the battle phase begins, with players firing cannons to repel waves of attacking enemies and rival castles.

Success depends on fast thinking and smart planning. Poor wall placement leaves cannons exposed, while inefficient repairs can spell disaster when the next assault begins. As levels progress, enemy pressure increases, forcing players to refine both construction and combat tactics.

Despite the Commodore 64’s technical limits, Rampart retains the addictive balance of strategy and arcade action that made the original stand out. Its innovative design helped define the castle defence genre and remains just as engaging today, whether played solo or with friends.

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Released in 1986 by Tigress Marketing and published by Ariolasoft under their Reaktör label, Deactivators is a highly original action-puzzle game built around bomb disposal and spatial problem-solving.

In the game, you control a squad of robotic “deactivators” sent into five dangerous research complexes to locate and neutralise bombs planted by terrorists.

Gameplay revolves around navigating interconnected rooms, picking up and throwing bombs, activating force-field switches, and using teleporters linked to hidden circuit boards.

Each room features shifting gravity orientations, where walls can become floors and ceilings can become walls, forcing players to constantly rethink movement and timing. Security droids patrol many areas, adding a tactical layer as you evade or manipulate them.

Visually, the Commodore 64 version uses a restrained colour palette, but impresses with clean layouts and clever spatial design. The standout feature is the atmospheric SID soundtrack by Simon PC Frost, which gives the game a distinctive identity.

Deactivators is widely regarded as an under-appreciated classic, praised for its inventive mechanics, demanding puzzles, and forward-thinking design. It remains one of the most creative strategy-puzzle titles on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1984 by First Star Software for the Commodore 64, Spy vs. Spy brings the anarchic rivalry of the MAD Magazine comic strip to life. You face off as the Black or White Spy in a frantic race to outwit your opponent, gather secret items, and escape the embassy before time runs out.

Gameplay is built around exploration, memory, and deception. You search rooms for essential items like passports, money, secret plans, and the all-important airport key, while laying traps to sabotage your rival’s progress. Every mistake costs precious seconds, especially when a deadly trap sends your spy floating off as an angel.

The split-screen design keeps both players constantly visible, turning every match into a tense battle of nerves and timing. Traps, bluffing, and last-second reversals create moments of genuine comedy, perfectly capturing the humour and style of Antonio Prohías’ original comic.

Today, Spy vs. Spy is remembered as one of the most inventive and entertaining multiplayer games on the C64. Its blend of strategy, chaos, and rivalry ensures it remains a timeless favourite for head-to-head play.

Released in 1984 by MC Lothlorien, Micro Mouse Goes De-Bugging is a distinctive action-educational title for the Commodore 64 that blends arcade gameplay with early programming concepts. Players take control of Micro Mouse, a digital fixer tasked with repairing corrupted BASIC code inside a malfunctioning computer system.

The action unfolds across side-view, flip-screen stages where players must retrieve missing characters from cages positioned around the screen and return them to their correct places in the code. At the same time, hostile bugs roam the area, attempting to steal characters and undo progress, forcing players to balance speed, accuracy, and survival.

A key mechanic is resource management. Micro Mouse can either carry a code character or a can of “datakill” to eliminate bugs, but never both at once. This simple restriction adds tension and strategy, requiring careful decision-making as threats increase and screens grow more chaotic.

Micro Mouse Goes De-Bugging stands out as a creative example of how educational ideas were woven into games during the early home computing era. Its mix of learning, arcade action, and playful presentation has earned it a fond reputation among Commodore 64 fans looking for something a little different.

Released in 1987 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64, Space Harrier is the home computer adaptation of Sega’s groundbreaking 1985 arcade hit, developed by Sega AM2 using “Super Scaler” technology.

Players control Harri as he flies through the surreal world of Dragonland, battling waves of enemies and gigantic bosses using fast-paced shooting and evasive movement. The gameplay centres on constant motion, reflexes, and precise positioning.

The C64 version delivers a scaled-down interpretation of the arcade’s pseudo-3D visuals, adapting the experience to 8-bit hardware while preserving the game’s core intensity and pace.

Two regional versions were released. The European version features flat terrain and simplified scrolling, while the North American release adds raster effects to simulate movement and includes alternative graphics and sound.

Despite technical limitations, the game captures much of the arcade original’s energy. Vibrant visuals and an energetic soundtrack composed by Mark Cooksey help maintain the sense of speed and spectacle.

Visually ambitious for its time, Space Harrier demonstrated how far the Commodore 64 could be pushed when handling complex arcade conversions.

Today, it’s remembered as one of the most impressive and influential shooters on the platform, representing an important step in the evolution of 3D-style gaming on home computers.

Released in 1992 by Cryo Interactive and published by Virgin Games, KGB is a dark and demanding point-and-click adventure for the Commodore Amiga, set against the backdrop of the collapsing Soviet Union in the summer of 1991. Players take on the role of Captain Maksim Rukov, a newly assigned KGB officer drawn into a murder investigation that quickly spirals into a far-reaching political conspiracy.

The game is built around realism and consequence. Actions unfold in real time, with events continuing whether the player is ready or not. A single poor decision can lead to immediate failure or trigger consequences that surface hours later, forcing players to think carefully, manage time, and pay close attention to dialogue, documents, and subtle clues.

Using the same engine as Cryo’s Dune, KGB features detailed hand-drawn locations and an interface designed to support complex investigation and interaction. The later CD-ROM release, Conspiracy, added voice acting by Donald Sutherland as Rukov’s father, reinforcing the game’s sombre tone and narrative weight.

Widely regarded as a cult classic, KGB is remembered for its mature themes, unforgiving structure, and immersive portrayal of Cold War espionage. It stands apart from traditional adventure games of the era, offering a tense and methodical experience that rewards patience, logic, and careful planning.

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Released in 1984 by Mindscape and developed by Michael J. Hanson, Indiana Jones in the Lost Kingdom is a puzzle-driven adventure for the Commodore 64 that stands apart from other Indy games by telling a completely original story. Rather than following a film plot, you guide Indiana Jones through a mysterious lost kingdom in a race against rival archaeologist Ivar Reiss to recover a powerful artifact.

The game is deliberately cryptic, offering almost no instructions and expecting you to work things out through experimentation and observation. Each of the six levels introduces new ideas and challenges, forcing you to think logically, test assumptions, and adapt your approach as the rules subtly change.

Unlike many puzzle games of the era, progress depends less on reflexes and more on insight. Success comes from paying attention to how each screen behaves and learning from failure, making every breakthrough feel earned rather than handed to you.

A two-player mode allows for cooperative play, adding an extra layer of discussion and shared problem-solving, though the game’s uncompromising design means patience is essential. For some, it’s frustrating; for others, it’s deeply rewarding.

Today, Indiana Jones in the Lost Kingdom is remembered as one of the more unusual licensed titles on the C64, praised for its originality and willingness to challenge players without holding their hand.

Pa8d9OA95uQ.title: Future Wars – The Amiga Adventure That Started with a Window Cleaner
Pa8d9OA95uQ.description:
🕹️ Future Wars (1989) – Commodore Amiga Cinematic Point-and-Click Adventure Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/future-wars/

Released in 1989 by Delphine Software International for the Commodore Amiga, Future Wars is an ambitious point-and-click adventure that marked the studio’s first step into cinematic storytelling. Created by Paul Cuisset and Éric Chahi, who would later go on to develop Another World, the game runs on Delphine’s proprietary Cinematique engine and laid the groundwork for their distinctive narrative style.

Players take on the role of an unlikely hero—a humble window cleaner—who stumbles upon a time machine and is thrown into a battle against the alien Crughons. His journey spans multiple eras, including medieval Europe, the distant 44th century, and the Cretaceous period, each offering unique environments, puzzles, and narrative twists.

Gameplay is driven by a streamlined interface designed to keep the screen uncluttered. Left-click controls movement, while right-click opens a verb menu featuring commands such as Operate, Examine, Take, Use, and Inventory. This system encourages careful observation and experimentation, while maintaining the game’s cinematic presentation.

Visually, Future Wars stands out with richly animated backdrops and subtle environmental details, from drifting smoke to background wildlife. Each time period features its own colour palette and artistic style, helping to reinforce the sense of time travel and progression. These visuals are complemented by an atmospheric soundtrack that was widely praised at release.

Despite its creative ambition, the game is notorious for unforgiving pixel hunting and potential dead-ends, a common issue in early adventure design. Even so, it received strong critical acclaim, earning awards for its soundtrack and securing a place in Amiga Power’s Top 100. Today, Future Wars is remembered as a visually striking, historically important adventure that helped shape the future of narrative-driven games.

Shadow Fighter (1994), developed by the Italian NAPS Team and published by Gremlin Interactive, is one of the most technically impressive 2D beat ’em ups on the Commodore Amiga.

Designed for standard OCS/ECS hardware, the game delivers smooth animation, vibrant sprites, and impressive multi-layer parallax scrolling that pushes the platform to its limits.

With 17 playable fighters, each featuring unique moves and backgrounds, the game uses a simple one-button control system that allows players to perform over 25 attacks per character through intuitive joystick motions.

A dedicated training mode introduces “Pupazz,” a practice opponent designed to help players master advanced techniques and special moves.

Graphically, Shadow Fighter stands out with its rich colour palette and dynamic arenas, while Patrick Phelan’s energetic soundtrack enhances the intensity of each battle.

Although later AGA and CD32 versions offered visual upgrades, the original OCS/ECS release remains a showcase of expert Amiga programming and fast-paced arcade-style combat.

Shadow Fighter is remembered as one of the platform’s finest fighting games and a highlight of 1990s European game development.

Gameplay centres on navigating maze-like rooms filled with traps, locked doors, and roaming enemies. Players must collect keys, avoid hazards, and carefully plan their routes in order to progress safely through each chamber and reach the next stage.

Progression relies on observation, timing, and problem-solving, as each new area introduces different layouts and obstacles. Quick reactions are essential, but success also depends on choosing the right path and managing risks effectively.

Gameplay revolves around careful movement and planning. Falling boulders can be pushed to clear paths, trigger chain reactions, or eliminate threats, but a single misstep can result in being crushed. Timing is crucial, as each level demands observation, patience, and an understanding of how the environment reacts to player actions.

The C64 version features bright, colourful graphics and a lively soundtrack that keeps the pace engaging while you work through increasingly demanding layouts. Although often compared to Boulder Dash, 20 Tons has its own identity, with tighter spaces and a greater emphasis on controlled movement and risk management.

While it may not be one of the system’s most famous puzzle titles, 20 Tons is fondly remembered by fans for its satisfying challenge and well-balanced design, making it a solid example of classic Commodore 64 puzzle gameplay.

Bill is a quirky prehistoric action game that blends arcade gameplay with light survival management. Players take on the role of Bill, a caveman determined to build and protect his growing family in a dangerous stone-age world.

Gameplay revolves around hunting animals for food, stunning cavewomen to bring back to your cave, and defending your home from roaming dinosaurs. Armed with only a club, Bill must carefully balance exploration, combat, and resource gathering to keep his family alive.

A distinctive feature is the changing seasonal cycle, which affects food supplies and family survival. Poor planning can lead to starvation, while successful hunts and rescues help expand your tribe. This adds a surprising strategic layer beneath the game’s humorous exterior.

Visually, B.C. Bill delivers colourful character sprites and lively prehistoric environments that give the game strong personality. The experience is elevated by Fred Gray’s catchy SID soundtrack, which provides memorable tunes that perfectly match the game’s playful tone.

Combining arcade action, light strategy, and tongue-in-cheek humour, B.C. Bill became a standout title of the early C64 era. Today, it remains fondly remembered as a charming and distinctive example of 1980s home computer creativity.

Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64 by Ocean Software, RoboCop is a side-scrolling action game based on Paul Verhoeven’s iconic sci-fi film. Developed under license from Orion Pictures, the home computer versions were produced by Ocean in collaboration with Data East, aiming to bring the film’s gritty atmosphere to 8-bit hardware.

Players step into the metal boots of RoboCop, patrolling the crime-ridden streets of Detroit across seven scrolling levels. Gameplay blends beat ’em up combat with run-and-gun shooting, as RoboCop uses punches and his Auto-9 pistol to clear enemies. Bonus shooting galleries add variety, rewarding accuracy and timing between the main stages.

On the Commodore 64, RoboCop delivers moody visuals and a strong sense of atmosphere that reflects the film’s tone. Jonathan Dunn’s powerful soundtrack is a standout feature, driving the action and becoming one of the most recognisable C64 game themes of the era. While movement and firing limitations add challenge, they also demand deliberate, methodical play.

A major commercial success in the UK, RoboCop became one of the best-selling home computer games of the late 1980s. Its mix of memorable music, solid action, and faithful use of the license has secured its reputation as a Commodore 64 classic.

Gameplay is split between fast-paced dogfighting and demanding aircraft carrier landing sequences. During combat missions, players engage enemy fighters using missiles, cannons, and defensive flares while carefully managing speed, altitude, and positioning. Success depends on timing and accuracy rather than brute force.

The landing sequences add an extra layer of tension, requiring precise control to line up correctly and touch down safely on the carrier deck. These sections are deliberately challenging and serve as a test of skill between combat encounters.

Presented using a distinctive 3D wireframe cockpit view, Top Gun delivers a strong sense of immersion for an 8-bit system. The atmospheric opening, complete with sunset visuals and the film’s famous theme, helped make it an instant talking point on release. While not as deep as dedicated simulators of the era, Top Gun remains a nostalgic favourite for its presentation and cinematic ambition.

Released in 1993 by Vision Software and published by Mindscape for the Commodore Amiga, Seek & Destroy is a fast-paced top-down helicopter shoot-’em-up that delivers arcade-style military action with strategic depth.

Players take control of a heavily armed Apache helicopter and are sent into hostile territory across a series of combat missions set in a fictional Middle Eastern conflict.

The game features a dynamic 360-degree scrolling playfield, allowing free movement in all directions and encouraging tactical positioning during intense firefights.

A wide range of weapons is available, including missiles, bombs, and machine guns, which can be used to engage tanks, enemy helicopters, ground forces, and defensive installations.

Success depends on balancing aggression with careful navigation, managing ammunition, and choosing the right weapons for each situation.

Visually, Seek & Destroy delivers detailed sprites and smooth scrolling environments, with the AGA-enhanced Amiga 1200 version offering improved colour depth and sharper presentation.

The soundtrack by Allister Brimble reinforces the military atmosphere with energetic, tension-building music throughout the campaign.

In 1994, the game was also released on the Amiga CD32, featuring enhanced CD audio and full-motion video cutscenes that expanded its cinematic feel.

Combining strong technical performance with accessible yet challenging gameplay, the game became a standout helicopter shooter on the platform.

Today, Seek & Destroy is remembered as a polished and underrated Amiga action title with lasting appeal among shoot-’em-up fans.

Exploration unfolds in an isometric 3D view across five interconnected decks, each filled with hostile skeletons, environmental puzzles, and hidden routes. Progress depends on careful navigation, combat timing, and gradually uncovering the ship’s secrets.

Survival hinges on knowing when to fight, when to retreat, and when to ring the ship’s mysterious bell to restore strength. Collecting scattered map pieces is essential to locating the captain’s imprisoned soul.

Although its structure closely follows earlier Pendragon titles, Blackwyche stands out for its eerie maritime atmosphere and unsettling sense of isolation. Today, it’s remembered as a distinctive and challenging cult favourite within Ultimate’s Commodore 64 catalogue.

Released in 1986 by Gremlin Graphics for the Commodore 64, Bounder is an inventive action-puzzle game that puts players in control of a constantly bouncing tennis ball navigating a series of suspended platforms high above dangerous voids.

The game spans 174 screens across 10 increasingly demanding levels, each built from hexagonal tiles filled with hazards, enemies, and obstacles. Players must carefully time their movements and landings while guiding the ball towards the exit on every screen. Precision and forward planning are essential for survival.

Scattered throughout the stages are special tiles that introduce strategic variety, including arrows that propel the ball forward, teleporters that remove sections of the level, and mystery tiles that can either reward or punish the player. Completing each stage unlocks a bonus screen, offering extra points and risk-based scoring opportunities.

Visually, Bounder stands out with its clever use of parallax scrolling and pseudo-3D perspective, creating a strong sense of depth on the C64. Its colourful palette, clean presentation, and responsive controls help maintain clarity even as the difficulty ramps up.

Praised on release for its originality and technical achievement, Bounder quickly earned a reputation as one of Gremlin’s most addictive titles. Today, it remains a standout entry in the Commodore 64 library and a favourite among fans of challenging, skill-based puzzle games.

Released in 1993 by Bullfrog Productions, Syndicate is a landmark cyberpunk strategy game set in a bleak future where megacorporations control the world through violence, surveillance, and technology. You command a squad of cybernetically enhanced agents, carrying out assassinations, sabotage, and corporate warfare across a global map of sprawling cityscapes.

The game unfolds in real time from an isometric top-down view, blending tactical planning with fast, often brutal action. Missions demand careful positioning, weapon choice, and agent upgrades, while urban environments are filled with civilians, enemy operatives, and destructible surroundings that can quickly turn chaos into opportunity.

One of Syndicate’s defining features is the Persuadatron, a mind-control device that allows you to convert civilians and enemies into loyal followers. Used well, it can completely shift the balance of a mission, turning hostile cities into walking armies under your control.

On the Amiga, Syndicate delivers detailed environments, moody lighting, and a dark visual tone that perfectly suits its dystopian setting. Russell Shaw’s industrial soundtrack adds an unforgettable layer of atmosphere, reinforcing the cold, corporate brutality at the heart of the game.

Decades later, Syndicate remains one of the most influential strategy titles of its era, remembered for its bold themes, innovative mechanics, and uncompromising vision of a cyberpunk future.

Deflektor (1987), developed by Vortex Software and published by Gremlin Graphics, is a top-down puzzle-action game that challenges players to guide a laser beam through complex mazes using movable mirrors.

With 60 increasingly demanding levels, Deflektor combines logical problem-solving with fast-paced arcade pressure, creating a uniquely tense gameplay experience.

Its inventive mechanics and elegant design have influenced many later puzzle games, securing Deflektor’s reputation as one of the finest cerebral action titles on the Commodore 64.

PVOQ9ijLrJw.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/guzzler/

Released in 1984 by Interceptor Software for the Commodore 64, Guzzler is a charming top-down maze action game that puts a clever twist on the classic arcade formula. Players control a hungry mouse navigating colourful labyrinths to collect keys and unlock food cells scattered throughout each level.

The core gameplay revolves around a unique “weight” mechanic. Every time the mouse eats, it grows fatter, making it impossible to squeeze through narrow passages until it gradually deflates over time. This creates a constant strategic balancing act between eating for points and staying slim enough to move freely through the maze.

Progression depends on careful route planning, timing, and risk management. Patrolling enemies add pressure to every decision, while Bonus Barry appears carrying letters that spell “GUZZLER”, rewarding exploration and skilful play with valuable extra points.

Visually, Guzzler stands out with bright, friendly graphics and clear maze layouts that keep the action easy to follow. The upbeat ragtime-style soundtrack reinforces the game’s playful personality and helps set it apart from more serious arcade-inspired titles.

Although often compared to Pac-Man, Guzzler earns its own identity through its inventive mechanics and thoughtful level design. Today, it is fondly remembered as a hidden gem of the Commodore 64 library, celebrated for its creativity, charm, and enduring replay value.

💬 Did you master the art of staying slim, or did greed always slow you down?

PwYUnlhPfbA.title: You Never Forget Your First Amiga Game… | 50 Essential Amiga Games
PwYUnlhPfbA.description:
🕹️ 50 Essential Amiga Games – The Classics That Defined the Commodore Amiga
🌐 Full games info, manuals & downloads:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk

You don’t forget your first Amiga game! For some, it was the speed of Lotus Turbo Challenge 2. For others, the atmosphere of Another World, the chaos of Worms, the depth of Dungeon Master, or the pure brilliance of The Secret of Monkey Island.

This video is my Essential 50 Amiga Games countdown — a personal but carefully considered look at some of the most memorable, influential and enjoyable games ever released for the Commodore Amiga. It is not meant to be a final word on the subject, because no Amiga list ever could be, but it is a celebration of just how much range the machine had.

Across arcade action, adventures, strategy games, simulations, shooters, dungeon crawlers, football, management, platformers and point-and-click classics, the Amiga delivered one of the richest libraries in gaming history. This countdown covers everything from Lotus Turbo Challenge 2, Cannon Fodder, Syndicate and Sensible World of Soccer to Monkey Island, Dune II, Another World, Populous, Lemmings 2 and many more.

Some of these games changed genres. Some pushed presentation, music or atmosphere to another level. Others were simply impossible to stop playing once they got their hooks into you. Together, they show why the Amiga still means so much to retro gamers today.

There will be omissions. There will be disagreements. That is part of the fun.

Released in 1985 by Gremlin Graphics, Monty on the Run is the third game in the Monty Mole series and one of the most celebrated platformers on the Commodore 64. The game follows Monty as he escapes from Scudmore Prison and attempts a perilous journey to France, dodging capture while navigating a hostile world packed with hazards.

Gameplay is built around fast-paced, multi-screen platforming that demands sharp reflexes and careful planning. Players must learn enemy patterns, master precise jumps, and make smart use of collected items to progress through the game’s varied environments. A defining feature is the opening item selection screen, where players choose five items from a larger list—some of which are essential to complete later sections—adding strategy and replay value while also acting as subtle copy protection.

The presentation makes full use of the C64’s strengths, with colourful, detailed backdrops and fluid character movement. Above all, Monty on the Run is legendary for its soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, whose energetic and technically impressive SID composition is widely regarded as one of the finest pieces of music ever produced for the Commodore 64.

Critically acclaimed on release, Zzap!64 awarded the game 90% and its prestigious “Sizzler” award. Today, Monty on the Run remains a defining example of mid-80s C64 game design, remembered for its challenge, innovation, and unforgettable music.

Released in 1984 by Concept Software and published by Argus Press Software for the Commodore 64, ALIEN is a tense hybrid of strategy and adventure inspired by Ridley Scott’s 1979 science-fiction classic. Set aboard the doomed spaceship Nostromo, the game challenges players to manage a vulnerable crew while a deadly alien stalks the corridors.

Gameplay unfolds in real time from a top-down perspective, with players controlling all seven crew members simultaneously. Each character has an individual emotional state, ranging from calm and confident to panicked and broken, directly affecting their performance and chances of survival. Balancing morale, positioning, and resources is essential to keeping the team alive.

Progression depends on careful exploration and intelligent decision-making. Players must search the ship for weapons, oxygen tanks, and vital equipment while tracking the alien’s movements and planning ambushes. Poor choices can quickly lead to crew deaths and a collapsing mission.

Visually simple but functionally effective, ALIEN uses a grid-based layout to represent the Nostromo’s claustrophobic interior. The atmosphere is dramatically enhanced by Paul Clansey’s haunting SID soundtrack, which maintains constant tension and reinforces the game’s sense of isolation and danger.

As one of the earliest licensed movie adaptations in video games, ALIEN stands out for its ambitious design and psychological depth. Today, it is remembered as a cult classic that successfully translated cinematic horror into strategic gameplay, earning its place among the most distinctive titles on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1986 by VIFI International for the Commodore 64, Serenade is a highly unusual and experimental title developed by French studio Jawx.

Players take on the role of a lovesick troubadour, depicted as a silhouetted figure, attempting to win the affection of a lady by performing music with a selection of instruments.

The game is presented entirely in French, adding to its distinctive atmosphere and reinforcing its European art-game sensibility. Rather than following traditional arcade or adventure conventions, Serenade focuses on mood and presentation.

Gameplay revolves around choosing musical pieces and attempting to perform them using four available instruments. However, interaction is deliberately minimal, and progress can feel ambiguous or even confusing.

Many players find it difficult to produce clear musical results, leading some to interpret the game as more of an interactive demo or artistic experiment than a conventional game.

Visually, the title features stark silhouettes and minimalist backgrounds, creating a theatrical, stage-like presentation that was rare on home computers at the time.

Its unusual structure and lack of clear objectives have made Serenade one of the more “mysterious” entries in the Commodore 64 library.

While never widely popular, the game stands as a fascinating example of the creative risks taken by smaller European developers during the 1980s.

Today, Serenade is remembered as a cult curiosity and a must-see title for collectors and enthusiasts interested in the stranger corners of retro gaming history.
