Released in June 1985 by Mastertronic and developed by Nigel P. Johnstone, The Captive is a tense top-down action-adventure that blends exploration, puzzle-solving, and careful planning. From the creator of The Prisoner, it delivers an unsettling atmosphere and an unusual sense of vulnerability for a Commodore 64 title.

The game is set on a mysterious island known as the Glen of Coloured Corpses. Players begin in a small town and must explore the surrounding areas in search of a way to escape. Progress is gated by colour-coded keys used to unlock doors scattered across the island, forcing players to think carefully about route planning and item usage.

Inventory management plays a central role, with only three items carriable at any time. Objects range from practical tools like guns and shovels to stranger items such as mushrooms, scrolls, and even a helicopter. Some items only become usable after discovering the correct scroll, encouraging experimentation and observation.

Adding constant tension are the Messengers of Doom, roaming entities that instantly end the game on contact. Their presence turns every journey into a risk, reinforcing the need for caution and strategic movement.

Despite its simple visuals and budget origins, The Captive stands out for its originality and atmosphere. Today, it’s remembered as an inventive and challenging puzzle-adventure that rewards patience, planning, and curiosity.

Released in 1985 by Gargoyle Games for the Commodore 64, Tir Na Nòg is a critically acclaimed arcade-adventure action-puzzle game inspired by Irish mythology, starring the legendary hero Cúchulainn.

Players are transported to the mystical Land of Youth, where Cúchulainn must recover four fragments of the Seal of Calum to restore balance while evading the mysterious and dangerous sídhe enemies.

The game world is vast and interconnected, featuring plains, forests, caverns, and hidden pathways that reward careful exploration and observation.

Movement is built around a unique rotating-view system, requiring players to change the camera direction before travelling left or right, adding strategic depth to navigation.

Progress depends on solving cryptic environmental puzzles and interpreting poetic clues, making inventory management and experimentation central to success.

Instead of traditional deaths, defeat sends Cúchulainn to another location and strips him of carried items, encouraging thoughtful risk-taking and frequent use of the built-in save system.

Visually, Tir Na Nòg was groundbreaking, with large animated characters, parallax scrolling, and richly detailed scenery that pushed the Commodore 64 to its limits.

The game earned widespread praise on release, with Zzap!64 famously calling it “a REAL arcade adventure” with stunning graphics and atmosphere.

Its blend of mythology, exploration, and cerebral puzzle design helped define a new style of adventure gaming.

Today, Tir Na Nòg is remembered as one of the most ambitious and influential titles in the Commodore 64 library.

Released in 1986 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64 and developed by Canvas Software, Miami Vice is an action-adventure title inspired by the hugely popular 1980s television series. Players take on the roles of detectives Sonny Crockett and Ricardo Tubbs as they attempt to dismantle a major drug operation led by the mysterious criminal known as “Mr. J.”

Gameplay is split into two distinct sections. The first involves top-down driving sequences, where players navigate a city map to reach crime scenes and suspect hideouts. These segments are notoriously challenging, with awkward steering, tight time limits, and frequent crashes making navigation a major test of patience and precision.

Once a destination is reached, the game shifts into side-scrolling action stages. Here, players confront criminals using basic combat mechanics and simple shooting elements. While functional, these sections lack depth and variety, contributing to the game’s mixed critical reception.

Progress depends on successfully balancing both driving and combat segments while managing limited resources and avoiding repeated failures. The structure encourages perseverance, as mistakes often result in restarting lengthy sections of gameplay.

One of the game’s strongest elements is its soundtrack, composed by Martin Galway. His energetic SID music captures the style and mood of the television series, providing a memorable audio experience that many players consider the highlight of the package.

Although Miami Vice struggled to live up to the quality of its source material, it remains an interesting example of 1980s licensed gaming. Today, it is remembered for its ambitious concept, tough difficulty, and outstanding music, securing its place in Commodore 64 history.

Released in 1988 by Interplay Productions and published by Electronic Arts for the Commodore 64, Neuromancer is an ambitious adventure game inspired by William Gibson’s groundbreaking cyberpunk novel. Blending hacking simulation, role-playing, and narrative exploration, it delivers one of the most immersive sci-fi experiences of the 8-bit era.

Set in 2058 in Chiba City, Japan, players take on the role of a struggling hacker trying to regain access to the Matrix after being cut off from cyberspace. The journey unfolds across neon-lit streets, shady bars, corporate offices, and virtual networks filled with danger and opportunity.

Gameplay is divided between real-world exploration and cyberspace infiltration. In the physical world, players gather information, earn money, buy equipment, and install skill chips that enhance abilities. In cyberspace, they battle hostile ICE programs, evade security systems, and confront powerful artificial intelligences guarding valuable data.

Progress depends on careful planning and character development. Choosing the right software, managing resources, and upgrading skills are essential for surviving increasingly complex hacking challenges. The interface combines joystick and keyboard controls, allowing smooth transitions between reality and the digital realm.

Visually atmospheric and enhanced by a memorable soundtrack featuring a Devo-inspired theme, Neuromancer perfectly captures the mood of cyberpunk fiction. Its futuristic style, layered systems, and freedom of approach set it apart from most adventure games of its time.

Critically acclaimed on release, Neuromancer won major awards and remains one of the most respected Commodore 64 titles. Today, it stands as a landmark fusion of literature, gaming, and technology, and a must-play for fans of sci-fi and retro adventures.

QDTysJJT9BM.description:
🕹️ C64 vs ZX Spectrum — the same games compared across two legendary 8-bit machines.

The Commodore 64 vs ZX Spectrum debate is one of the longest-running arguments in retro gaming history. In this video, I’m taking a slightly different approach: comparing the same games across both systems to see how they actually play, look, sound and feel.

Yes, the Commodore 64 is technically the more powerful machine, with stronger sound hardware, more colourful graphics and smoother sprite handling. But once you put these games side by side, power is not always the whole story.

Many classic 8-bit games were originally designed around the ZX Spectrum, which means the timing, controls, structure and screen layout often suited that machine first. That creates an interesting comparison. The C64 versions often look and sound better, but the Spectrum versions can sometimes feel tighter, faster or more natural to play.

Featured games include Head Over Heels, Skool Daze, Manic Miner, Sabre Wulf, Jet Set Willy, Saboteur!, Dizzy, Nodes of Yesod, Exolon, The Great Escape, Chimera, The Way of the Exploding Fist, Target: Renegade, Chase H.Q. and RoboCop.

Rather than simply declaring a winner, this video looks at where each version came from, what changed between machines, and how those differences affect the experience today.

Sometimes the C64 takes control and delivers the stronger version. Other times, the Spectrum original still shows why it worked so well in the first place.  Looking back, both machines gave us something special. Whether you were a Commodore 64 owner, a ZX Spectrum fan, or just someone who loves 8-bit gaming history, this is really about the games themselves.

Released in 1983 by Llamasoft for the Commodore 64, Hover Bovver is an offbeat maze-action game designed by Jeff Minter that blends humour with fast-paced arcade gameplay.

Players take on the role of a mischievous homeowner who “borrows” his neighbour’s lawnmower to cut his own overgrown garden. The objective is to mow every patch of grass while avoiding flowerbeds and escaping angry pursuers.

Gameplay revolves around navigating tight garden layouts while being chased by an enraged neighbour and gardener. Quick reactions and careful route planning are essential to avoid capture and complete each level.

A unique feature is the player’s dog, which can be commanded to distract enemies and create escape routes. However, misuse can cause the dog to turn hostile, adding an extra layer of risk and strategy.

Visually, the game features simple but charming character sprites and clearly defined playfields. The whimsical tone is enhanced by a SID rendition of Percy Grainger’s “Country Gardens,” arranged by James Lisney.

Typical of Jeff Minter’s early work, Hover Bovver embraces eccentric design and playful mechanics. Its blend of comedy and challenge helped it stand out in the crowded early C64 market.

Today, it’s remembered as a cult favourite and a perfect example of Llamasoft’s distinctive creative style during the formative years of home computing.

qgA5R-JZrKo.title: Quinx – The Bizarre C64 Game Set Inside a Student’s Exam Nightmare
qgA5R-JZrKo.description:
🕹️ Quinx (1984) – Commodore 64 Surreal Single-Screen Arcade Oddity
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/quinx/

Released in 1984 by Supersoft for the Commodore 64, Quinx is a bizarre and memorable arcade game built around a dreamlike premise. Players take on the role of Arthur Crown, a student at the London School of Economics, trapped in a nightmare where ink worms threaten to consume the very paper he stands on.

Gameplay takes place on a single screen viewed from above, with worms emerging from the edges and leaving trails of ink as they move. The goal is simple but demanding: squash the worms before they hatch. If a worm survives too long, it destroys part of the paper, steadily shrinking the playable area and pushing the game toward failure.

The challenge comes from speed and positioning, as multiple worms can appear at once and hesitation quickly leads to irreversible damage. There are no power-ups or complex mechanics, just constant pressure to react quickly and stay in control as the screen becomes more chaotic.

On the Commodore 64, Quinx uses a stark and minimal presentation that suits its surreal concept. The visuals are clean and functional, allowing the unusual idea to take centre stage rather than relying on spectacle or arcade excess.

Although it lacks common features like a high-score table, Quinx stands out for its originality and strange narrative framing. Today, it’s remembered as a distinctive early-80s experiment that highlights how inventive and unconventional C64 games could be during the platform’s formative years.

Released in 1986 by Ocean Software and developed by Platinum Productions, Rambo: First Blood Part II adapts the 1985 action film into a tense top-down action-adventure for the Commodore 64. Rather than straightforward run-and-gun chaos, the game leans into survival, stealth, and tactical decision-making.

Players guide Rambo through dense jungle environments on a mission to rescue prisoners of war from enemy camps. Progress requires careful navigation, avoiding patrols, and choosing when to strike. Rambo can arm himself with a knife, bow and arrows—including explosive variants—and an M16 rifle, each weapon offering different risks and rewards.

A standout mechanic is how noise affects enemy behaviour. Loud weapons attract reinforcements, encouraging a more considered approach and rewarding players who balance stealth with aggression. Limited lives and tough enemy placement make every encounter feel high stakes.

The Commodore 64 version is elevated by a powerful soundtrack from Martin Galway, featuring themes inspired by the film’s score and adding intensity to the action. Despite its difficulty, the game was praised for capturing the tone of the movie and offering a more thoughtful take on licensed action gameplay.

Released in 1987 by Binary Design and published under Mastertronic’s Bulldog Software label, Feud is a unique action-adventure built around magical rivalry and spellcraft.

In the Commodore 64 version, you play as the sorcerer Learic, locked in a deadly feud with your evil brother Leanoric. To win, you must explore the map, gather herbs and ingredients, brew powerful spells, and hunt down your rival.

Spells range from fireballs and lightning to invisibility and zombification, giving the game a strong tactical element. Success depends on learning spell recipes, managing resources, and predicting your opponent’s movements.

The C64 edition differs notably from the Spectrum and Amstrad versions, featuring altered object placement and more unpredictable enemy tracking, which makes each encounter more tense and unpredictable.

Visually, Feud features bold character sprites, a striking title screen by Ste Pickford, and an atmospheric soundtrack by David Whittaker that reinforces the game’s mystical tone.

Despite some technical quirks, Feud remains highly regarded for its inventive mechanics, sibling rivalry theme, and its place among the most ambitious budget titles of the 1980s C64 scene.

Released in 1990 by Codemasters, Prince Clumsy is a tongue-in-cheek platformer that playfully pokes fun at the Ghosts ’n Goblins formula. You guide the hopelessly accident-prone Prince Clumsy on a quest to rescue the princess from her evil sister, armed with an unlimited supply of throwing daggers and very little dignity.

The game keeps things approachable with smooth, forgiving jumping and straightforward combat, making it far less punishing than its inspirations. Along the way you’ll battle zombies, grim reapers, and other familiar foes while collecting bread and ale to restore health and avoiding hazards like poison and sticky traps.

Levels are designed to be readable and welcoming, encouraging steady progress rather than memorisation. The light-hearted tone runs throughout, helped along by Allister Brimble’s upbeat music, which perfectly matches the game’s playful mood.

Simple, fun, and self-aware, Prince Clumsy remains a fondly remembered C64 platformer, celebrated for its humour, accessibility, and relaxed take on a famously brutal genre.

Released in 1989 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore Amiga, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Graphic Adventure is a landmark point-and-click adventure built on the SCUMM engine. Designed by Ron Gilbert, Noah Falstein, and David Fox, the game expands on the events of the film, allowing players to guide Indy and his father through iconic locations including Venice, Brunwald Castle, and Berlin in a race to secure the Holy Grail.

Gameplay centres on puzzle-solving, exploration, and narrative-driven progression, with multiple ways to approach and complete many challenges. The introduction of the “Indy Quotient” (IQ) scoring system rewards experimentation and creative thinking, encouraging players to discover alternative solutions and aim for the maximum 800-point score.

Progression is shaped by player choice, observation, and careful interaction with the environment. Conversations, item combinations, and branching puzzle paths give the adventure a high level of replayability, setting it apart from many linear titles of the era.

Early releases included a physical Grail Diary feelie, which served both as immersive storytelling material and a vital puzzle-solving reference. It also functioned as a form of copy protection, blending real-world artefacts seamlessly into the gameplay experience.

With its atmospheric visuals, intuitive interface, and faithful yet expanded adaptation of the movie, the Amiga version remains one of the finest cinematic adventures of the late 1980s. Today, it stands as a beloved classic, praised for merging film-quality storytelling with thoughtful interactive design.

qody-Yqd19o.title: Amiga Guru Meditation Error Explained | The Commodore Amiga Crash Screen That Became Legend
qody-Yqd19o.description:
🕹️ The Amiga Guru Meditation error explained — the famous Commodore Amiga crash screen that became a retro computing legend.

First appearing with the Commodore Amiga in 1985, the Guru Meditation error became one of the most recognisable system crash messages in computing history, displayed as a red-bordered box with cryptic diagnostic codes. Unlike generic error screens on other platforms, the Amiga’s approach combined technical seriousness with a strange bit of personality, helping it become part of the machine’s identity and culture.

The name came from early Amiga development, when frustrated programmers would sit cross-legged on a Joyboard to “meditate” through crashes, inspiring the unusual but now iconic message. When triggered, the system displayed a numerical error code and offered limited recovery options, including rebooting with the left mouse button or accessing ROMWack debugging tools with the right button.

For most users, though, it simply meant restarting the Amiga and hoping the problem would not return. Despite indicating a serious system failure, the Guru Meditation screen became a shared experience for Amiga owners and a badge of honour among enthusiasts.

Its bold visual style, unusual name and development backstory helped set the Commodore Amiga apart from rival systems of the era. Today, the Guru Meditation error remains a nostalgic symbol of retro computing and one of the most memorable crash screens ever created.

qOO0QuGaRqc.title: Judge Dredd – Why Did the C64 Get TWO Different Mega-City One Games?
qOO0QuGaRqc.description:
🕹️ Judge Dredd (1986 / 1991) – Commodore 64 Licensed Action Platformer
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/judge-dredd/

Judge Dredd made his Commodore 64 debut in 1986, with a later reimagined version released in 1991, both drawing on the iconic 2000 AD comic and its dystopian vision of Mega-City One. Each game offers a different interpretation of the lawman, reflecting changing design trends across the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The 1986 release from Melbourne House, developed by Beam Software, mixes arcade action with light strategy. Players patrol the city via a crime map before tackling flick-screen platform levels, choosing how to deal with perps using commands like Halt, Warn, or Kill. The Lawgiver’s multiple ammo types add tactical flexibility, reinforcing Dredd’s role as judge, jury, and executioner.

In contrast, the 1991 version from Virgin Mastertronic and Random Access shifts to a scrolling platform format with structured missions spread across Mega-City One. Each assignment focuses on eliminating threats or objectives while keeping the city’s crime rate under control, blending fast action with time pressure and forward planning.

Together, these two games highlight different eras of licensed design on the Commodore 64. While neither fully captures the scale of Dredd’s comic universe, both remain fondly remembered by fans for their atmosphere, ambition, and distinctly British approach to arcade action.

💬 Which version do you prefer — the crime-map tactics of 1986, or the mission-driven action of 1991?

Released in 1990 by Cinemaware, Antheads: It Came from the Desert II is a direct sequel to the cult classic It Came from the Desert, pushing the story five years into a darker, more unsettling future. The once-quiet town of Lizard Breath is again under threat—this time from townsfolk mutating into terrifying ant-headed creatures.

Players step into the role of Brick Nash, now a war veteran turned truck driver, drawn back into the mystery as the town unravels. The game retains Cinemaware’s signature blend of real-time exploration, dialogue-driven encounters, and action sequences, all unfolding under a strict 15-day countdown that keeps the pressure firmly on.

While it reuses much of the original game’s structure and assets, Antheads introduces new story beats, locations, and a heavier emphasis on investigation. The tone is noticeably darker, with paranoia and body-horror elements replacing some of the B-movie camp of its predecessor.

Visually, the game maintains Cinemaware’s cinematic presentation, with detailed character portraits and moody scenes that help sell the narrative. Music by Jim Simmons and Gregory Haggard reinforces the tension, supporting the game’s sense of urgency and creeping dread.

Though often viewed as an expansion rather than a full sequel, Antheads remains a fascinating continuation of the series, valued by fans for its storytelling ambition and its place within Cinemaware’s distinctive catalogue.

Released in 1987 by Magnetic Scrolls for the Commodore Amiga, The Guild of Thieves is a landmark interactive fiction adventure set in the richly imagined medieval world of Kerovnia. You play as an aspiring thief seeking admission to the notorious Guild, tasked with proving your skill by stealing priceless treasures from heavily guarded locations.

Gameplay is driven by a powerful text parser that allows detailed and flexible interaction with the environment. Players must carefully explore towns, castles, and vaults, using observation, logic, and precise timing to overcome devious puzzles and security systems. Every command matters, and experimentation is often the key to progress.

The Amiga version enhances the experience with around 30 high-quality illustrations that bring key moments and locations to life, adding atmosphere without breaking the flow of the text-driven gameplay. Puzzle design is demanding but fair, rewarding patience and careful thinking rather than trial and error alone.

Adding to the immersion were the famous “feelies” included in the original release, such as the What Burglar? newsletter, a Bank of Kerovnia account card, a guild contract, and a six-sided die. These physical extras deepened the sense of inhabiting a living world beyond the screen.

Today, The Guild of Thieves is regarded as one of the finest examples of interactive fiction ever created. Winner of the Golden Joystick Award for Best Adventure Game of 1987, it remains a defining title of the genre and a standout classic of the Commodore Amiga.

Released in 1986 by Hewson Consultants and developed by Stephen Crow, Firelord drops you into the cursed kingdom of Torot as Sir Galaheart, a lone knight tasked with reclaiming the sacred Firestone from the Evil Queen. To restore peace, you must recover four charms of eternal youth while surviving a land filled with danger, temptation, and consequence.

The game blends exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving into a surprisingly deep experience. You begin unarmed, forced to explore cautiously until you obtain an enchanted crystal to fight off spectral enemies. As you roam forests, villages, and dungeons, you’ll trade, bargain, steal, or face trials that can end in execution if you fail.

Firelord stands out for its layered systems. You must manage health, trading energy, and weapon energy while navigating a dynamic economy and morality system where your choices directly affect outcomes and progression. Every decision nudges your journey in a different direction.

Visually, the side-scrolling world is richly detailed and atmospheric, brought to life further by Ben Daglish’s evocative SID soundtrack. Your adventure concludes with a ranking system, awarding titles from humble Serf to the ultimate Firelord, reflecting not just success, but how you achieved it. Today, Firelord is remembered as one of the Commodore 64’s most ambitious and thoughtful fantasy adventures.

Released for the Commodore Amiga in 1994 by Virgin Interactive, Aladdin is a colourful platform game based on Disney’s hugely successful animated film. Developed from the same design as the Mega Drive version, the Amiga port brought the adventure of Agrabah to home computer players with detailed sprites, lively animation, and fast arcade-style gameplay.

Players take control of Aladdin as he runs, jumps, and fights his way through stages inspired by the movie. From the busy rooftops of Agrabah to the treacherous Cave of Wonders and the Sultan’s palace, each level mixes precise platforming with combat using Aladdin’s scimitar or thrown apples to defeat enemies.

The game also includes collectible gems, bonus tokens, and special mini-games featuring Genie and Abu. These extra challenges provide opportunities to earn additional lives and rewards, encouraging players to explore levels carefully rather than simply rushing to the exit.

Visually, Aladdin impressed many Amiga players with smooth character animation and vibrant environments inspired by Disney’s original artwork. Combined with lively music and effects adapted for the Amiga sound hardware, the game captured much of the energy of the film.

Today, Aladdin is remembered as one of the better Disney-licensed games of the era and a solid example of how film adaptations could work well on the Amiga when handled by the right team.

Released in December 1985 by Richard Darling and published by Mastertronic under its M.A.D. label, Master of Magic is a fast-paced dungeon adventure that drops players into a dangerous high-fantasy world of spells, monsters, and maze-like peril. Transported by the mysterious Thelric, your unnamed hero must recover the legendary Amulet of Immortality before being trapped forever.

Gameplay blends action-oriented role-playing with constant exploration. Players navigate interconnected mazes while battling creatures such as skeletons, bats, and spiders, carefully managing health and magical energy as danger escalates. Progress depends on learning layouts, reacting quickly in combat, and making smart decisions under pressure.

The screen layout is clean and functional, combining a live map, text messages, command options, and clear visual representations of enemies and items. This structure keeps the action flowing while allowing tactical choices during exploration and combat.

A major highlight is the soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, featuring an arrangement of Shibolet by Synergy. The music adds atmosphere far beyond what was expected from a budget release, helping elevate the experience and giving the game a lasting identity.

Despite its budget origins, Master of Magic earned praise for its engaging gameplay and outstanding audio. Today, it’s regarded as a cult favourite on the Commodore 64 and a strong example of how ambition and craftsmanship could shine even in low-cost releases.

Released in 1984 by Infocom and designed by Douglas Adams alongside Steve Meretzky, The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy arrived on the Commodore 64 as one of the most ambitious interactive fiction titles of the 8-bit era. Based directly on Adams’ bestselling novel, the C64 version faithfully recreated the absurd humour and unpredictable sci-fi storytelling that made the book a cult phenomenon.

On the Commodore 64, gameplay is entirely text-driven, powered by Infocom’s advanced Z-machine engine. Players must type precise commands to explore environments, solve layered puzzles, and survive increasingly bizarre situations — from escaping a bulldozer to navigating interstellar travel. The parser is famously demanding, often requiring exact phrasing and lateral thinking, making experimentation essential. The C64 release also shipped with Infocom’s signature “feelies” in the box, physical props that enhanced immersion and reinforced its narrative depth.

Technically impressive for an 8-bit machine, the game demonstrated how the Commodore 64 could deliver complex logic structures and expansive storytelling without graphics. Its difficulty became legendary, with many players remembering unexpected instant deaths and obscure puzzle solutions as part of the experience. Unlike arcade titles of the time, this was pure imagination-driven gameplay.

Today, The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy is regarded as one of the finest text adventures ever released on the Commodore 64. It stands as a milestone in interactive fiction history and remains a defining example of how strong writing alone could create an unforgettable gaming universe.

Released in October 1987 by Superior Quality Software and published by Datasoft, Force 7 is a unique hybrid of arcade shooting and squad-based strategy on the Commodore 64.

In this sci-fi action game, you command a crack special-forces team of seven operatives sent to infiltrate an alien-infested energy facility on the planet Karis and rescue trapped Earth colonists.

Only one operative is active at a time, and each squad member has specialised abilities — including welding tools, flame-throwers, hydro-guns, and demolition equipment — requiring tactical switching to survive.

Gameplay focuses on navigating multi-level rooms using teleporters, collecting ammo and health packs, battling alien “mother” units, and deploying the powerful Battle Unit (BU) mech turret for temporary invincibility.

The C64 version delivers strong graphics for the platform and features an atmospheric soundtrack by Rob Sisinni that builds tension throughout each mission.

Force 7 remains notable in the retro community for its ambitious design, blending fast-paced action with team management and problem-solving. Often compared to the film Aliens, it stands out as one of the more inventive sci-fi shooters on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1984 by Craig Communications and developed by A.V.S. for the Commodore 64, System 15000 is one of the earliest video games to realistically simulate computer hacking.

Designed by Lee Kristofferson, the game places players in the role of a digital investigator tasked with recovering $1.5 million stolen from Comdata by the criminal organisation Realco.

Armed with only a phone number and access code, players must dial into remote systems using a simulated modem interface, decipher passwords, analyse data, and bypass security protocols.

Gameplay unfolds as a text-based adventure, carefully recreating the experience of early online computing. Dial tones, slow screen rendering, and realistic command prompts mirror the behaviour of 300-baud modems.

Progress depends on logical thinking, careful note-taking, and understanding system structures rather than fast reflexes, making it a uniquely cerebral experience.

The game’s detailed presentation and immersive pacing have often been compared to the atmosphere of the film WarGames, reinforcing its authentic hacking theme.

Praised for its realism and originality, System 15000 offered a rare “white-hat” hacking experience long before the genre became popular.

Today, it’s remembered as a pioneering digital simulation and an important milestone in the evolution of computer-based adventure games.

Endorsed by professional snooker legend Jimmy White, the game delivers a remarkably authentic and feature-rich snooker experience.

Players are given complete control over the table, with the ability to rotate the view, zoom in on any ball, and apply spin or swerve to shots. Multiple modes are included, ranging from competitive one- and two-player matches to practice sessions, trick shots, and demo play, all supported by four adjustable skill levels.

What truly sets the game apart is its smooth 3D presentation and highly accurate ball physics. Each break-off plays differently, maximum 147 breaks are possible, and games can be saved mid-frame. Digitised crowd applause and sound effects add to the atmosphere, while playful visual touches appear if players take too long to line up a shot.

Widely regarded as one of the finest snooker simulations ever made, Jimmy White’s Whirlwind Snooker remains a standout Amiga title. Its blend of realism, accessibility, and personality ensures its lasting reputation as a true sports gaming classic.

Inspired by Atari’s iconic arcade machine, this version reimagines the experience within the limits of the C64 while aiming to preserve the feel and structure of the original.

The game is split into three distinct sequences. First, players engage in a space battle against swarms of TIE Fighters defending the Death Star. This is followed by a surface assault, flying low across the station while avoiding obstacles and targeting defensive emplacements.

The final and most memorable section is the trench run, where precision flying and sharp reflexes are required to survive enemy fire and line up the decisive shot into the exhaust port. While the C64 cannot reproduce true vector graphics, the game’s presentation captures the spirit of the arcade with fast-paced, forward-scrolling action.

Although technical limitations are evident, Star Wars remains an engaging and nostalgic experience for fans of the franchise. Its faithful recreation of the film’s climax helped secure its place among the more memorable licensed titles on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1988 by Target Games and designed by Julian Gollop, Laser Squad is a landmark turn-based tactical strategy game that helped define the genre on home computers. Often described as the spiritual forerunner to X-COM, it introduced ideas and systems that would influence tactical design for decades.

Players command a small squad of elite soldiers across a range of mission scenarios, including hostage rescues, search-and-destroy operations, and item recovery. Viewed from an isometric perspective, each mission demands careful positioning, awareness of enemy movement, and smart use of cover.

Every unit operates using a limited pool of action points per turn, forcing players to plan movement, attacks, and reactions with precision. A wide selection of weapons and equipment—each with distinct strengths and limitations—allows for varied tactical approaches, while line-of-sight rules and fog of war keep tension high.

Laser Squad was widely praised on release, earning strong review scores and recognition for its depth and replayability. Its influence is unmistakable, later evolving into X-COM: Enemy Unknown, which originally began life as Laser Squad II. Today, it stands as one of the most important strategy games ever released on the Commodore 64.

Players begin their journey in rural Thailand and fight their way toward the legendary Lumpini Stadium in Bangkok, facing eight opponents along the way. Each fighter has their own style and behaviour, forcing players to adapt rather than rely on a single tactic throughout the game.

A clever multi-load system keeps the action flowing without breaking immersion.

The game was praised for its large character sprites, fluid animation, and depth of mechanics, especially impressive on the C64. While the learning curve can be steep and timing is unforgiving, mastery is rewarding and skill-based rather than luck-driven.

With streamlined controls, recognisable wrestlers, and strong presentation, the game captures the spectacle of early ’90s WWF in 8-bit form.

r2v9K15Clr4.title: Final Fight – Why Was Guy Missing from the Amiga Conversion?
r2v9K15Clr4.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/final-fight/

Final Fight (1991), developed by Capcom and ported to the Amiga by Creative Materials under U.S. Gold, is the home-computer adaptation of the classic 1989 arcade beat ’em up.

Players can choose from two of the three main heroes — Mike Haggar, Cody, and Guy — as they battle through Metro City to defeat the Mad Gear gang and rescue Haggar’s daughter, Jessica.

Gameplay follows traditional side-scrolling brawler mechanics, featuring punches, kicks, throws, jumping attacks, and waves of on-screen enemies.

However, the Amiga conversion is notably less fluid than the arcade original. Animation frames are reduced, certain sections are missing, and performance issues such as slowdown affect the pacing.

Some iconic stages and elements are simplified or removed, including parts of the Industrial Area and the elevator sequence.

Graphically, the game attempts to preserve the arcade’s pixel-art style, but lacks polish and smoothness. The soundtrack is also heavily limited, with most in-game music omitted in favour of sound effects.

Despite its shortcomings, Final Fight on the Amiga remains historically significant as part of the early wave of arcade-to-home conversions, demonstrating how hardware limits shaped classic ports.

Today, it is often cited by retro fans as a case study in both the challenges and compromises of adapting arcade hits to home systems.

You race across seven increasingly challenging tracks packed with ramps, bumps, and tight corners, aiming to complete three laps before the timer runs out. Released in 1987 by Ocean Software, Short Circuit is an action-adventure game for the Commodore 64 based on the popular 1986 sci-fi comedy film. Players take control of Number 5, a military robot accidentally brought to life by a lightning strike and determined to escape captivity without harming humans.

The game is split into two contrasting gameplay styles. The first section is a top-down adventure set inside a laboratory complex, where players search for items, avoid guards, and solve puzzles to build a robot decoy. Careful exploration and planning are essential, reflecting Number 5’s ethical refusal to cause harm.

Once outside, the game shifts into a side-scrolling action phase focused on speed and precision. Players must guide Number 5 through hazardous environments while avoiding security forces, obstacles, and enemy robots as the difficulty steadily increases.

The Commodore 64 version features detailed graphics and a memorable soundtrack composed by Martin Galway, helping capture the personality and atmosphere of the film. While opinions were mixed at release, Short Circuit is now remembered as an ambitious licensed title that blended adventure and arcade action in a distinctive way.

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Master of the Lamps is a highly original title developed by Peter Kaminski and Russell Lieblich and published by Activision. Blending action, rhythm, and puzzle-solving, the game offers a calm yet demanding experience that stood apart from the more aggressive arcade releases of the era.

Players take on the role of an Eastern prince on a mystical journey to restore three shattered magical lamps and reclaim his palace. Gameplay alternates between two very different challenges. The first involves piloting a magic carpet through winding tunnels, passing precisely through diamond-shaped gates where even a single mistake sends you back to the start.

The second core mechanic introduces rhythm and memory-based gameplay. Players face musical duels with genies, repeating increasingly complex sequences of tones. Across three sets of seven genie dens, the challenge escalates from audio and visual cues, to visual-only prompts, and finally to sound alone, testing timing, memory, and pitch recognition.

Russell Lieblich’s soundtrack is deeply woven into the experience, not just accompanying the gameplay but forming its foundation. Praised for its creativity and non-violent design, Master of the Lamps remains one of the Commodore 64’s most distinctive and thoughtful games, offering a uniquely meditative alternative to traditional action titles.

💬 Did your skills lie in perfect carpet control, or mastering the genie’s musical challenges?

Released for the Commodore Amiga, Lost Patrol places you in command of a stranded U.S. infantry squad after a helicopter crash in the Central Highlands of Vietnam. Cut off from support and deep in hostile territory, your mission is simple in theory but brutal in execution: lead the survivors safely to the nearest U.S. base while an unseen enemy hunts you at every step.

Most of the game unfolds on a strategic map of Vietnam, where you guide your squad across dangerous terrain. Managing morale, health, food, water, ammunition, and rest is essential, as exhaustion and poor decisions can be just as deadly as enemy fire. Every move carries risk, forcing you to weigh speed against safety.

When the patrol reaches key locations such as villages, rivers, or jungle clearings, the game shifts into illustrated scenario screens that present critical decisions. Encounters with snipers, patrols, ambushes, or minefields can trigger tense arcade-style sequences, including firefights and desperate hand-to-hand combat.

Lost Patrol stands out for its grim atmosphere and unconventional design. Interspersed video footage from the Vietnam War reinforces the sense of realism and tension, making the journey feel relentless and unforgiving. It remains one of the Amiga’s most distinctive war games, remembered for its focus on survival, leadership, and consequence rather than heroics.

Released in 1985 by Orpheus, Elidon is an atmospheric fantasy adventure for the Commodore 64 that sends you fluttering through an enormous enchanted world of forests, flowers, strange creatures and hidden pathways.

You control a fairy tasked with preparing for the return of the Fairy Queen. Her crown, Finvarra, needs seven magical flowers before the celebrations can begin – but first you must explore Elidon and track down seven bottles of magic water needed to make them bloom.

And there is plenty of exploring to do. Elidon contains over 300 flick-screen locations, creating a surprisingly large maze for a C64 game from 1985. Your fairy can walk or fly between screens, squeezing through narrow passages and avoiding enemies and obstacles that gradually drain her energy.

Various objects can be collected along the way, although you can only carry three at once. Fairy dust restores lost energy, while other items including a torch and musical instruments help you reach or survive different areas of the enchanted landscape.

The presentation was one of Elidon's biggest strengths. John B. Marshall's detailed backgrounds give each screen its distinctive storybook appearance, while Jon Maskill's SID soundtrack features an arrangement of Anitra's Dance from Edvard Grieg's Peer Gynt.

The game received some strong reviews at the time, including 83% from Zzap!64 and 9/10 from Computer & Video Games. Its combination of exploration, arcade movement and a huge interconnected world made it a rather unusual C64 release – and one that could easily leave you completely lost without a map.

Released in June 1984 by Sight & Sound Music for the Commodore 64, Kawasaki Rhythm Rocker is a unique interactive music-making tool created by jazz fusion musician and programmer Ryo Kawasaki.

Rather than focusing on traditional gameplay, the software allows users to compose and perform music in real time using four independent tracks: drums, bass, synthesiser, and vocal-style effects.

Players select an instrument channel, input rhythms and notes, and loop their creations while adjusting tempo, bass levels, and dub-style effects on the fly.

The interface is designed to be intuitive and expressive, encouraging experimentation and live-style performance rather than rigid composition.

High-resolution animated visuals pulse and react to the music, creating a hypnotic, psychedelic display that enhances the creative experience.

Powered by the SID chip, Rhythm Rocker showcases the sound hardware’s expressive range, blending sequencing, synthesis, and performance into one package.

Its design bridges the worlds of music production and home computing, offering a glimpse into early digital creativity on 8-bit systems.

Never intended as a competitive game, it instead invites exploration, improvisation, and artistic play.

Today, Kawasaki Rhythm Rocker is regarded as a cult classic among chiptune artists and retro enthusiasts, celebrated for its originality and ambition.

Released in 1988, MicroProse Soccer is an arcade-style football game developed by Sensible Software and published by MicroProse for the Commodore 64. Often seen as the foundation of the legendary Sensible Soccer series, it redefined how football games felt on 8-bit systems with speed, flow, and immediate control.

The game offers both full 11-a-side outdoor matches and fast-paced 6-a-side indoor soccer, alongside single matches, tournaments, and full World Cup campaigns. Players can save progress and customise teams using the Name Bank, adding long-term appeal rarely seen in football games of the era.

Controls are simple yet expressive, allowing crisp passing, chipped balls, powerful shots, and the famous “banana kick” for curling efforts on goal. The top-down scrolling pitch is enhanced by weather effects, player fatigue, and dynamic replays that mimic video rewinding, adding style and atmosphere to every match.

Critically acclaimed on release, MicroProse Soccer earned top scores across the gaming press and won the Golden Joystick Award for Best 8-bit Simulation. Its balance of arcade fun and tactical depth secured its legacy as one of the most influential sports games ever released on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Bocce is a digital adaptation of the traditional Italian lawn bowling game, developed and published by Simulmondo. As the company’s debut title, it holds an important place in European gaming history and helped introduce Italian-developed games to the wider home computer scene.

Gameplay faithfully recreates the real-world sport of bocce, tasking players with rolling large balls as close as possible to the smaller target ball, known as the jack. Players can fine-tune each throw by adjusting direction, power, and spin, with success relying more on precision and strategy than speed.

Matches can be played across different environments, including outdoor courts with uneven terrain and indoor bocciodromes that offer more controlled conditions. A distinctive split-screen interface enhances the experience, combining a top-down tactical view of the court with a 3D-style perspective of each throw.

While audio is minimal, the focus on realistic mechanics and thoughtful presentation gives Bocce a surprising depth. Remembered today as both a solid sports simulation and a milestone release for Simulmondo, it remains a fascinating example of early international game development on the Commodore 64.

Released in 1985 by Lucasfilm Games for the Commodore 64, The Eidolon is a pioneering first-person adventure that blends exploration, combat, and surreal science fantasy. Set in a mysterious, steampunk-inspired world, players discover a strange 19th-century machine and are transported into a vast network of otherworldly caves guarded by powerful creatures.

Gameplay focuses on navigating fractal-generated labyrinths, collecting coloured energy orbs, and battling hostile enemies. Each orb provides unique abilities, such as freezing time, transforming foes, or boosting attack power, encouraging players to experiment and adapt their strategy to survive.

Progression depends on careful resource management and tactical combat, as players must gather the right combination of orbs to defeat the fearsome dragon guardians that block advancement. With no save feature, every decision carries weight, making concentration and planning essential.

Visually, The Eidolon stands out for its use of fractal technology, previously seen in Rescue on Fractalus!, creating deep, atmospheric environments unlike anything else on the C64. Minimalist sound design and eerie effects reinforce the game’s sense of isolation and mystery.

Praised for its innovation and technical ambition, the game earned critical acclaim, including a 97% score and Gold Medal from Zzap!64. Although demanding and unforgiving, The Eidolon remains a cult classic, celebrated for helping shape the future of first-person adventure games.

rn_hzXvVYes.title: Insects In Space – The Bizarre C64 Defender Clone That Scored 94%
rn_hzXvVYes.description:
🕹️ Insects In Space (1989) – Commodore 64 Shoot-'Em-Up by Sensible Software
🌐 Full game info & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/game/insects-in-space

Released in 1989 by Hewson, Insects In Space is a bizarre Commodore 64 shooter from Sensible Software, heavily inspired by Defender. You take control of St. Helen, flying across a strange two-level landscape while battling giant alien insects and attempting to rescue helpless human babies.

The insects can grab the babies and carry them away, draining their life energy and eventually turning them into new creatures. A radar helps you keep track of what is happening across the playfield, while you race around trying to save as many babies as possible.

Rescuing the babies isn't simply about earning points either. They can provide useful power-ups, while a mysterious teleporting dust cloud can transport you around the landscape when you need to reach another part of the level quickly. Despite its wonderfully strange premise, Insects In Space was very well received by the C64 magazines. 

📰 Zzap!64 awarded it an impressive 94%, while The Games Machine gave it 86% and Commodore Force later gave it 90%.

The game was developed by Sensible Software, with programming by Chris Yates and music by legendary C64 composer Martin Galway. Interestingly, Insects In Space did not receive a conventional standalone release. The C64 version appeared as part of Hewson's 4th Dimension compilation alongside Head the Ball, Cyberdyne Warrior and Mission Impossibubble.

That makes this one of those fascinating examples of a game that was relatively easy to overlook at the time, despite being made by one of the most important British developers of the era and receiving a huge 94% from Zzap!64. There's plenty of Sensible Software personality here too, from the bizarre concept and chunky graphics to the frantic Defender-style gameplay, strange insect enemies and wonderfully noisy C64 sound effects.

Released in October 1985 for the Commodore 64, Little Computer People is a groundbreaking life simulation game developed by David Crane and published by Activision. Long before virtual pets became mainstream, this title offered a novel idea: sharing your computer with a living digital companion.

After loading, players are presented with a three-storey house and, after a short wait, a Little Computer Person moves in and begins living an independent daily routine. The character cooks meals, watches television, reads, and relaxes, all without direct control. Interaction is subtle, with players influencing behaviour through gifts, card games, and observation rather than commands.

A defining feature is that each copy of the game generates a unique character with its own name and personality traits. The LCP responds to care and neglect, encouraging a sense of responsibility and long-term engagement rather than traditional goals or scoring systems.

Praised for its originality and emotional connection, Little Computer People is widely regarded as one of the earliest examples of virtual life simulation. Its quiet, experimental design helped pave the way for later simulation and companion-based games, securing its place as a true Commodore 64 classic.

rng9n0SNeDg.title: The Magical Melodies Of Silence: Commodore Amiga Music Demo (1990) | Hq
rng9n0SNeDg.description:
♫ Sounds of Silents (1990) – Commodore Amiga Music Disk by The Silents
🌐 Visit the Cheeky Commodore Gamer website for retro gaming features, videos & archives:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk

Released in 1990, Sounds of Silents isn’t a traditional scene demo but a dedicated Amiga music disk—and it absolutely earns its place here on the strength of its soundtrack alone. Featuring compositions by Jesper Kyd, this release highlights just how powerful and expressive Amiga music could be when placed front and centre.

The disk presents its tracks through a custom music selector coded by The Crux and illustrated by Mikael Balle. From here, listeners can choose individual compositions while watching responsive “sound to light” animations and VU meters that pulse and shift in time with the music, keeping the experience visually engaging without distracting from the audio.

The collection includes seven tracks: Apocalypse, Next Decade, China Girl, Slide, Spirit, and Space Song. Apocalypse stands out as a rich, atmospheric piece, while Space Song brings a more upbeat, rhythmic energy that feels effortlessly infectious. The remaining tracks maintain a consistently high standard, showcasing Kyd’s range and musical identity even at this early stage.

Originally released on a single disk at The Bounty Copyparty in Horsens, Sounds of Silents remains a superb example of why Amiga music disks mattered. More than three decades later, it still holds up as a focused, confident celebration of composition, timing, and mood on Commodore’s 16-bit machine.

rqqqYRSgSBI.title: Go For The Gold – The £2.99 C64 Game That Reached UK No.1
rqqqYRSgSBI.description:
🕹️ Go For The Gold (1986) – Commodore 64 Multi-Event Sports Game
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/go-for-the-gold/

Released by Americana in 1986, Go For The Gold is a multi-event Commodore 64 sports game featuring sprinting, hurdles, long jump, archery, diving and weightlifting. You can practice individual events or compete across the full programme, with up to six participants battling for the best scores. Some events demand the traditional left-and-right joystick treatment, while archery, diving and weightlifting rely more heavily on timing and technique.

The game originally appeared in America as HESGames in 1984. That version was only available on disk in the UK and cost £27.95, leaving it competing with considerably cheaper sports games such as Daley Thompson’s Decathlon and Summer Games.

Two years later, Americana brought it back under the new title Go For The Gold. The revised version was released on cassette for just £2.99, transforming a largely overlooked game into one of the biggest C64 budget successes of 1986. It eventually climbed to number one in the Gallup/Microscope UK combined-format chart for the week ending 13 September 1986. Not bad for a renamed two-year-old sports game costing less than three quid.

Go For The Gold also received excellent reviews. Zzap!64 awarded it 95%, Computer & Video Games and Commodore User both gave it 8/10, while Your Commodore went all the way with 10/10. The chunky athletes and their celebrations give the events plenty of personality. The sprinter punches the air with delight, the long jumper checks his backside after falling over, and one of the diving judges appears to have found something more interesting to look at. Archery remains my favourite, even though its aiming cursor looks suspiciously like a tiny boat with a white sail.

rRKBcyiWO2I.title: The Commodore 64 SID Chip Explained | The Sound That Defined C64 Music
rRKBcyiWO2I.description:
🕹️ The Commodore 64 SID chip explained — the legendary sound chip that helped define C64 music, 8-bit game soundtracks and chiptune culture.

The MOS Technology SID, short for Sound Interface Device, was the sonic heart of the Commodore 64. Designed by Bob Yannes and launched with the C64 in 1982, it helped turn the machine into far more than just another home computer.

With three independent voices, selectable waveforms, ADSR envelopes, ring modulation, sync and filtering, the SID gave musicians and game composers a level of sound control that stood apart from many rival systems of the time.

In this retro computing feature, we look at how legendary Commodore 64 composers such as Rob Hubbard, Martin Galway, Ben Daglish and David Whittaker pushed the SID chip far beyond what many people expected from an 8-bit machine. From rapid arpeggios and clever waveform tricks to sample playback, basslines, filters and unforgettable loading music, the SID became part of the C64’s identity.

The demo scene pushed it even further, using technical tricks, experimental routines and musical imagination to create sounds that still impress retro gaming fans, chiptune artists and C64 collectors today. The SID’s influence did not stop in the 1980s. Its sound still lives on through emulation, hardware recreations, live performances, modern chiptune music and a global fanbase that continues to celebrate Commodore 64 music decades later.

For many C64 owners, the SID chip was not just a component. It was the sound of loading screens, high scores, late nights, tape decks, joystick battles and games that stayed in your head long after the computer was switched off.

This is the story of the SID chip — the sound that helped make the Commodore 64 legendary.

Released in 1983 by Commodore Business Machines (UK) Ltd., Dancing Monster is an unusual first-person action game developed by Peter Dekany and Denes Baan for the Commodore 64. Blending fantasy themes with shooter-style mechanics, it stands out as one of the system’s more experimental early titles.

Players are tasked with rescuing a princess who has been transformed into a grotesque dancing monster by an evil wizard. Using a crosshair, the goal is to destroy specific parts of the creature in a strict sequence, with each required body part displayed on screen. Speed and accuracy are essential, as mistakes cause previously destroyed parts to regenerate.

The challenge ramps up as players must complete the entire sequence within a limited time while managing an action gauge that steadily drains. Missed shots, hesitation, or targeting the wrong area can quickly undo progress and lead to failure.

With its strange premise, rule-driven gameplay, and distinctive presentation, Dancing Monster remains a memorable curiosity in the Commodore 64 library. It’s a prime example of early 8-bit experimentation, offering something truly different from more conventional action games of the era.

The Commodore 64 version faithfully preserves the tense gameplay of the original, offering smooth scrolling, responsive controls, and a constant sense of pressure. Released in 1994 by International Computer Entertainment, Total Carnage brings all-out arcade chaos to the Commodore Amiga as the spiritual successor to Smash TV. It delivers relentless top-down action with an unapologetically explosive tone.

Set in the fictional war zone of Kookistan in 1999, you step into the boots of Captain Carnage or Major Mayhem, members of the Doomsday Squad sent to topple the deranged dictator General Akhboob. Each of the three stages throws swarms of enemies, environmental hazards, and screen-filling carnage at you, building toward a boss showdown.

The twin-stick control scheme keeps movement and firing independent, making precision and positioning critical as the pace ramps up. Power-ups, screen-clearing bombs, and rescued prisoners add tactical choices to the constant pressure, while two-player co-op doubles the chaos.

On the Amiga, Total Carnage stands out for its bold visuals, smooth scrolling, and faithful arcade energy. Today it’s remembered as one of the platform’s most intense action shooters and a must-play for fans of fast, uncompromising arcade design.

Blagger Goes To Hollywood is a 1985 action-arcade game developed and published by Alligata Software for the Commodore 64.

A follow-up to the original Blagger trilogy, this quirky title sends the infamous burglar on a chaotic adventure through a Hollywood studio packed with famous movie characters and recognisable theme tunes.

In this C64 classic, you guide Blagger through an isometric, side-view world, collecting and using the correct props to defeat characters inspired by Batman, Superman, Jaws, Tarzan, The Incredible Hulk, and more.

Each opponent requires a specific item to be launched at the right moment, blending fast arcade action with puzzle-solving and pattern recognition — a fairly unusual concept for mid-80s Commodore 64 games.

The game is especially remembered for its catchy chiptune adaptations of film and TV themes, cleverly recreated within the limits of the SID chip, and for its playful pop-culture mash-ups.

While reviews were mixed at the time, Blagger Goes To Hollywood has since earned appreciation for its ambition, originality, and nostalgic charm, making it a fascinating entry in C64 gaming history.

Savage Pond stands out for its ambition and originality, offering a demanding experience that feels very different from typical 8-bit action games. Its focus on nature, growth, and survival has earned it a distinctive place in the Commodore 64’s early library.

Set across the Caribbean during the golden age of piracy, it drops you into a living world shaped by exploration, politics, and personal ambition.

You take command of a pirate ship and choose how to carve out your legend, whether that means serving European powers, turning rogue against everyone, or switching allegiances as fortunes change. These systems combine strategy, action, and role-playing elements in a way that was far ahead of its time.

On the Commodore 64, the game delivers expressive sprites, fluid animations, and atmospheric sound that bring the high seas to life. Sid Meier’s Pirates! is widely regarded as a landmark title that helped define open-ended game design and remains a gold standard of emergent gameplay today.

The adventure unfolds over three distinct stages. First, players control Jonathan Harker as he explores Count Dracula’s castle, searching for vital documents while evading supernatural dangers. The second stage shifts to the town of Wismar, where Van Helsing and Jonathan battle the spreading vampire threat using tools such as garlic and stakes. Presented in an isometric perspective, the game delivers a striking visual style that reinforces its eerie tone. The monochromatic graphics enhance the sense of dread, while sparse music and sound effects build an unsettling atmosphere that mirrors the film’s slow-burn horror.

Unusual, moody, and unmistakably dark, Nosferatu the Vampyre stands out as one of the Commodore 64’s most distinctive horror titles. It remains fondly remembered for its ambition, presentation, and commitment to gothic storytelling.

sCn0FCZBbAU.title: Aliens: The Computer Game – Why Did the C64 Get Two Completely Different Versions
sCn0FCZBbAU.description:
🕹️ Aliens: The Computer Game (1986) – Commodore 64 Action-Strategy Movie Tie-In
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/aliens-the-computer-game/

Released in 1986 for the Commodore 64, Aliens: The Computer Game arrived in two distinct versions. The US release was developed by Activision, while the European version was handled by Software Studios and published by Electric Dreams. Both were based on James Cameron’s Aliens, but each took a very different approach to translating the film onto 8-bit hardware.

The Activision version is built around six mini-missions that mirror key moments from the movie. These range from piloting the Sulaco dropship and navigating air-duct mazes to managing a squad of marines and confronting the Alien Queen. Gameplay switches between fast joystick-driven action and tactical decision-making inside the Mobile Tactical Operations Bay, where players monitor stamina, ammunition, and marine status.

Exploration plays a major role, with a sprawling maze of up to 255 rooms filled with aliens, acid pools, and limited resources. The Electric Dreams version strips things back into a more straightforward action experience, but focuses heavily on atmosphere, tension, and mood, earning praise for how well it captured the dread of the film on the Commodore 64.

Together, both versions stand out among licensed games of the era. By blending action, strategy, and early digitised cutscenes, Aliens: The Computer Game remains one of the most atmospheric and inventive movie tie-ins on the C64. Today, it’s remembered as a challenging, memorable experience that dared to do more than simply reskin an arcade shooter.

Developed by Clive Townsend with music by Rob Hubbard, the game introduces Nina, sister of the original protagonist, on a mission driven by revenge and infiltration rather than brute force.

The game unfolds across nine missions spanning more than 700 interconnected screens, forming a vast industrial compound filled with hazards and security systems. Progress depends on exploration and careful planning as players collect punched tape fragments to disable defences and work towards a daring motorcycle escape.

Combat is deliberately de-emphasised in favour of stealth and evasion. Robotic guards, wild animals, electrified fences, and surveillance systems force players to observe enemy patterns, choose routes wisely, and solve environmental challenges rather than rely on direct confrontation.

Despite its demanding difficulty and maze-like design, Saboteur II is widely regarded as a bold and innovative sequel. Its emphasis on stealth gameplay, strong atmosphere, and the introduction of a female lead helped it stand out in the Commodore 64 library, securing its reputation as a classic of the genre.

Released in 1987 by Mirrorsoft and developed by Blitter Animations, Andy Capp brings the iconic British comic strip to the Commodore 64 in a surprisingly ambitious life-simulation adventure. Players step into the shoes of Andy himself, attempting to survive a chaotic week of everyday life without running out of money—or patience.

Gameplay unfolds across fixed-screen locations as time rapidly ticks through the days of the week. Players must juggle Andy’s priorities, including securing unemployment benefits, managing cash, visiting the pub, dodging the police, and dealing with his long-suffering wife, Flo. Choices and timing are crucial, as certain locations and characters are only available at specific times.

The presentation leans heavily into the comic’s roots, with monochrome visuals that closely resemble the original artwork. The soundtrack famously features a rendition of Dvořák’s New World Symphony, an unusual but memorable choice that gives the game a distinctive identity.

Andy Capp stands out as an early experiment in life-simulation gameplay, blending humour, routine, and mild chaos into a format rarely seen on the C64 at the time. Its satirical take on everyday struggles has earned it lasting affection among retro gaming fans.

SLx3YOQVWE4.title: Highlander – Ocean Turned Connor MacLeod Into a C64 One-on-One Fighter
SLx3YOQVWE4.description:
🕹️ Highlander (1986) – Commodore 64 Film Tie-In Fighting Game
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/highlander/

Released in 1986 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Highlander is a one-on-one fighting game based on the cult classic fantasy film. Developed by Canvas, the game puts players in control of Connor MacLeod, the immortal swordsman, as he faces key opponents from the movie in a bid to claim “The Prize.”

Combat is presented as a series of duels against Ramírez, Fasil, and the Kurgan. Each encounter focuses on sword-based fighting, with the goal of defeating every opponent in turn. While the premise promises cinematic clashes, the gameplay itself is very limited, offering a small move set and little tactical depth.

Controls are awkward and unresponsive, making combat feel sluggish and unrefined. Movement and attacks lack precision, which often turns fights into drawn-out exchanges rather than tense duels. Presentation does little to elevate the experience, with stiff character animation and basic arenas that fail to convey the atmosphere of the film.

Highlander was widely criticised on release, receiving poor reviews for its execution and overall design. Despite a strong licence and recognisable characters, it’s remembered as a disappointing movie adaptation that never captured the excitement or drama of its source material.

💬 Did you ever persevere with Highlander, or was this one you quickly moved on from?

Released in 1990 by Ocean Software for the Commodore 64, Total Recall is an action-heavy platform game based on the hit science-fiction film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger. You play as Doug Quaid, a man caught in a web of shifting memories, corporate conspiracies, and deadly secrets that stretch all the way to Mars.

The game blends multiple styles as you move through its stages, combining platforming, shooting, and light puzzle elements across varied locations. From hostile city streets to high-security interiors, progression depends on sharp reactions, careful movement, and dealing with enemies quickly before they overwhelm you.

Despite the limitations of the hardware, the C64 version delivers a tense, atmospheric experience. Large character sprites, smooth scrolling, and moody screen design help capture the darker tone of the film, while Jonathan Dunn’s soundtrack adds a constant sense of urgency and futuristic grit.

Total Recall stands out as one of Ocean’s stronger late-era licensed games, offering a solid mix of action and atmosphere. It remains a memorable example of how ambitious movie adaptations could still shine on the Commodore 64.

stPD0I9cvv8.title: Lazarian – Five Space Trials and a Giant Flying Eye on the C64
stPD0I9cvv8.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/lazarian/

Released in 1983 by Commodore for the Commodore 64, Lazarian is an early arcade-style shoot-’em-up programmed and scored by Andy Finkel and inspired by Bally Midway’s 1981 arcade title.

Players pilot a spacecraft through a series of increasingly challenging combat zones, battling waves of alien enemies, navigating dense meteor fields, and surviving fast-paced attack patterns.

The game unfolds across five distinct stages, each introducing new mechanics and enemy behaviours. Progression requires sharp reflexes, precise movement, and careful positioning.

The final phase culminates in a showdown with the powerful “Evil Eye” boss, providing a demanding conclusion to the multi-stage campaign.

Visually, Lazarian delivers simple but effective space-themed graphics that suit its fast-moving gameplay. Enemy formations and environmental hazards are clearly presented, allowing players to react quickly.

Sound design and music by Andy Finkel enhance the experience, adding tension and atmosphere to each stage. Several audio elements are shared with Commodore’s Dragon’s Den, reflecting common development practices of the era.

While overshadowed by later shooter classics, Lazarian represents an important step in bringing arcade-style action to home computers during the early 1980s.

Today, it’s remembered as a solid and historically significant example of Commodore’s early in-house game development.

💬 Did you manage to defeat the Evil Eye, or did the later stages prove too intense?

T_WmUbbiD8E.title: Commodore 64 Budget Games – Incredible C64 Classics Under £3 (80s & 90s)
T_WmUbbiD8E.description:
🕹️ Cheap Commodore 64 Games That Defined the £1.99 Era
🌐 Full game info, manuals & more:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/

Commodore 64 budget games in the 1980s and early 90s typically cost just £1.99 to £2.99, making them some of the most accessible and important games of the era. This video looks back at those original budget prices — not modern retro values — and explores how these low-cost titles helped define a generation of gaming.

Back in the UK, budget labels like Mastertronic, Codemasters and Firebird reshaped the gaming landscape. Instead of paying full price, players could take a chance on cheaper cassette releases — sometimes rough, sometimes brilliant, but always memorable.

Featured in this video are classic and cult Commodore 64 budget titles including Kikstart II, Kane, Rogue, Thrust, Spore, CJ’s Elephant Antics, BMX Simulator and more — alongside hidden gems, underrated favourites, and a few that didn’t quite hit the mark.

We also explore how the budget ecosystem expanded through re-release labels like Americana, Rack-It, Encore and Kixx, bringing full-price classics back to the shelves at £1.99.

Technically, these games pushed the Commodore 64 to its limits. With cassette loading, tight memory constraints, and innovations like Invade-a-Load, developers created simple but highly addictive gameplay experiences that are still remembered today.

For many of us, this wasn’t just part of gaming — this was gaming.

T0GsTIt4xAE.title: Uridium – Andrew Braybrook Made the C64 Move at Ridiculous Speed
T0GsTIt4xAE.description:
🕹️ Uridium (1986) – Commodore 64 High-Speed Sci-Fi Shoot ’Em Up Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/uridium/

Released in 1986 by Hewson Consultants and developed by Andrew Braybrook of Graftgold, Uridium is a blisteringly fast horizontal shooter that redefined what the Commodore 64 could do. You pilot the agile Manta fighter across fifteen vast super-dreadnought carriers, each named after metallic elements, in a relentless fight for survival.

Each carrier demands precision flying as you skim across its surface, destroying defences, dodging drones, and avoiding lethal barriers. Once the core is breached, you must land successfully to trigger the self-destruct sequence before making a clean escape, turning every stage into a nerve-wracking test of control and timing.

Uridium is famous for its technical brilliance, using clever manipulation of character graphics to simulate pseudo-parallax scrolling. The result is a sense of speed, depth, and smooth motion that was astonishing on C64 hardware at the time.

Backed by a driving soundtrack from Steve Turner and razor-sharp controls, Uridium delivers constant intensity from start to finish. Praised by Zzap!64 as “technically stunning” and winner of the 1986 Golden Joystick Award for Best Arcade-Style Game, it remains one of the most celebrated and influential shooters of the 8-bit era.

💬 Did you master the carrier landings, or did the speed push you to the limit every time?

Released in 1984 by Timothy G. Martin and published by Brøderbund Software, with the Commodore 64 version distributed in Europe by Ariolasoft, Spelunker is infamous for its unforgiving difficulty and remarkably fragile hero. Few games on the C64 punish carelessness quite like this one.

The goal is to descend deep into a sprawling multi-level cave system while collecting keys, treasure, bombs, and flares, all under constant pressure from a limited air supply. Hazards are everywhere, from deadly traps and roaming ghosts to sheer drops where even the smallest fall results in instant death. Every movement demands patience, precision, and absolute caution.

Progression relies on mastering elevators, ropes, ladders, and careful item use as you work through six increasingly dangerous stages. The Commodore 64 version delivers smooth scrolling, colourful cave environments, atmospheric sound effects, and an eerie soundtrack that reinforces the sense of isolation and danger.

Notorious yet unforgettable, Spelunker has earned its cult status by being relentlessly fair but utterly uncompromising. Decades on, it’s still remembered as the game where every single step truly matters.

Players pilot a high-speed spacecraft across a horizontally scrolling alien landscape, tasked with protecting stranded astronauts from waves of invading enemies. Combat is intense and demanding, with smart bombs available to clear the screen in emergencies and hyperspace jumps offering a risky escape option. Mastery comes from learning enemy behaviour, rescuing humans before they mutate, and maintaining control while navigating the terrain at speed.

The Commodore 64 version preserves the core mechanics and challenge that made the arcade original famous. Defender remains a landmark arcade-to-home conversion and is still regarded as one of the most influential and punishing shooters of its era.

Released in 1992 by Digital Design and published by Codemasters for the Commodore 64, Slicks is a fast-paced overhead Formula One racing game designed by Ashley Routledge and David Saunders, with music composed by Allister Brimble. It delivers an arcade-driven racing experience that pushes the C64 hard in its later years.

Players choose from six racing teams, each with different performance characteristics, and compete across circuits inspired by real-world Formula 1 tracks. The focus is on speed, precision, and maintaining control through tight corners while jostling for position against rival cars.

While the handling is immediate and accessible, Slicks adds a strategic layer through fuel consumption and tyre wear. Knowing when to push hard and when to drive conservatively becomes key to finishing races successfully, especially over longer events.

The game is widely praised for its smooth scrolling, responsive controls, and energetic presentation. A two-player mode adds extra excitement, making it a popular competitive choice for head-to-head racing on the same screen.

Today, Slicks is regarded as one of the finest top-down racers on the Commodore 64, remembered for its polished gameplay, excellent soundtrack, and lasting appeal among C64 racing fans.

Players take control of Clyde Radcliffe, a member of the Fuzzy Wuzzies, as he explores a hostile island to rescue his captured friends from sinister demons. Traditional side-scrolling platforming is blended with puzzle-solving, most notably in the infamous “torture screens,” where careful planning and precise execution are required to save trapped creatures from elaborate mechanisms.

Creatures is widely praised for its technical achievements, including smooth parallax scrolling, richly detailed environments, and expressive character animation. Steve Rowlands’ energetic soundtrack drives the action and complements the game’s shifting moods, balancing cute visuals with a darker edge.

Critically acclaimed on release, Creatures earned a Zzap!64 Gold Medal and is still regarded as a landmark C64 title. It stands as a showcase of what the hardware could achieve in the hands of skilled developers and remains a favourite among platform fans.

Players take on the role of a new recruit pushed through a series of gruelling training exercises designed to weed out the weak. These include the obstacle course, firing ranges, the Iron Man race, arm wrestling contests, and hand-to-hand combat against the drill instructor, before putting everything together in a hostage rescue mission. Each event tests different abilities, from precise timing to raw stamina.

The gameplay is infamous for its intense joystick-waggling mechanics, requiring fast reactions and physical endurance from the player. Success depends on mastering each discipline and maintaining consistency across events, closely mirroring the structure and challenge of the original arcade machine.

Combat School was widely praised for its faithful conversion, varied mini-games, and Martin Galway’s driving soundtrack. Today, it stands as one of the Commodore 64’s most memorable arcade adaptations and a defining example of Ocean Software’s expertise in bringing coin-op experiences to home computers.
