Released in 1984 by Jimmy Huey and published by Creative Software for the Commodore 64, Trolls and Tribulations is an inventive platformer that blends action, puzzles, and strategy into a distinctly unusual experience. Players take control of a lone troll exploring sewer-like mazes in search of hidden relics, while facing constant danger from hostile creatures and unforgiving layouts.

Gameplay is split into two interconnected phases. First comes Cretin Elimination, where enemies must be neutralised using a water gun that turns them into eggs. These eggs must then be disposed of correctly, or they’ll hatch back into active threats. Once the area is cleared, the focus shifts to maze exploration, collecting treasures and keys while avoiding indestructible monsters that force careful route planning.

Movement is deliberately grid-based, with the troll moving one tile at a time, giving the game a strong puzzle-like rhythm rather than traditional free-flowing platform action. This unique control system rewards foresight and precision, making every move count.

Adding to its distinctive personality is the use of classical music from composers such as Bach and Mozart, lending the game an unexpectedly atmospheric tone. Unusual mechanics, clever level design, and a clear sense of identity have helped Trolls and Tribulations earn a lasting cult following among Commodore 64 fans.

Released in 1984 by David and Richard Darling and published by Mastertronic for the Commodore 64, Bionic Granny is one of the most unconventional arcade-style titles of the early home computer era. Players take control of an elderly woman with bionic enhancements, tasked with chasing down schoolchildren after class and tapping them with her walking stick.

The game is presented from a top-down perspective, with the screen divided into three lanes where children walk steadily across the playfield. Players move left and right along the bottom of the screen, positioning Granny to intercept each child at the right moment.

Timing and positioning are essential, as players must also avoid lollipops thrown by the crossing guard, which can cost lives and interrupt progress. The simple control scheme keeps the focus on reflexes and rhythm rather than complex mechanics.

Visually, Bionic Granny uses basic graphics and minimal animation, reflecting its budget-label origins. While often criticised for repetitive gameplay and limited depth, the presentation suits the game’s straightforward arcade design.

Despite mixed reception on release, Bionic Granny has developed a cult following thanks to its bizarre premise and distinctive personality. Today, it’s remembered as a curious slice of 1980s game design and a talking point within the retro gaming community.

Gameplay blends fast-paced arcade shooting with light simulation elements. Missions involve strafing ground installations, bombing bunkers, and torpedoing enemy ships, while carefully managing fuel, ammunition, and aircraft damage. Successful pilots must return safely to the carrier to refuel, rearm, and make repairs before heading back into combat.

The Amiga version stands out for its smooth animation, detailed visuals by John Boechler, and an atmospheric soundtrack composed by Kris Hatlelid, all of which enhance the sense of scale and tension during each sortie. Precision flying and smart resource management are just as important as reflexes.

Wings of Fury is remembered as one of the Amiga’s standout flight action games, praised for its balance of challenge and immersion. Today, it remains a respected classic that captures the thrill and pressure of carrier-based air warfare.

Gear changes play an important role too, forcing you to manage effort carefully as terrain and pace shift throughout each stage.

Rather than racing visible opponents, Tour de France focuses entirely on time trials. Success depends on efficiency, stamina management, and maintaining a smooth rhythm, with overall victory decided by cumulative stage times rather than single-race wins.

Visually, the game makes strong use of smooth scrolling and high-resolution graphics, giving a convincing sense of forward motion that stands out among mid-1980s sports titles. The soundtrack supports the action with original music that reinforces the steady intensity of long-distance racing.

Today, Tour de France is remembered as an ambitious early sports simulation on the C64, valued for its inventive controls and its attempt to capture the feel of cycling at a time when the genre was still finding its footing.

Despite being a single-load game, it delivers a demanding and memorable challenge.

Praised on release for its originality and presentation, Zamzara earned high review scores and has since become regarded as one of the more distinctive and ambitious platform shooters on the Commodore 64.

Released in early 1992 by Ubisoft and developed by Hudson Soft, Dynablaster is the Amiga’s take on the legendary Bomberman formula, delivering fast-paced maze action built around timing, positioning, and glorious chaos. Known as Bomberman on other platforms, this version became a firm favourite for Amiga multiplayer sessions.

Gameplay takes place in grid-based arenas where players drop bombs to clear blocks, uncover power-ups, and outmanoeuvre opponents. Power-ups increase bomb range, allow multiple bombs, and boost movement speed, turning each round into a tense battle of prediction and quick thinking.

Dynablaster truly shines in multiplayer, supporting up to five players using a joystick adaptor, with four on joysticks and one on the keyboard. Matches are frantic, tactical, and endlessly replayable, making it a staple of living-room gaming during the Amiga’s peak years.

Single-player mode offers structured challenges across castle-style labyrinths filled with AI enemies, timers, and increasing difficulty. Strong visuals, tight controls, and a memorable soundtrack by Romeo Knight help keep the pace sharp and the pressure high.

Praised by Amiga magazines for its arcade-perfect conversion and outstanding multiplayer, Dynablaster remains one of the most iconic party games on the platform and a defining example of bomber-style gameplay done right.

Set in a dark sci-fi future, you control Saint Dragon as it rebels against a ruthless cyborg empire.

Action unfolds across five steadily escalating stages, each ending with a huge screen-filling guardian that tests positioning and firepower. Movement is deliberate and weighty, demanding careful control as enemy patterns close in from all angles.

The weapon system takes clear inspiration from R-Type, with collectible power-ups that upgrade pulse shots, lasers, and the dragon’s distinctive segmented tail, which can be used defensively as a shield. A temporary hyper mode boosts firepower and grants brief invulnerability, adding a risk-reward layer to the combat.

Despite inevitable limits compared to the arcade, the C64 version impressed with smooth scrolling and detailed animation, achieved using clever pre-shift techniques. Today, Saint Dragon is remembered as a cult favourite, praised for its atmosphere, originality, and its bold blend of fantasy and sci-fi within the shoot ’em up genre.

Players command a party of four iconic heroes — the Barbarian, Dwarf, Elf, and Wizard — as they venture into grid-based dungeons to defeat monsters, uncover treasure, and ultimately thwart the evil sorcerer Morcar. Despite the C64’s limitations, HeroQuest delivers atmospheric visuals with detailed sprites and dungeon layouts that successfully capture the look and feel of the tabletop experience. The music and sound effects reinforce the fantasy setting, adding tension and drama as each room is revealed.

Widely regarded as one of the strongest board game adaptations on the Commodore 64, HeroQuest stands out for its depth, accessibility, and strategic gameplay. It remains a beloved title among retro fans and a high point for fantasy strategy games of the early 1990s.

Released in 1983 for the Commodore 64, Miner 2049er is a landmark platform game developed by Bill Hogue and published by Big Five Software. Players take on the role of Bounty Bob, a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, sent deep into an abandoned uranium mine to capture the criminal Yukon Yohan.

Gameplay is built around precision movement and route planning. Each level is cleared by walking over every section of the mine’s platforms while avoiding radioactive enemies and environmental hazards. Timing is critical, as each stage is governed by a strict time limit that pushes players to balance speed with accuracy.

Strategic depth comes from collectible items such as drills and candles, which temporarily turn enemies harmless and allow Bob to defeat them on contact. Learning enemy patterns and choosing the safest order to claim platforms becomes essential as the levels grow more complex.

With colourful visuals, responsive controls, and tightly designed stages, Miner 2049er earned widespread praise and is often cited as one of the finest early platformers on the Commodore 64. Its influence can still be felt in later exploration-based platform games.

Released in 1988 by Superior Software and developed by Jason Benham, By Fair Means or Foul is a boxing game that stands apart by encouraging players to fight smart—or fight dirty. Alongside standard punches like jabs and uppercuts, players can sneak in illegal moves such as headbutts and low blows when the referee isn’t paying attention.

A key feature is the referee awareness system, shown via an on-screen indicator that lets players know when fouls can be committed without being caught. This adds a layer of strategy rarely seen in sports games of the era, forcing players to balance risk and reward inside the ring.

Single-player mode tasks players with defeating six increasingly tough opponents on the road to becoming World Champion, while two-player mode offers competitive bouts against a friend. The Commodore 64 version also includes a dedicated training mode, allowing players to practise moves on a punching bag before stepping into real matches.

Although reviews at the time were mixed, praising the inventive mechanics while criticising presentation and control response, the game left a lasting impression. Its later re-release as Pro Boxing Simulator by Codemasters in 1990 sparked controversy, but only reinforced its reputation as an unusual and memorable boxing title.

ujl4c2-3fUY.title: Banned Commodore 64 Games Explained | Germany’s BPjS Index
ujl4c2-3fUY.description:
🕹️ Banned C64 games, hidden Commodore 64 classics, and Germany’s secret BPjS Index — this is the story of the games that were restricted, indexed, or pushed out of public view.

In 1980s Germany, some Commodore 64 games were not always “banned” in the simple sense. Many were placed on the BPjS Index, meaning they could not be advertised, openly displayed, or sold normally to young people.  If you wanted them, you often had to know what to ask for — “unter dem Ladentisch”, or under the counter.

This video looks at banned and indexed Commodore 64 games connected with Germany’s youth protection rules, including Beach-Head, Raid Over Moscow, Blue Max, Castle Wolfenstein, Ikari Warriors, Platoon, Death Wish 3, Operation Wolf, Judge Dredd, S.W.A.T., Highlander, Infernal Runner, Mandroid and more.

Were these C64 games genuinely too violent for the time, or was this classic 1980s moral panic?

Some choices make sense when you look at military violence, political themes, crime, war, vigilante action and arcade shooting. Others feel much harder to justify today.

This is not just about censorship. It is also about how different countries treated games, how moral panic shaped the 8-bit era, and why retro game restrictions are still fascinating decades later.

💬 Which C64 game on this list most deserved to be restricted?
💬 And which one was absolutely ridiculous?

As a movie tie-in, the game leans heavily on its concept rather than technical ambition. Controls and repetition were widely criticised at the time, but the structure still reflects late-80s licensed design, with clear stages, boss battles, and a relentless push forward.

Today, The Running Man is remembered less for its gameplay strengths and more as a curiosity of the era. For fans of Arnold Schwarzenegger films and retro movie adaptations, it remains an interesting snapshot of how big cinema licenses were translated to the Commodore 64.

Released in 1993 by Teque London and published by Millennium Interactive for the Commodore Amiga, Brutal Sports Series Football is a chaotic and ultra-violent sports title that blends American football and rugby with explosive arcade-style action.

Set in a dystopian arena, the game combines traditional scoring objectives with brutal combat mechanics, allowing players to punch, kick, and even decapitate opponents to gain control of the match.

Power-ups such as bombs, weapons, and speed boosts are scattered across the pitch, encouraging aggressive play alongside tactical positioning. Matches are fast, unpredictable, and packed with confrontations.

The Amiga version is especially remembered for its frenetic multiplayer mode, distinctive sprite designs, and unusual hybrid of sports and beat-’em-up gameplay. It is often compared to Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe, even though opinions on pacing and scrolling were mixed.

Visually, the game embraces a bold, exaggerated style that matches its violent tone, supported by energetic sound effects and a hard-hitting soundtrack that keeps the action intense.

While controversial at release, Brutal Sports Series Football went on to achieve cult status among Amiga fans. It pushed the boundaries of sports game design in the early 1990s and remains one of the platform’s most provocative and memorable titles.

Today, it’s remembered as a wild and unapologetic fusion of sport and combat that still stands out in the Amiga library.

Released in 1992 by the Norwegian demo group Spaceballs, State of the Art arrived as something genuinely different on the Commodore Amiga. Technically, it wasn’t pushing the hardware as far as some contemporaries, but what it delivered instead was style, cohesion, and timing that felt fresh and confident.

Built around rhythm, motion, and presentation, the demo focuses on tightly synchronised visuals driven by music, creating an experience that feels deliberate and polished rather than purely technical. The animation, pacing, and clean design work together to form a demo that’s easy to watch and instantly memorable.

Spaceballs began in 1988 as a one-man project by Dark Helmet, later expanding with members recruited from Halden, Norway. Early additions like Lone Starr helped shape the group’s identity, which leaned toward strong presentation and artistic direction rather than brute-force effects alone.

Today, State of the Art is remembered as a defining demo of the early 1990s scene, often cited for its influence on rhythm-based visuals and its confidence in doing something different. It remains a standout example of how creativity and timing could outshine raw technical excess on the Amiga.

The game is split into two contrasting gameplay styles. One section has you flying on a broomstick, collecting keys and magical ingredients while fending off enemies. Cauldron stands out for its strong atmosphere, with detailed sprites and smooth scrolling that bring its eerie world to life. The experience is reinforced by Keith Miller’s haunting soundtrack, which adds tension and mood throughout both gameplay sections.

Known for its demanding difficulty, Cauldron requires careful management of magic points and sharp platforming skills. While unforgiving at times, this challenge became part of its identity, helping it earn cult status among Commodore 64 fans. Today, Cauldron is remembered as an inventive and atmospheric genre-blender that dared to do things differently.

Released in 1985, Rags to Riches is an ambitious life simulation for the Commodore 64 developed by Bob Keener and published by Melody Hall Publishing. Unusually for its time, the game places players in the role of a homeless character with a single long-term objective: work your way up from nothing and accumulate one million dollars.

The journey begins on the streets, where survival comes first. Players collect bottles, search for spare change, and take on low-paying jobs to build a small income. Gradual progression allows lifestyle upgrades such as getting a haircut, pursuing education, and securing better employment, turning small decisions into meaningful long-term consequences.

The city is divided into distinct districts, each presenting its own opportunities and risks. Navigating these areas requires careful planning, as threats like police, thieves, and the IRS can quickly undo progress. Time management and strategic choices are essential, making every in-game day count.

Rags to Riches stands out for its open-ended structure and satirical take on wealth, ambition, and social mobility. Despite simple visuals, its depth and originality helped it earn cult status, and it remains one of the Commodore 64’s most unconventional and thought-provoking simulation games.

Gameplay revolves around exploration and problem-solving inside a gloomy castle. You move between rooms, collect strange items, and deal with creatures that emerge from the trap door, all while working out how each task fits together. Time pressure keeps the tension high, as each task must be completed before the Thing Upstairs loses patience. The flip-screen, pseudo-3D presentation lets Berk move into the depth of rooms, while expressive animations and dark humour capture the atmosphere of the TV show perfectly.

Today, The Trap Door is remembered as one of the most original licensed games on the C64. Its creativity, humour, and distinctive style earned it cult status and helped it stand out as something truly different in the 8-bit era.

Players can choose to pilot either the chopper or the jeep, while two-player mode allows cooperative play with one player controlling each vehicle. Together, you battle waves of tanks, aircraft, and ground forces as they flood in from all directions.

The C64 conversion retains the arcade feel with smooth scrolling, power-up shields, destructible scenery, and intense enemy patterns. The port was programmed by Warren Mills, with graphics by Edward Langman and music by Barry Leitch.

Although less technically advanced than the arcade and Amiga versions, the Commodore 64 edition stands out as one of the system’s strongest co-op shooters, delivering true simultaneous two-player action.

Players take on the role of an ageing wizard descending into a deadly dungeon to rescue his mentor, Mordamir, uncovering a grim story of ancient civilizations, betrayal, and the pursuit of immortality along the way.

The game spans eight perilous dungeon levels packed with traps, puzzles, monsters, and environmental hazards. Progress relies heavily on experimentation and learning from failure, with death often serving as a lesson rather than a setback. Combat is slow, deliberate, and unforgiving, requiring precise timing and smart use of magic rather than button-mashing. Encounters are tense and often brutal, with graphic death animations reinforcing the constant sense of danger and vulnerability that defines the experience.

Widely praised for its atmosphere, depth, and challenge, The Immortal earned cult-classic status for its mature presentation and demanding gameplay. Progression relies on memory, observation, and precise movement, as new abilities and equipment gradually open up previously unreachable areas. The game blends arcade-style combat with exploration elements, creating a rewarding sense of discovery as the world slowly unfolds.

Visually, Switchblade stands out with its distinctive NES-style presentation, detailed environments, and polished animated intro and title screen. The atmosphere is further enhanced by one of Ben Daglish’s most memorable Commodore 64 soundtracks, widely regarded as his final major work on the platform.

Balancing technical ambition with engaging gameplay, Switchblade pushed the C64 to its limits and demonstrated just how far the system could be taken in the early 1990s. Today, it remains a respected cult classic, celebrated for its scope, presentation, and enduring appeal among retro fans.

Released in 1982 by HAL Laboratory and published by Commodore for the Commodore 64, Night Driver is an early milestone in racing games, bringing first-person driving to home computers. Originally debuting as a 1976 Atari arcade title, it helped define the foundations of the genre long before modern racing sims existed.

Gameplay drops you behind the wheel on a pitch-black road, guided only by glowing roadside reflectors. The aim is simple but demanding: cover as much distance as possible within a strict 90-second time limit without crashing. Four track modes—beginner, pro, expert, and random—gradually increase the challenge, while manual gear shifting adds an extra layer of skill and tension.

The Commodore 64 version improves on the arcade original with higher resolution visuals and smoother scrolling, enhancing the sensation of speed as the road twists ahead. Sparse presentation and minimal audio place full focus on timing, control, and staying on the road under pressure.

As one of the earliest first-person racers available on a home system, Night Driver holds an important place in gaming history. Today, it’s remembered as a fascinating and influential example of how much atmosphere and challenge could be created with very simple elements.

Praised on release for its variety and two-player mode, Beach-Head II earned a 90% rating from Zzap!64 and remains one of the most distinctive and entertaining action games on the system, still remembered fondly for its ambition and personality.

Released in 1986 by Activision and designed by Peter J. Favaro for the Commodore 64, Alter Ego is a pioneering life simulation RPG that broke away from traditional game design. Instead of focusing on combat or high scores, it invites players to shape the life of an imaginary character and experience the long-term consequences of their decisions.

The game begins with a detailed personality test that determines core attributes such as confidence, intelligence, and physical health. From there, players guide their alter ego through seven stages of life, from infancy to old age, facing moral, social, and practical choices that influence relationships, careers, and personal development.

Progression is entirely choice-driven, with each decision subtly altering future opportunities and risks. Some paths lead to success and fulfilment, while others can result in failure, regret, or even premature death, giving the game remarkable emotional depth and replay value.

Alter Ego was released in two distinct versions, depicting either a male or female life, each offering unique scenarios and perspectives. Its text-driven interface and thoughtful writing create an intimate, reflective experience rarely seen in 1980s home computer games.

Widely praised for its originality and psychological insight, the game earned critical acclaim, including a five-star rating from Info magazine. Today, Alter Ego is remembered as a bold experiment in interactive storytelling and remains one of the most thought-provoking titles in the Commodore 64 library.

🌐 Visit the Cheeky Commodore Gamer website for retro gaming features, videos & archives:

Released at the Anarchy Easter Party 1991, Enigma by Phenomena achieved first place at a highly competitive Amiga demo party held at Oppeby-Skolan in Nyköping, Sweden. With around 500 attendees and strict competition rules in place, the demo stood out immediately for its confidence, polish, and consistency from beginning to end.

Phenomena delivered a production where every element feels deliberate and refined. The visuals are varied yet cohesive, flowing naturally from scene to scene, while the pacing keeps the experience engaging throughout. It’s the kind of demo that feels complete, with no weak sections, and one that clearly deserved its top ranking at the event.

A major part of Enigma’s lasting reputation comes from its music, widely regarded as one of the greatest Amiga demo tunes of all time. Instantly recognisable and deeply addictive, the soundtrack elevates the entire production and helped reinforce the Amiga’s reputation as a serious multimedia powerhouse rather than just a games machine.

Founded in 1987, Phenomena were one of the most influential Swedish demo groups during the formative years of the Amiga demoscene. Enigma remains one of their defining works and a true legend of the era—an Amiga demo that still demands preservation and appreciation today.

In the game, you pilot a sleek Moon Shuttle spacecraft through layered asteroid fields and hostile alien formations, blasting narrow pathways while avoiding deadly collisions.

Stairways (1985), developed and published by Thor Computer Software, is a quirky and highly distinctive action-shooter for the Commodore 64, set almost entirely inside a chaotic pub.

You play as a bar patron on a mission to collect seven fragments of the legendary amulet of the great budgie WONGA — all while trying to avoid being thrown out by the doorman.

Gameplay takes place in a side-view scrolling environment where you must balance three key attributes: energy, hunger, and drunkenness. Hallucinations drain your energy, spilled drinks anger staff, and sobering up makes defending yourself more difficult.

To survive, you can return to the bar to get more intoxicated, grab food from a burger kiosk, and carefully manage your condition while shooting “thought bubble” enemies.

Each level is timed, adding extra pressure to collect all amulet pieces before advancing. The mix of arcade shooting, resource management, and pub-based chaos creates a truly unusual gameplay experience.

Although it never achieved mainstream success, Stairways is fondly remembered for its bizarre setting, inventive mechanics, and tongue-in-cheek humour.

Creatures 2: Torture Trouble (1992), developed by Apex Computer Productions and published by Thalamus, is one of the most technically impressive late-era releases on the Commodore 64.

You play as Clyde Radcliffe, whose children have been kidnapped by demons and hidden across three dangerous islands. To rescue them, you must survive a series of intricate “torture screens,” trampoline bonus stages, boss encounters, and hazardous island-hopping sections.

Rather than focusing on traditional platforming, Creatures 2 emphasises puzzle-solving and experimentation. Each torture chamber is filled with elaborate mechanisms that must be activated in the correct order to progress.

The game is famous for its detailed cartoon-style graphics, featuring advanced multicolour sprites and smooth animation that pushed the C64 hardware to its limits. Steve Rowlands’ energetic soundtrack and sound effects further enhance the experience.

Critically acclaimed on release — including a famous 97% score from Zzap!64 — the game was praised for its ambition and presentation. However, its shift toward complex puzzle mechanics divided some players who preferred the simpler style of the original Creatures.

Today, Creatures 2 is widely regarded as one of the finest Commodore 64 exclusives, showcasing what was still possible on 8-bit hardware in the early 1990s.

Sensible Golf (1995) is a 2D arcade-style golf game developed by Sensible Software and published by Virgin Interactive for the Commodore Amiga.

Featuring the familiar “pin-like” characters seen in Sensible Soccer and Cannon Fodder, the game delivers a fast-paced, no-frills take on golf that focuses on fun over realism.

Gameplay is built around a simple three-click system — aim, set power and curve, then strike — with automatic club suggestions and slope indicators to help guide each shot.

Rather than simulating wind and terrain height, the game concentrates on hazards such as water and sand across 25 imaginative courses, totalling 72 holes. This makes it ideal for quick rounds, full seasons, or tournament play with large groups.

Despite its charm, Sensible Golf received mixed reviews at release, including a 66% score from Amiga Power, and proved to be one of Sensible Software’s weaker commercial performers.

Today, it retains a small but dedicated following, with its minimalist mechanics, quirky course designs, and nostalgic visuals offering a distinctive slice of mid-90s Amiga gaming.

You create rainbows that double as weapons and platforms, trapping enemies beneath them or using them to climb higher. Mastery comes from chaining jumps, controlling enemy movement, and collecting power-ups that enhance speed, range, and scoring potential.

The adventure spans seven main islands, each ending with a boss encounter, while skilled players can unlock secret islands by collecting all seven rainbow-coloured diamonds. This adds depth and replay value for those aiming to see everything the game has to offer.

On the Amiga, Rainbow Islands shines with bright visuals, smooth animation, and a catchy soundtrack that captures the arcade original’s energy and charm. The port was widely praised on release, with Amiga Format awarding it an impressive 95% for its faithful and polished conversion.

Today, Rainbow Islands is remembered as one of the finest arcade platformers of its era, celebrated for its inventive mechanics, upbeat presentation, and enduring appeal on the Commodore Amiga.

Released in 1992 by Team17 for the Commodore Amiga, Project-X is a brutally challenging horizontally scrolling shoot ’em up set in a futuristic war against rogue military droids that have turned on humanity. It quickly earned a reputation as one of the toughest shooters of the 16-bit era.

Players pilot a heavily armed spacecraft equipped with seven distinct weapon systems, including Guns, Buildup, Side Shots, Homing Missiles, Plasma, Magma, and Laserbeam. Choosing the right loadout and managing upgrades is essential, as enemy placement and bullet patterns leave little room for error.

The game spans five lengthy levels, each ending with large, multi-phase boss encounters. Difficulty is relentless, with many players struggling to progress beyond the early stages. In response, Team17 released Project-X Special Edition in 1993, offering a reduced difficulty option while preserving the core experience.

Technically, Project-X showcases the Amiga at its peak, with detailed visuals, smooth scrolling, and dense on-screen action. The soundtrack by Allister Brimble is a standout, delivering driving, atmospheric music that perfectly complements the intensity of the gameplay.

Despite its unforgiving nature, Project-X remains a landmark Amiga shooter. It’s remembered as a bold, uncompromising title that defined Team17’s reputation for high production values and hardcore design.

Critically acclaimed on release, Theme Park was praised for its depth, humour, and addictive gameplay loop. Its success spawned sequels and helped establish the theme park management genre, making it one of the most influential simulation games of the 1990s.

Released in 1990 by Rainbow Arts and developed by Manfred Trenz, Turrican is widely regarded as one of the most ambitious and technically impressive action games ever created for the Commodore 64. Designed as a run-and-gun platformer with a strong emphasis on exploration, it raised expectations for what the C64 could deliver late in its lifespan.

Players control a lone warrior encased in a powerful assault suit, battling through five expansive worlds across 13 interconnected levels. The game blends fast-paced side-scrolling combat with open-ended level design, rewarding exploration with hidden areas, secret bonuses, and powerful upgrades. A defining feature is the rotating laser weapon, which can be aimed freely through 360 degrees, adding tactical depth to both combat and traversal.

From a technical standpoint, Turrican is a standout achievement on the Commodore 64. Smooth multi-directional scrolling, detailed sprite animation, and large environments push the hardware to its limits. The experience is further elevated by an iconic soundtrack composed by Chris Hülsbeck, with additional contributions from Ramiro Vaca and Stefan Hartwig, delivering memorable themes that perfectly complement the game’s scale and intensity.

Turrican’s innovative design, technical mastery, and sense of freedom left a lasting mark on the genre. It spawned multiple sequels and influenced countless action games, securing its place as a must-play classic for fans of Commodore 64 gaming.

Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Everyone’s a Wally is an arcade adventure developed by Chris Hinsley and published by Mikro-Gen. Acting as a follow-up to Pyjamarama, the game expands the world of Wally Week, a builder trying to get through a hectic day alongside his family and friends.

The action takes place across a lively town made up of more than 30 locations, including streets, shops, offices, and public buildings. Players can switch between five characters — Wally, his wife Wilma, and friends Tom, Dick, and Harry — each with their own jobs to complete. Progress depends on managing time, energy levels, and movement efficiently across the map.

Each completed task earns a letter, and collecting them all reveals the password needed to open the bank safe and collect everyone’s wages. The challenge comes from juggling multiple characters, avoiding hazards, and planning the most efficient order to finish every job before energy runs out.

The town feels alive thanks to non-playable characters following their own routines, adding unpredictability and depth. A hidden mini-game inspired by Asteroids can also be found in phone booths, adding a surprising extra layer of gameplay. The original cassette release even included a song by Mike Berry, which doubled as the game’s theme tune.

Today, Everyone’s a Wally is remembered as one of the most inventive arcade adventures on the Commodore 64. Its colourful presentation, ambitious design, and character-driven gameplay have secured it a lasting place in C64 history.

Released in 1983 by Cosmi and developed by Paul Norman, Forbidden Forest is one of the earliest and most influential horror-themed action games on the Commodore 64. You take on the role of a lone archer venturing into a dark, hostile forest where every step forward brings new danger.

Gameplay revolves around careful positioning, precise timing, and strict arrow management as you face off against giant spiders, bees, mutated frogs, dragons, and other nightmarish creatures. Each enemy has distinct movement patterns, forcing you to react quickly while conserving ammunition and avoiding lethal contact.

What truly sets Forbidden Forest apart is its atmosphere. Parallax scrolling gives depth to the forest, a dynamic day-to-night cycle steadily ramps up the tension, and context-sensitive music shifts as threats appear on screen. The game was also one of the first to feature animated blood, pushing boundaries and helping define the visual language of survival horror.

Simple in structure but relentlessly tense, Forbidden Forest became a cult classic and a blueprint for later horror-focused games. Today, it remains a landmark Commodore 64 title, remembered for its unsettling mood, bold design choices, and lasting influence on the genre.

Gemstone Warrior (1985) is a 2D action-adventure game developed by Paradigm Creators and published by Strategic Simulations, Inc., originally released on the Apple II before being ported to the Commodore 64.

Set within a dangerous labyrinth beneath a volcanic fortress, you guide an armoured hero armed with a crossbow and limited magical attacks in search of five hidden gemstone fragments.

Each run takes place across randomly generated dungeon rooms filled with skeletal warriors, demons, gas-trap plants, and deadly hazards. Supplies and magical items can be looted from chests, coffins, and fallen enemies.

Useful tools include healing goblets, screen-clearing crystal balls, illusion spells, invisibility, and freezing magic, all of which must be used carefully. Mapping, saving, and strategic planning are essential for survival.

One of the game’s most memorable features is its haunting title-screen music, a variation of J.S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier, setting an eerie tone from the outset.

Gemstone Warrior stands out for its blend of procedural dungeon design, real-time combat, and survival mechanics, earning its place as an influential early action-adventure classic.

Players take on the role of Elidaan the Loremaster, a wizard tasked with recovering the legendary Coronet of Arien — an artifact said to grant immortality.

The game world is built around a vast 16×16 screen map, encouraging careful exploration, note-taking, and classic hand-drawn mapping.

Progress depends on finding the eight fragments of the Riddlescroll of Wurslea, solving environmental puzzles, mastering spells, and defeating powerful enemies including dragons.

Doriath places heavy emphasis on non-linear progression, allowing players to tackle challenges in different orders while gradually unlocking new abilities.

Its detailed visuals by Richard Murray and atmospheric music by Chris Cox help create a rich fantasy setting rarely seen in budget C64 releases.

Despite its modest price point, Doriath stands out for its depth, difficulty, and innovative structure, often compared to later exploration-based classics such as Metroid and Zelda.

Released in 1985 by Activision and developed by Steve Cartwright for the Commodore 64, Hacker is a distinctive graphic adventure that places players in the role of a digital spy infiltrating secret computer systems. Opening with the now-iconic “Logon Please” prompt, the game immediately sets a tense, puzzle-driven tone that defines the entire experience.

Gameplay blends text-based interaction with strategic exploration as players guide a small robot through a complex underground tunnel network. The objective is to locate and assemble fragments of a classified document hidden across multiple global locations, all while managing limited money, time, and access privileges.

Progression depends on careful planning, memory, and precision. Surveillance systems, security checkpoints, and restricted routes force players to think several steps ahead, especially since the absence of a save feature means that mistakes can result in starting over from the beginning.

Visually, Hacker adopts a minimalist, functional style that reinforces its themes of secrecy and infiltration. Sparse sound effects and subdued presentation heighten the sense of pressure, making every decision feel consequential despite the game’s restrained audiovisual design.

Praised for its originality and cerebral challenge, Hacker offered something very different from action-heavy titles of the era. Today, it is remembered as a pioneering example of stealth-based strategy on the Commodore 64 and a cult favourite among fans of thoughtful, methodical gameplay.

wuZcVW4DTLs.title: Flip & Flop – The C64 Platformer Played on the Ceiling
wuZcVW4DTLs.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/flip-and-flop/

Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64 by State Soft, following its original Atari debut in 1983 from First Star Software, Flip & Flop is an isometric action-platformer created by Jim Nangano that blends arcade reflexes with strategic puzzle design.

Players alternate control between Flip the kangaroo and Mitch the ape, each tackling separate stages built around climbing ladders, navigating 3D-style platforms, and flipping marked tiles.

The main objective is to activate every highlighted tile by jumping onto them, sometimes requiring precise double-jumps on higher levels while avoiding a relentless pursuer.

Depending on the character, players are chased by either a zookeeper or a creeping net, forcing constant movement and quick decision-making.

Sticky tiles act as temporary traps, briefly halting enemies and creating vital breathing space to plan routes and recover control.

Every five stages, a short circus-themed interlude provides a playful break before the difficulty increases.

As the game progresses, layouts become more complex, timing windows shrink, and safety tiles are removed entirely, demanding sharper strategy and faster reactions.

Visually, the game features colourful isometric environments inspired by arcade hits like Q*Bert, while the catchy SID soundtrack by Jerry White adds energy and charm.

Highly praised on release, including recognition from German magazine 64’er, Flip & Flop earned a reputation as one of the finest examples of its genre.

Today, it remains fondly remembered for its clever design, rising challenge, and timeless arcade appeal.

💬 Did you master the tile-flipping patterns, or did the chase always catch up with you?

Martin Wheeler’s soundtrack underlines the game’s tense atmosphere, reinforcing its identity as a tough but inventive experience. Originally released individually in 1983 by Infocom, the Zork series brought sophisticated interactive fiction to home computers, inviting you into the vast and dangerous Great Underground Empire through pure text and imagination. Zork I, Zork II, and Zork III each build on the same rich fantasy world, gradually expanding its scope, puzzles, and narrative ambition.

Gameplay revolves around exploration, logic, and language. You type commands to move, examine objects, solve devious puzzles, and survive encounters with trolls, thieves, and wizards, all guided by Infocom’s famously advanced text parser. Success depends on careful observation, memory, and lateral thinking rather than reflexes.

On the Commodore 64, the trilogy retains the full depth and complexity of the original releases, translating Infocom’s storytelling and puzzle design faithfully to the platform. Each entry refines the formula, with Zork III introducing more structured challenges and a stronger sense of purpose.

Zork helped define the interactive fiction genre and set a benchmark for narrative-driven adventure games. Decades later, the trilogy remains a landmark in gaming history and a rewarding test of wit for anyone willing to slow down and think.

The western atmosphere is reinforced by a rendition of Do Not Forsake Me: The Ballad of High Noon, arranged by David Dunn. Simple but effective visuals and arcade pacing make High Noon an early standout among themed shooters on the Commodore 64, and a fondly remembered classic of the era.

Today, Give My Regards to Broad Street is remembered as an early example of a music-driven video game, blending adventure and puzzle mechanics with pop culture in a way that set it apart within the Commodore 64 library.

Released in 1992 by Virgin Interactive and developed by Cryo Interactive, Dune is a bold adventure-strategy hybrid set in Frank Herbert’s iconic sci-fi universe. You step into the role of Paul Atreides, navigating the harsh desert world of Arrakis as rival houses battle for control of the all-important spice.

Gameplay blends first-person exploration with strategic management. You travel across the planet, meet key characters, forge alliances with the Fremen, and oversee spice production while making decisions that shape the balance of power. Recruiting warriors, deploying ornithopters, and managing resources are all essential to pushing back the Harkonnen threat.

As the story unfolds, Paul’s growing psychic abilities add narrative depth and influence how events play out. Progress isn’t just about military strength, but understanding Arrakis, its people, and the consequences of your choices.

On the Amiga, Dune shines with atmospheric visuals, cinematic cutscenes, and a memorable MIDI soundtrack by Stéphane Picq and Philippe Ulrich. Gameplay revolves around movement, survival, and growth. By eating brine shrimp and other food, your fish grows in size and strength, allowing it to leap into larger tanks and eventually out of the house entirely. Fail to eat enough, and your fish shrinks, becoming weaker and closer to death.

Hazards are constant and varied, including aggressive piranhas, swooping fishnets, and even cats’ paws reaching in from above. Players must keep the fish moving at all times to avoid suffocation, adding an extra layer of pressure to every moment.

The mechanics are simple but surprisingly tense, with size, health, and momentum all closely linked. The game’s bright visuals and playful premise mask a genuine challenge that rewards careful timing and route awareness.

Today, CHOMP! is fondly remembered as one of the Commodore 64’s more unusual ideas. Its inventive concept, lighthearted tone, and demanding gameplay have helped it earn a lasting cult following among 8-bit fans.

Originally developed by Namco and released in arcades in 1982, Pole Position arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1984 as a home conversion of one of the most influential racing games ever made. Players take control of a Formula One car and attempt to qualify for pole position by completing a fast, clean lap of the iconic Fuji Racetrack.

Gameplay is split into two phases, beginning with a solo time trial where precision and memorisation are essential. Successfully qualifying unlocks the main race, where players must compete against rival cars while managing speed, positioning, and a strict time limit. Collisions with other vehicles or trackside objects quickly end a promising run.

The Commodore 64 version recreates the arcade’s behind-the-car perspective with smooth forward scrolling and recognisable track landmarks. While simplified compared to the original cabinet, the core mechanics remain intact, focusing on rhythm, reaction time, and learning the course layout corner by corner.

Audio is handled with a faithful SID interpretation of the arcade’s memorable tunes and sound effects, helping maintain the atmosphere and tension of high-speed competition. The presentation prioritises clarity and speed, ensuring the racing remains readable even at higher velocities.

Pole Position is widely regarded as a landmark title that defined the template for future racing games. On the Commodore 64, it remains a nostalgic and historically important experience, capturing the spirit of arcade racing during the early years of home computing.

xH3wDOLAqds.title: Daley Thompson’s Decathlon – The C64 Game That Punished Joysticks
xH3wDOLAqds.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/daley-thompsons-decathlon/

Released in 1984 by Ocean Software, Daley Thompson’s Decathlon brought the intensity of Olympic athletics to the Commodore 64 in a way few games had managed before. Officially licensed by double Olympic gold medallist Daley Thompson, it challenges you to survive all ten events of the modern decathlon across two gruelling in-game days.

Day one tests raw speed and power with the 100 metres, long jump, shot put, high jump, and 400 metres. Day two raises the stakes with the 110 metre hurdles, pole vault, discus, javelin, and the exhausting 1500 metres. Each event demands qualifying standards, and failure costs one of your limited lives. Complete the full decathlon and the challenge resets with even tougher requirements.

The gameplay is infamous for its joystick-waggling controls, where running speed is generated by rapidly moving the stick left and right. This physical input became legendary, earning the game its reputation as a true joystick destroyer and turning every race into a test of endurance for both you and your hardware.

A massive commercial and critical success, Daley Thompson’s Decathlon became one of the UK’s best-selling computer games of the mid-80s and won multiple awards, including the Golden Joystick Award for Best Arcade-Style Game. Today, it remains one of the most recognisable and talked-about sports games in Commodore 64 history.

Released in 1984 for the Commodore 64, Mutant Monty is a fixed-screen arcade game developed by John Prince and published by Artic Computing. Players take control of Monty, an ambitious adventurer determined to become rich and heroic by collecting gold nuggets scattered across a series of increasingly demanding levels.

The game is built around 40 single-screen rooms, each packed with enemies, hazards, and tight time limits. To progress, Monty must collect every gold nugget on the screen and reach the exit door before time runs out. Contact with enemies or failure to escape in time costs one of Monty’s limited lives.

Movement is a key part of the challenge. Monty continues moving in the chosen joystick direction until he hits an obstacle, with longer joystick holds increasing his speed. This creates a risk-and-reward balance, where precision and planning are just as important as quick reactions.

What gives Mutant Monty its lasting appeal is its imaginative setting, featuring bizarre locations such as the Pit of Eternal Slime, a neutron accelerator interior, and the desolate wastes of Pithor. Combined with colourful visuals and tense gameplay, it stands as a memorable and distinctive entry in the Commodore 64’s collect-’em-up library.

Released in 1987 by Ocean Software, Match Day II is a landmark football simulation for the Commodore 64 that built upon and refined the foundations laid by the original Match Day. Developed by Jon Ritman, with graphics by Bernie Drummond and music by Guy Stevens, the game introduced new systems that significantly raised the bar for 8-bit sports titles.

The game offers league and cup competitions for up to eight teams, alongside quick exhibition matches. Played with seven players per side, Match Day II allows direct control of the goalkeeper, adding an extra tactical layer rarely seen at the time. The action is fast, fluid, and highly responsive, rewarding anticipation and positioning rather than simple button-bashing.

A defining innovation is the Diamond Deflection System, which calculates realistic ball rebounds based on angle and impact, creating unpredictable and natural-feeling play. The Kick-o-meter further deepens control, letting players adjust shot power and elevation to curl efforts past defenders or lift the ball over advancing goalkeepers.

Praised for its depth and control, Match Day II is widely regarded as one of the most important football games on the Commodore 64. While its speed could be demanding, it delivered a level of realism and tactical freedom that helped shape the future of football video games on home computers.

🕹️ The Rats (1985) – Commodore 64 Horror Strategy Adventure
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/the-rats/

Released in 1985 by Five Ways Software and published by Hodder & Stoughton for the Commodore 64, The Rats is an unusual hybrid of strategy and interactive fiction based on James Herbert’s best-selling horror novel.

Players take on the role of Harris, head of the rat extermination commission, as London faces a devastating invasion of genetically mutated rats. Using a detailed city map, players must deploy emergency services, manage resources, and fund research into advanced extermination technologies.

Strategic planning is balanced with crisis management, as rising panic levels and civilian casualties can quickly overwhelm your efforts. Careful coordination and long-term investment are essential for survival.

At key moments, the game shifts into real-time, text-based scenarios where players experience the invasion from the perspective of trapped civilians. These sequences present tense decision-making situations supported by eerie sound effects and minimalist visuals.

The combination of heartbeat audio, atmospheric writing, and limited presentation creates a strong sense of dread that was rare on 8-bit systems. These sections help transform the game from a simple management simulation into a genuine horror experience.

Praised for its originality and faithful tone, The Rats remains a standout title in the Commodore 64 library. Its ambitious design, immersive storytelling, and genre-blending gameplay have earned it cult classic status among retro horror fans.

Today, it’s remembered as one of the most distinctive and unsettling strategy-adventure games of the 1980s.

💬 Did this game genuinely scare you back in the day, or did you manage to keep London safe?

xTIc4AKoMuI.title: Archon – The C64 Chess Game Where the Pieces Fought Back
xTIc4AKoMuI.description:
🕹️ Archon: The Light and the Dark (1983) – Commodore 64 Strategy Board Game with Real-Time Combat
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/archon-the-light-and-the-dark/

Released in 1983 by Free Fall Associates and published by Electronic Arts, Archon: The Light and the Dark is a pioneering hybrid that blends turn-based strategy with fast-paced real-time combat. Designed by Jon Freeman and Paul Reiche III, with programming by Anne Westfall, the game challenges players to command either the forces of Light or Dark in a battle for control of a magical board.

The board resembles a chess layout, but instead of static captures, opposing pieces trigger one-on-one real-time battles when they meet. Each creature has unique movement patterns, strengths, and special abilities, making positioning and timing just as important as combat skill. Control is achieved by occupying five power points or eliminating the opposing army entirely.

Light and Dark units offer distinct play styles, from agile and precise to powerful and aggressive, ensuring that no two matches play out the same. The shifting balance of the board and the pressure of live combat create a constant sense of tension, especially during head-to-head multiplayer games.

As one of Electronic Arts’ earliest releases, Archon quickly earned classic status. Its inventive fusion of genres and competitive depth helped define a new style of strategy gaming, securing its place as one of the most influential titles in the Commodore 64 library.

💬 Did you side with the forces of Light, or embrace the chaos of the Dark?

XUgrbMKPGJ8.title: Ghosts ’N Goblins – Could Capcom’s Brutal Arcade Classic Survive on the C64?
XUgrbMKPGJ8.description:
🕹️ Ghosts ’N Goblins (1986) – Commodore 64 Hardcore Action Platformer Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Ghosts ’N Goblins on the Commodore 64 delivers Capcom’s brutal arcade platformer in full side-scrolling form, challenging you across six punishing levels packed with relentless enemies and hazards. Each stage must be cleared within a strict time limit, or a life is lost, keeping the pressure high from start to finish.

You play as Arthur, a brave knight on a desperate mission to rescue his beloved Princess from the Demon King Astaroth. Along the way, you face waves of undead horrors including ghosts, zombies, bats, ogres, and goblins, all while navigating ladders, moving platforms, and deadly fire and water traps.

Combat and movement demand absolute precision. Weapon upgrades help, but even the best gear offers little mercy, and losing your armour leaves Arthur painfully vulnerable. Memorisation, timing, and patience are essential to survive the game’s famously unforgiving design.

Renowned for its difficulty and atmosphere, Ghosts ’N Goblins became a rite of passage for 8-bit players. Today, it remains a legendary test of skill and endurance, and one of the most iconic platform games ever released on the Commodore 64.

xxqb6JkNOE8.description:
🕹️ Paperboy (1986) – Commodore 64 Arcade Cycling Action Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/paperboy/

Released in 1986 by Atari Games and ported to the Commodore 64 by Elite Systems, Paperboy turns a simple daily job into frantic arcade chaos. You take control of a newspaper delivery kid pedalling through suburban streets, trying to complete your route while everything around you seems determined to knock you off your bike.

Gameplay revolves around accurate newspaper throwing and quick reactions. You must deliver papers to subscribers, avoid smashing windows at non-subscribers’ houses, and steer clear of traffic, pedestrians, dogs, lawnmowers, and other unpredictable hazards. Balancing speed, accuracy, and survival is the key to making it through each day.

The C64 version captures the spirit of the arcade original, translating its distinctive diagonal viewpoint and fast-paced action to home hardware. While visuals and animation are pared back, the colourful presentation and recognisable layouts keep the experience instantly familiar.

Reception was mixed at the time, but Paperboy has endured thanks to its originality and memorable design. Today, it remains a much-loved arcade conversion and a perfect snapshot of mid-80s game creativity on the Commodore 64.

💬 Did you aim for perfect deliveries, or just try to survive the street in one piece?

Xzgcz7n7Kxw.title: Bionic Commando – Did Capcom’s Arcade Platformer Survive the Move to C64?
Xzgcz7n7Kxw.description:
🕹️ Bionic Commando (1988) – Commodore 64 Grappling Hook Action Platform Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/bionic-commando/

Released in 1988 for the Commodore 64, Bionic Commando is a side-scrolling action-platformer developed by Software Creations for the UK release and Pacific Dataworks International for the US version, published by U.S. Gold, GO!, and Capcom.

Unlike most platform games of the era, the hero cannot jump. Instead, movement is based entirely around a powerful bionic arm that functions as a grappling hook for swinging, climbing, attacking enemies, and collecting items.

The C64 version closely follows the arcade structure across five demanding levels, requiring careful planning and precise execution to survive hostile terrain.

Players must shoot supply crates dropped by parachutes to upgrade weapons, then skillfully use the bionic arm to traverse gaps, scale platforms, and avoid deadly hazards.

Gameplay focuses on timing, positioning, and momentum, rewarding players who master the unique swinging mechanics.

The UK release is known for smoother scrolling and stronger audio, while the US version is often criticised for rushed development and technical shortcomings.

With strict time limits, tough enemy patterns, and unforgiving level design, the game delivers a formidable challenge even for experienced players.

Despite its difficulty, Bionic Commando is respected for its originality and ambitious mechanics on 8-bit hardware.

Today, it is remembered as one of the most distinctive and demanding action-platformers in the Commodore 64 library.

💬 Did you master the bionic arm, or did the no-jumping rule defeat you?

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Released in 1989 by Rainbird Software, Weird Dreams is a cinematic platformer that drags you deep into a nightmarish subconscious. You play as Steve, a young man undergoing brain surgery who becomes trapped inside a sequence of hostile dreams shaped by the sinister presence of Zelloripus, a corrupting force linked to his colleague Emily.

Each dream world is visually striking and deeply unsettling, ranging from twisted fairgrounds to vast deserts filled with impossible creatures. Progression relies on careful movement, observation, and precise timing, with every screen presenting hazards that punish impatience and reward methodical play.

The game’s imagery takes clear inspiration from surrealist art, creating scenes that feel deliberately uncomfortable and unpredictable. This atmosphere is reinforced by David Whittaker’s haunting Amiga soundtrack, which gives the game a constant sense of tension and unease.

Packaged with a 64-page novella by Rupert Goodwins that expands the narrative, Weird Dreams stands out as one of the Amiga’s most distinctive and challenging experiences. It remains a cult favourite, remembered for its ambition, visual identity, and uncompromising difficulty.

💬 Did you persevere through the dream worlds, or did Weird Dreams get inside your head?

y-H_XRlwKkA.title: Tusker – The C64 Adventure That Wanted to Be Indiana Jones
y-H_XRlwKkA.description:
🕹️ Tusker (1989) – Commodore 64 Action-Adventure Exploration Classic
🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/tusker/

Released in 1989 by System 3, Tusker is an action-adventure game for the Commodore 64 that blends exploration, combat and puzzle solving in a cinematic African expedition. Developed by Duncan Meech with music by SID composer Matt Gray, the game follows a young explorer attempting to finish his father’s final quest: locating the legendary Elephant Graveyard hidden deep within the African wilderness.

Gameplay combines side-view exploration with item-based puzzles and survival mechanics. Players travel across deserts, villages and ancient ruins while collecting weapons such as knives, machetes, guns and slingshots. These tools are not only used to defeat enemies but also to interact with the environment and solve progression puzzles scattered across the game’s locations.

A unique mechanic in Tusker is the survival system. Energy and water levels must be carefully managed as the harsh environments slowly drain your resources. Finding ways to refill your canteen or avoid unnecessary damage becomes crucial to surviving the journey deeper into the wilderness.

Visually, Tusker pushes the Commodore 64 with colourful scenery, large animated characters and atmospheric environments. The experience is further elevated by Matt Gray’s memorable soundtrack, which uses tribal-inspired rhythms and ambient jungle effects to create a tense expedition atmosphere through the SID chip.

Although often compared to System 3’s Last Ninja series, Tusker offers its own style of adventure with a stronger emphasis on exploration and puzzle solving. Today it remains a fascinating late-era C64 title that attempted to combine cinematic adventure with arcade action.

Released in 1985 by Elite Systems for the Commodore 64, Airwolf is a licensed action-shooter based on the popular television series, placing players in control of Stringfellow Hawke’s advanced military helicopter.

The mission centres on rescuing five trapped scientists from a vast underground complex, requiring careful navigation through narrow caverns filled with hazards and enemy defences.

Gameplay focuses on precise flying, with players managing momentum, gravity, missiles, shields, and fuel while blasting through walls and activating switches to open new routes.

Progress demands accurate positioning and timing, as falling debris, tight corridors, and hostile fire punish even minor mistakes.

Visually, the game delivers colourful 8-bit sprites and smooth side-scrolling environments that maintain a strong sense of speed and tension.

The experience is enhanced by a looping rendition of the iconic Airwolf television theme by Sylvester Levay, adapted effectively for the SID chip.

Despite its technical polish, Airwolf became notorious for its extreme difficulty, with unforgiving controls and one-hit deaths making survival a serious test of skill and patience.

Today, it remains a cult favourite and a memorable example of both the ambition and frustration found in licensed C64 titles.

Released in 1990 by Teque Software Development and published by Domark, Escape from the Planet of the Robot Monsters is a multidirectional shooter for the Commodore 64, adapted from Atari Games’ 1989 arcade release. The game embraces a tongue-in-cheek 1950s sci-fi theme, blending action with humour and distinctive presentation.

Set on Planet X, players control interplanetary agents Jake and Duke on a mission to rescue Dr. Sarah Bellum and other hostages from the evil Reptilons. Using an isometric viewpoint, the game tasks players with navigating maze-like environments, destroying robotic enemies, and activating switches and mechanisms to progress through each level.

Combat introduces an extra layer of strategy, allowing players to crouch, rotate, and fire in eight directions while stationary. This system rewards positioning and timing rather than constant movement, setting it apart from many shooters of the era. Despite the Commodore 64’s limitations, controls remain responsive and collision detection is reliable.

The atmospheric soundtrack by Matt Furniss enhances the sci-fi mood, helping deliver a surprisingly faithful home conversion. Today, this version is remembered as one of the stronger arcade adaptations on the C64, praised for retaining the feel and challenge of the original.

y58m3nrHqvg.title: The Dolphin’s Rune – Was This More Interactive Art Than C64 Game?
y58m3nrHqvg.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/the-dolphins-rune/

Released in 1985 by Mindscape for the Commodore 64 and developed by John O’Neill under the Admacadiam label, The Dolphin’s Rune: A Poetic Odyssey is a highly unconventional action-puzzle game that prioritises atmosphere and reflection over traditional arcade thrills. Designed as an interactive art experience, it stands apart from most titles of its era.

Players take control of a dolphin swimming through a vast ocean environment, where survival depends on awareness and restraint rather than speed. Avoiding sharks, surfacing for air, and steering clear of dangerous fishing nets form the core challenges, encouraging slow, thoughtful exploration from the dolphin’s perspective.

Progression is shaped by observation, rhythm, and environmental understanding. Instead of score-chasing or time pressure, the game rewards patience and immersion, inviting players to absorb its unusual tone and subtle mechanics.

Visually, the game employs minimalist graphics that evoke the scale and emptiness of the open sea. This is reinforced by ambient sound design that plays a central role in creating its calm, dreamlike atmosphere. As part of Mindscape’s “Book Street Inter-Arts Series,” it blurred the boundaries between literature, art, and interactive media.

Although it struggled commercially on release, The Dolphin’s Rune has since gained a dedicated cult following. Today, it is recognised as an early example of video games as artistic expression, showcasing how the Commodore 64 could be used to deliver introspective and emotionally resonant experiences.

💬 Did you embrace the calm, meditative pace, or wish for more traditional arcade action?

Released in 1983 by Cosmi and developed by Paul Norman, Aztec Challenge throws you into a relentless series of seven deadly trials inspired by ancient temple myths. Each challenge demands sharp reflexes, precise timing, and sheer endurance as you fight to survive rather than explore.

The opening trial, The Gauntlet, sets the tone immediately as you sprint toward a distant temple while dodging and leaping over spears hurled by Aztec warriors. From there, the game constantly shifts perspective and mechanics, forcing you to adapt as you climb collapsing stairs, avoid falling stones, navigate trap-filled corridors, swim through piranha-infested waters, and cross a crumbling bridge with missing planks.

Every stage feels deliberately unforgiving, turning simple actions into high-pressure tests of nerve. There’s no margin for error, and success comes only through memorisation, rhythm, and persistence.

Paul Norman’s tense soundtrack reinforces the pressure, heightening the sense that each mistake could be your last. Infamous for its difficulty, Aztec Challenge has earned cult status over the years and remains one of the Commodore 64’s most punishing and memorable action games.

💬 How far did you make it before the temple claimed another victim?

Players take on the role of Buster Baloney, a would-be film star navigating a frantic studio complex in a bid to collect five Oscar statues and make it big in Hollywood.

Gameplay blends arcade platforming with resource management and quick decision-making. Buster defends himself by hurling custard pies at enemies, with supplies replenished via a strategically placed cream tap. The studio itself is a maze of interconnected rooms, doors, and hazards, with some exits leading to hectic street scenes filled with fast-moving policemen that demand sharp reflexes and careful timing.

The isometric presentation gives the game a strong sense of depth and movement, while colourful visuals help sell its cartoonish, slapstick tone. Completing the package is a memorable soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, whose energetic music perfectly complements the game’s playful atmosphere.

With its distinctive theme, challenging layout, and comedy-driven design, Hollywood or Bust remains a charming and unusual entry in the Commodore 64 library, fondly remembered for its humour and character.

Originally released by Sega in 1987, Thunder Blade is a high-energy shoot-’em-up that puts you in control of a heavily armed attack helicopter blasting through enemy territory. Famous in the arcades for its pseudo-3D visuals and dramatic motion cabinets, the game later made its way to home computers with mixed but fascinating results.

On the Commodore 64, published by U.S. Gold in 1988, Thunder Blade takes a top-down approach combined with behind-the-helicopter stages. You pilot the Gunship Gladiator through vertically scrolling combat zones, taking out tanks, gun turrets, and enemy helicopters. Clever programming techniques attempt to recreate depth and scale, delivering fast action even if movement and detail can feel rough at times.

The Amiga version, also released in 1988 by U.S. Gold, offers smoother scrolling and richer visuals, making better use of the hardware while keeping the arcade’s alternating perspectives intact. Although it still falls short of the spectacle of the original cabinet, it delivers a more polished and playable experience overall.

Both versions highlight the ambition and compromises of late-80s arcade conversions. Thunder Blade remains a memorable example of Sega’s push to bring large-scale arcade action into the home, and a notable entry in the shoot-’em-up libraries of both the Commodore 64 and Amiga.

Players take charge of a Ghostbusters team, managing money, hiring staff, buying equipment, and responding to supernatural outbreaks across New York City. Choosing when to upgrade gear or invest in better vehicles directly affects success, especially as ghost activity escalates toward the endgame.

Ghostbusters remains one of the most respected licensed games of the era, praised for capturing the spirit of the film while delivering inventive gameplay. Its mix of management and action helped secure its place as a true classic of 1980s home gaming.

YJmnLrEebyQ.title: Stormbringer – How Did the Magic Knight Saga End on the Commodore 64?

Released in 1987 by Mastertronic under the M.A.D. (Mastertronic Added Dimension) label, Stormbringer is a fantasy adventure game for the Commodore 64 developed by David Jones. It serves as the fourth and final entry in the Magic Knight series, following Finders Keepers, Spellbound, and Knight Tyme, while shifting the formula toward a more action-focused arcade-adventure style.

The story centres on Magic Knight facing his own evil alter ego, the Off-White Knight, also known as Stormbringer. A time travel accident has created this destructive duplicate, and the only way to restore balance is for Magic Knight to confront and ultimately merge with his darker self. This narrative twist gives the game a more personal and dramatic tone than earlier entries in the series.

Gameplay takes place across 64 interconnected screens filled with hazards, puzzles, and environmental challenges. Players must navigate carefully, avoiding threats such as lightning bolts and spinning axes while solving puzzles that block progression. Interaction is handled through a menu-driven system, allowing spells to be cast, objects examined, and actions selected without relying on reflex-heavy controls alone.

On the Commodore 64, Stormbringer is supported by atmospheric music composed by David Whittaker, adding tension and weight to the fantasy setting. The presentation and mechanics mark a clear evolution from the earlier Magic Knight titles, prioritising immediacy and danger over exploration-heavy design.

Although reception at the time was mixed, with some critics noting a loss of depth compared to its predecessors, Stormbringer remains an important and distinctive entry in the series. Today, it stands as a bold and experimental finale that closed out one of the Commodore 64’s most recognisable fantasy adventure franchises.

You pilot a ship through a grid-based maze, facing relentless waves of alien enemies attacking from all directions. Movement and firing are possible in four directions, forcing you to think quickly at intersections while staying one step ahead of incoming threats.

Released in 1989 by Strategic Simulations Inc. for the Commodore 64, Curse of the Azure Bonds is a classic role-playing game and the acclaimed follow-up to Pool of Radiance in the legendary Gold Box AD&D series.

Players build and command a party of adventurers as they journey through the Forgotten Realms, uncovering the mystery of the magical “azure bonds” marked on their arms. The game blends exploration, questing, and tactical turn-based combat.

Gameplay alternates between first-person dungeon crawling and overhead battlefield encounters, delivering the deep strategic feel that defined the Gold Box engine. Careful party management, spell selection, and positioning are essential for survival.

The game expands on its predecessor with richer quests, more character classes, and improved balance, including options such as paladins and rangers. Its design closely mirrors tabletop AD&D, offering strong replay value and long-term depth.

Visually, the C64 version presents detailed character portraits, clear dungeon layouts, and functional combat screens that prioritise readability and gameplay. The presentation supports long play sessions without sacrificing clarity.

While demanding by modern standards, Curse of the Azure Bonds stands as one of the most ambitious RPGs on the Commodore 64. It remains a beloved entry in the Gold Box series and a favourite among retro RPG fans.

Today, it’s remembered as a landmark fantasy adventure that helped define computer role-playing on 8-bit systems.

Released in 1986 by Firebird Software and developed by Andrew Rogers, Spiky Harold is a distinctive single-screen platform adventure for the Commodore 64. You take control of Harold the hedgehog, who must gather enough food to survive hibernation while navigating an underground maze of interconnected screens.

The game spans 57 linked areas beneath a hedgerow, each filled with hazards, collectables, and routes that demand careful planning. Food keeps Harold going, coins earn extra lives, and enemies such as wasps, rodents, and drifting sulfur clouds constantly threaten progress.

A unique twist comes from the wine glasses scattered throughout the maze. If Harold drinks one, he becomes drunk, making movement unpredictable and turning simple platforming into a risky balancing act. This mechanic adds humour while increasing the challenge at exactly the wrong moment.

All of this unfolds against a 24-hour in-game clock, pushing you to memorise routes and move efficiently rather than wandering aimlessly. Success depends on strategy, patience, and learning how the maze fits together.

Today, Spiky Harold is remembered as a creative and slightly eccentric C64 platformer, fondly recalled for its quirky ideas and the demanding challenge it presents to determined players.

Released in 1984, Breakdance is a rhythm-based game developed by Beck-Tech and published by Epyx for the Commodore 64, drawing inspiration from the early 1980s breakdancing explosion and films such as Flashdance and Beat Street. Rather than traditional arcade action, the game focuses on timing, memory, and performance, placing dance culture front and centre.

The gameplay is split across several distinct modes. Hot Feet is a memory-based dance contest where players must repeat increasingly complex move sequences, while Battle the Rocket Crew pits players against rival dancers in competitive copycat showdowns. Perfection’s Dance Puzzle adds a timed challenge element, requiring players to assemble and perform routines in the correct order.

A standout feature is Choreograph Mode, which allows players to create custom dance routines using a set of 14 moves, then perform and replay them. This creative option helped set Breakdance apart from other C64 titles of the era, offering experimentation rather than pure score chasing.

Although reception at the time was mixed, with criticism aimed at repetitive music and limited depth, Breakdance remains a memorable snapshot of 1980s pop culture. Today it’s remembered as an inventive and unusual entry in the Commodore 64 library, capturing a moment when breakdancing briefly ruled the world.

Released in 1984 by T. Owen and published by Bubble Bus Software for the Commodore 64, Flying Feathers is a fast-paced arcade-style shooter that challenges players to protect helpless fish from relentless swooping eagles. Taking control of a warden in a small boat, players use a crosshair to shoot down incoming birds before they can steal their prey.

Gameplay takes place on a single screen, where quick reactions and accurate shooting are essential. Players begin with five fish to defend, and even if an eagle manages to grab one, well-timed shots can force it to drop the fish back into the water. After a set time, a passing duck and her family provide an extra fish, giving players a valuable second chance to extend their run.

At the start of each session, players can choose from eight different skill levels, allowing the game to scale from accessible arcade fun to a demanding test of reflexes. This adjustable difficulty helps keep the experience engaging and encourages players to push for higher scores.

While limited to a single-screen format, Flying Feathers delivers tightly focused gameplay built around timing, precision, and concentration. Its simple mechanics make it easy to pick up, while its increasing pace ensures that survival becomes steadily more challenging.

Though some critics noted the repetitive nature of its design, the game remains fondly remembered for its addictive “one more go” appeal and straightforward arcade action. Today, it stands as a nostalgic favourite among Commodore 64 fans who appreciate classic score-chasing shooters.
