Released in 1985 by Mastertronic and developed by Clive Brooker, One Man and His Droid is a clever puzzle-action game that puts a futuristic spin on herding. Set on the alien world of Andromadous, you control a droid tasked with rounding up strange sheep-like creatures known as Ramboids and guiding them safely into teleporters.

Each of the game’s 20 levels is split into two distinct phases. First, you navigate maze-like caverns filled with roaming Ramboids and environmental hazards. Then the real challenge begins, herding them into teleporters in the correct order against a strict time limit. The ability to dig and tunnel through the terrain adds a strategic layer, letting you reshape levels to manage the Ramboids’ unpredictable movement.

The Commodore 64 version is especially memorable thanks to its colourful presentation and smooth animation, but it’s Rob Hubbard’s outstanding SID soundtrack that truly elevates the experience. His music gives the game a sense of pace and atmosphere that perfectly complements the thoughtful, sometimes frantic gameplay.

Today, One Man and His Droid is fondly remembered as one of Mastertronic’s more inventive titles, blending logic, timing, and action into a uniquely British take on puzzle design that still holds up for retro fans.

Sound effects and music help reinforce the lively, high-energy atmosphere.

Released in 1986 by Software Communications and published by Martech Games for the Commodore 64, Samantha Fox Strip Poker is an early adult-themed poker simulation featuring British model Samantha Fox.

Players compete in 5-card or 7-card stud matches, with opponents adapting their play style as each game progresses and victories unlocking progressively revealing images.

Despite its provocative premise, the game focuses heavily on genuine card strategy, requiring careful betting, bluffing, and risk management to succeed.

The minimalist presentation keeps attention firmly on the gameplay loop, blending gambling mechanics with reward-based progression.

A standout feature is the soundtrack by Rob Hubbard, credited as John York, including SID chip versions of “The Entertainer” and “The Stripper,” which became legendary among C64 music fans.

These distinctive tunes helped elevate the experience and remain one of the game’s most memorable elements.

With surprisingly solid AI and polished mechanics for its era, the game stood out among early adult-oriented titles.

Today, it is remembered as a cult classic that combined British cheek, technical skill, and iconic SID music into a uniquely 1980s package.

ZNDkyuUkL74.title: Darkseed – The Amiga Horror Adventure Built Around H.R. Giger’s Art
ZNDkyuUkL74.description:

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Released in 1992 by Cyberdreams for the Commodore Amiga, Darkseed is a psychological point-and-click adventure that blends science fiction horror with deeply unsettling themes. You play as Mike Dawson, a successful advertising executive who moves into a quiet mansion, only to discover he has been implanted with an alien embryo while unconscious.

Gameplay revolves around exploration, puzzle-solving, and navigating between the real world and a nightmarish parallel dimension known as the Dark World. Every action is governed by a strict in-game time limit, forcing careful planning as the alien embryo slowly matures. Missed clues or wasted time can permanently lock you out of progress, making tension a constant companion.

One of Darkseed’s defining features is its striking visual presentation. The game uses high-resolution 640×350 graphics on the Amiga to showcase the biomechanical artwork of H.R. Giger, whose designs lend the environments a disturbing, organic quality rarely seen in games of the era. Each location feels oppressive, alien, and deliberately uncomfortable.

Darkseed is remembered for its atmospheric storytelling, ambitious art direction, and unforgiving design. While its difficulty divided players, it remains a standout example of psychological horror on the Amiga and a bold experiment in blending fine art with interactive storytelling. Today, it’s regarded as a cult classic that still leaves a lasting impression.

Released in 1990 by Vectordean and published by Millennium Interactive for the Commodore Amiga, James Pond: Underwater Agent introduces a humorous aquatic spy adventure inspired by the world of James Bond.

Players take control of James Pond, a suave mudskipper secret agent, as he embarks on a series of eco-themed missions to protect the underwater world from pollution and danger.

The game features twelve varied levels where objectives include rescuing trapped sea creatures, sealing toxic leaks, and escorting fish to safety, all while racing against the clock.

Gameplay centres on trapping enemies inside bubbles and then popping them to turn foes into useful collectibles. Exploration is encouraged through branching tunnels, hidden rooms, and interconnected pipe systems.

Visually, the Amiga version stands out for its bright cartoon-style graphics, detailed sprites, and parallax-scrolling backgrounds. Humorous level titles such as “Licence to Bubble” and “A View to a Spill” reinforce the game’s playful tone.

The experience is enhanced by Richard Joseph’s energetic soundtrack and atmospheric sound effects, which help create a distinctive underwater espionage atmosphere.

Praised for its polished presentation, responsive controls, and mission-based variety, the Amiga version is widely regarded as the definitive edition of the game.

Today, James Pond: Underwater Agent is remembered as the start of a beloved franchise and one of the standout platformers of the early 1990s Amiga era.

Released in November 1994 by Sensible Software and published by Virgin Interactive for the Commodore Amiga, Cannon Fodder 2 builds on the explosive foundations of the original with a bold time-travel twist. This sequel sends your tiny four-soldier squad across wildly different eras, from deserts and medieval battlefields to alien worlds, each with its own tactical challenges.

Gameplay retains the tight overhead run-and-gun mechanics that made the series famous. Players command troops armed with machine guns, grenades, rockets, and vehicles such as jeeps, tanks, and helicopters. Success depends on positioning, timing, and knowing when to sacrifice firepower for survival as enemy numbers and hazards escalate.

Level design was handled by journalist-turned-designer Stuart Campbell, introducing more complex, puzzle-like layouts packed with hidden routes and pop-culture references. While some critics noted a sharp increase in difficulty and lighter narrative framing, the moment-to-moment action remains fast, precise, and punishing.

Though opinions were divided on how much it innovated beyond the original, Cannon Fodder 2 is fondly remembered by Amiga fans for its responsive controls, distinctive visual style, and relentless challenge. It stands as a cult favourite that preserves the series’ anti-war tone while pushing players to their tactical limits.

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:

Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64, Blade Runner was developed by Ian Foster and Andy Stodart and published by CRL Group. This early cyberpunk shooter casts you as a bounty hunter tracking down dangerous “Replidroids” across a dystopian future city inspired by Ridley Scott’s iconic film.

The game opens with an ambitious two-minute rendition of Vangelis’s Blade Runner soundtrack, immediately setting a brooding sci-fi mood that was striking on the C64. From there, gameplay alternates between top-down city navigation in a hover-skimmer and side-scrolling street chases where targets must be eliminated while avoiding traffic and pedestrians.

As the game progresses, the pace increases and the Replidroids become faster and more elusive, demanding sharper reactions and better route planning. The mix of overworld scanning and street-level action aims to recreate the feel of a futuristic manhunt rather than straightforward arcade shooting.

While the atmosphere and music were widely praised, the game struggled with sluggish controls, repetitive encounters, and limited presentation. Contemporary reviews were mixed, and its gameplay never quite matched the ambition of its concept.

Today, Blade Runner is remembered as a curious and bold Commodore 64 release. Though flawed, its attempt to capture the noir sci-fi tone of the film has earned it a cult following and a unique place in C64 history.

ZtSDw6HOKPE.title: SimCity – How Did Will Wright Squeeze an Entire City Builder into the C64?
ZtSDw6HOKPE.description:
🕹️ SimCity (1989) – Commodore 64 Simulation | Retro Classic

🌐 Full game info, manual & download:
👉 https://www.cheekycommodoregamer.co.uk/games/simcity/

SimCity (1989), developed by Maxis and designed by Will Wright, is the groundbreaking city-building simulation that helped define the genre on home computers.

The Commodore 64 version condenses the full SimCity experience into just 64 KB of memory — a remarkable technical achievement for the time.

You build and manage your city zone by zone, laying residential, commercial, and industrial areas, constructing roads and waterways, setting taxes, balancing budgets, and responding to disasters such as earthquakes.

To fit within tight memory limits, features like police stations, fire departments, stadiums, railways, and advanced statistics were removed. However, core systems such as pollution tracking, growth charts, water systems, and tax controls remained intact — with some elements appearing on C64 before the PC version.

Despite its minimalist, mostly monochrome visuals, performance is smooth and responsive, turning technical limitations into part of the game’s charm.

SimCity on the Commodore 64 stands as a testament to smart design and technical ingenuity, and remains a fascinating chapter in the history of simulation gaming.

Released in 1987 by Mastertronic and developed by Richard Aplin, Invade-a-Load is one of the most inventive ideas to appear on the Commodore 64. Rather than staring at a static loading screen, you’re dropped straight into a Space Invaders-style shooter that runs while the main game loads from cassette in the background.

You control a small ship at the bottom of the screen, blasting descending alien waves as they speed up and become more aggressive. It’s simple, immediate, and surprisingly addictive, turning unavoidable loading time into a playable challenge instead of dead air.

What makes Invade-a-Load truly special is how seamlessly it integrates with the fast loader itself, running without slowing the loading process. Add Rob Hubbard’s unmistakable SID music into the mix and you’ve got a loading screen that became more memorable than some full games.

Invade-a-Load stands as a brilliant example of 8-bit ingenuity, proving that even technical limitations could be transformed into something clever, playful, and unforgettable.

Released in 1987 by MicroProse for the Commodore 64, Project Stealth Fighter is an ambitious combat flight simulator developed by Jim Synoski and Arnold Hendrick. Set against the backdrop of Cold War tensions, the game places players in the cockpit of a fictional stealth aircraft tasked with high-risk missions across global hotspots including Libya, the Persian Gulf, Scandinavia, and Central Europe.

Before take-off, players engage in detailed mission planning, selecting weapons, fuel loads, flight routes, and tactics. Conflict levels ranging from Cold War to Conventional War alter enemy behaviour and engagement rules, giving each mission a different strategic flavour and level of risk.

Once airborne, the simulation focuses on immersion and tactical awareness. The cockpit view features a comprehensive HUD, external 3D perspectives, reconnaissance systems, and electronic countermeasures. A key gameplay mechanic is managing radar exposure, as enemy detection strength is constantly measured against the aircraft’s stealth profile.

Flying low, adjusting heading, and controlling altitude all play vital roles in avoiding radar locks and surface-to-air threats. Combined with realistic flight handling and dynamic atmospheric conditions, the game delivers a sense of tension and authenticity rarely seen on the C64 at the time.

Today, Project Stealth Fighter is recognised as a landmark simulation title on the Commodore 64. Its depth and realism influenced later stealth flight sims, including MicroProse’s own F-19 Stealth Fighter, and it remains a respected classic among fans of serious flight simulation.

Released in 1983, Blagger is a classic single-screen platform game for the Commodore 64 developed by Antony Crowther and published by Alligata Software. Players step into the role of Roger the Dodger, tasked with collecting keys scattered around each screen in order to unlock the safe before time runs out.

The game spans 30 increasingly challenging levels, each packed with hazards such as collapsing platforms, conveyor belts, and an assortment of bizarre enemies including giant mouths and alien creatures. Movement is tightly controlled, with fixed jump arcs that demand precise timing and careful positioning.

Rather than fast reflexes alone, Blagger rewards planning and pattern recognition. Knowing when and where to jump is critical, as a single mistake can quickly end a run. This balance of risk, timing, and spatial awareness gives the game its enduring appeal.

Simple in concept but tough to master, Blagger stands as a strong example of early 1980s platform design and remains a fondly remembered title among Commodore 64 fans, spawning sequels and cementing its place in retro gaming history.
